fact_uses.text: [F1] $|K_j(x)|\le c_n|x|^{-n}$ for $x\ne0$; $|K_j(x-h)-K_j(x)|\le C_n|h|\,|x|^{-(n+1)}$ with $C_n=c_n2^{n+1}(3n+4)$ whenever $|h|\le|x|/2$; and $\int_{S^{n-1}}K_j(r\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega)=0$ for every $r>0$ ([[lem-riesz-transform-kernels-have-explicit-size-difference-and-spherical-cancellation-bounds]]).

proof_steps.claim: The published estimates give the size bound $|K_j(x)|\le c_n|x|^{-n}$, the first-difference bound $|K_j(x-h)-K_j(x)|\le C_n|h||x|^{-(n+1)}$ for $|h|\le|x|/2$, and the vanishing of every spherical mean. The explicit kernel is smooth on the punctured space, hence Borel measurable and locally integrable there.

By [F6], the size bound gives $\int_{R\le|x|\le2R}|K_j(x)|\,dx\le c_n|S^{n-1}|\int_R^{2R}dr/r=c_n|S^{n-1}|\log2$. For every $h\ne0$, directly integrating the difference bound gives $\int_{|x|\ge2|h|}|K_j(x-h)-K_j(x)|\,dx\le C_n|h||S^{n-1}|\int_{2|h|}^\infty r^{-2}dr=|S^{n-1}|C_n/2$. Thus $K_j$ is a base Calderón–Zygmund kernel with $A_1=c_n|S^{n-1}|\log2$ and $A_2=|S^{n-1}|C_n/2$; its first-difference estimate now establishes standard $1$-Hölder status with $A_2'=C_n$.

proof_steps.claim: Its multiplicities give degree $N=2+1=3$ and distributional source $4\pi(2\delta_{z_0}+\delta_{z_1})=8\pi\delta_{z_0}+4\pi\delta_{z_1}$. Apply [F2] to the explicit effective divisor $|n|[0]$ of degree $|n|$ (the empty divisor if $n=0$) and conjugate when $n<0$. Its signed flux is $2\pi n$, and [F3] gives $T_n=2\pi\xi|n|$.

Here $P=(z-z_0)^2(z-z_1)$ and $s=2\log|P|$. The reconstruction in [F2] extends smoothly over both centers, solves the positive critical equations, and has flux $2\pi N=6\pi$. Since it is a fixed-divisor reconstructed solution, [F3] gives its attained absolute transverse energy $2\pi\xi N=6\pi\xi$. The argument determines the profile by the unique scalar boundary-value problem and supplies no elementary closed form.

proof_steps.claim: For each chosen effective divisor of degree $|n|$, apply [F3] with $e=g$ and $\xi=2v^2$, using its conjugate for negative n. [F4] fixes its finite energy and flux normalization. The polynomial phase correction relative to $n\theta$ is degree zero and tends to zero; the cutoff cleanup used in [F5] removes only this correction globally, preserving the divisor. The resulting embedded fields have a=p=0 and satisfy the appropriate critical equations, so all residuals in step 2.1 vanish and the full-model energy is exactly $T_n$. The same identity bounds every competing full-model profile below by $T_n$, proving absolute minimality. Compactly supported smooth variations preserve the flux/vacuum class, so differentiability of their energy at the minimum gives vanishing first variation. This proves actual existence and stationarity for every divisor, without a radial or unit-winding restriction.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] [[pthm-qftx-n2-linear-monopole-bps-vortex-bound]]: in the frozen-metric linear truncation, actual mathematical arbitrary-divisor vortices embed as stationary absolute full-model minima with $T_n=4\pi v^2|n|$; actual canonical full-model collars give $T_nL+O(1)$ for fixed-flux cylinder infima. Its nonlinear stationarity obstruction and screened dual-electric response keep this exact critical result separate from generic nonlinear confinement.

proof_steps.claim:
Under the additional vortex/minimization hypothesis in the Statement,
[F4] gives nonzero quantized original electric flux and a tension
$\sigma>0$. The interior of a translation-invariant tube of length $L$
contains the same transverse profile at each longitudinal coordinate, so
its bulk energy is $\sigma L$. The uniformly bounded endcap contribution
therefore gives $V(L)=\sigma L+O(1)$, which is linear confinement in this
effective model. This last conclusion is conditional: no preceding step establishes existence or minimization of the required profile. Original electric probes correspond to dual magnetic flux; the condensed original magnetic charges are dual electric charges and are screened in the linear response about the dual Higgs vacuum described by [F5]. This conclusion concerns classical effective energy, not a quantum Wilson-loop area law.

In the explicitly linear truncation, assume [A3] and apply [F5] with $\xi=2v^2$ to each chosen effective divisor of degree $|n|$. It supplies an actual smooth stationary full-model minimum of tension $T_n=2\pi\xi|n|=4\pi v^2|n|$, and actual finite collars from every fixed canonical full-model end trace in the stated valid neutral disk. Thus $T_nL\le I_L\le T_n(L-2\ell)+C_0+C_1$, proving $I_L=T_nL+O(1)$; matching minimizing traces attain $T_nL$ exactly. No solution or endcap existence is assumed for this critical boundary problem. The nonlinear obstruction in [F5] prevents extending its exact BPS assertion to generic u.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-qftx-taubes-arbitrary-divisor-plane-vortex]]: for every effective finite divisor of degree $|n|$ there is a smooth finite-energy planar critical pair with flux $2\pi n$ (using conjugation for $n<0$); for the empty divisor it is the vacuum. The local unwound exterior gauge has $q=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}$ and $A=-\tfrac12*dh$; that degree-changing exterior gauge is not asserted to extend globally. Separately, removing only the smooth degree-zero polynomial phase correction relative to $n\theta$ by a global cutoff gauge yields the canonical winding representative $q=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}e^{in\theta}$, $A=n\,d\theta-\tfrac12*dh$.

proof_steps.claim: For an end trace with exterior phase $n\theta+\phi$, choose a smooth radial cutoff $\eta$ which is zero on a disk containing the noncanonical region and one outside a larger disk. The real function $\chi=-\eta\phi$ extends smoothly by zero to the whole plane; the allowed gauge transformation $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ therefore makes the exterior phase exactly $n\theta$. This constructs the asserted degree-zero exterior phase cleanup without attempting to extend a degree-$n$ angular map across the disk. For the planar minimizer in [F2], write $P=|P|e^{i\vartheta}$ on the exterior; $\vartheta-n\theta$ is single-valued, smooth and tends to zero because $P(z)=z^n(1+O(|z|^{-1}))$ for $n\ge0$ (use the conjugate construction for $n<0$). Applying the same cutoff extension to $-(\vartheta-n\theta)$ changes its exterior fields to $q^*=\rho_*e^{in\theta}$ and $A^*=n\,d\theta-\tfrac12*dh$; hence $A^*-n\,d\theta$ decays exponentially.

In canonical exterior gauge write $q=\rho e^{in\theta}$ and $\alpha=A-n\,d\theta$. Directly, $D_Aq=e^{in\theta}(d\rho-i\rho\alpha)$, so the real and imaginary terms are orthogonal and $|D_Aq|^2=|d\rho|^2+\rho^2|\alpha|^2$. Uniform convergence gives $\rho\ge\sqrt\xi/2$ outside a disk; thus finite kinetic energy implies $\alpha\in L^2$ there. Also $|\rho-\sqrt\xi|\le |\rho^2-\xi|/\sqrt\xi$, so finite potential energy gives $\rho-\sqrt\xi\in L^2$ there. On compact disks all fields are smooth and bounded. Consequently, for any two cleaned end traces and the cleaned minimizer, differences of connections and Higgs fields are globally in $L^2$; each Higgs field is bounded.

Apply step 3.1 first to $p_0$ and $p_*$, defining its finite energy to be $C_0$, and then to $p_*$ and $p_1$, defining its finite energy to be $C_1$. For $L\ge2\ell$, place the first collar on $[0,\ell]$, the constant planar minimizer on $[\ell,L-\ell]$, and the second collar on $[L-\ell,L]$. The profiles match smoothly because the collar cutoff is constant near its ends. The middle has no longitudinal energy and contributes exactly $T_n(L-2\ell)$ by [F2]–[F3]. At $L=2\ell$ this middle interval has zero length; the two collars meet at the constant value $p_*$, so the same upper bound holds. This admissible concatenation proves $\inf\mathcal E_L\le C_0+T_n(L-2\ell)+C_1$.

Combining steps 1.1 and 4.1 gives $0\le\inf\mathcal E_L-T_nL\le C_0+C_1-2\ell T_n$ for every $L\ge2\ell$; the right side is a finite constant independent of $L$, proving the bounded-remainder conclusion. If $p_0=p_1=p_*$, the constant extension $(A_1,A_2,q)=(A^*,q^*)$, $A_3=0$, has energy $T_nL$ and satisfies the angular and no-leakage conditions. The lower bound from step 1.1 then proves it is an exact translation-invariant minimum.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-qftx-taubes-arbitrary-divisor-plane-vortex]]: for each effective finite divisor of degree $|n|$, the reconstructed smooth critical fields satisfy the corresponding first-order equations, have finite energy, and have flux $2\pi n$ with sign set by the orientation.

proof_steps.claim: For each fixed divisor, [F2] supplies a smooth pair satisfying the relevant first-order equations. Its square terms in step 1.1 vanish identically; the sequence estimates of steps 1.2–2.1 apply because [F2] gives finite energy and the same boundary sector. Hence its energy is exactly $2\pi\xi|n|$. The lower bound of step 3.1 applies to every admissible same-winding configuration, so this pair is an absolute transverse energy minimum, without radial or unit-winding assumptions.

Let $(a,\eta)$ be a smooth compactly supported variation of a minimizing pair, and set $A_t=A+ta$, $q_t=q+t\eta$; for any field expression $F$, define $\delta F:=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}F(A_t,q_t)$. For sufficiently small $t$, the fields remain in the same boundary sector; outside the compact support they equal the original fields. Thus the boundary-current limit in the disk identity is unchanged and the flux is unchanged by Stokes applied to $d a$. The energy along this variation is the constant $2\pi\xi|n|$ plus the squared $L^2$ norms of the two first-order residuals in step 1.1. Both residuals vanish at $t=0$; differentiating the squared norms gives $E'(0)=0$ and
$$E''(0)=2\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(|\delta(D_{A,1}\pm iD_{A,2})q|^2+\frac{|\delta(B\mp e^2(\xi-|q|^2))|^2}{2e^2}\right)dx_1dx_2\ge0,$$
with the upper signs for $n\ge0$ and lower signs for $n\le0$ (either choice when $n=0$). Therefore the first variation vanishes and no smooth compactly supported same-sector perturbation lowers the energy. Distinct divisors give distinct possible minimizing fields, so no cross-divisor uniqueness follows.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] [[thm-interior-w-two-p-estimate-for-uniformly-elliptic-equations]]: for $p>2$ on a two-dimensional ball, the interior $W^{2,p}$ norm is bounded by the local $L^p$ norms of the solution and its Laplacian.

proof_steps.claim: To obtain derivative decay, fix $\alpha<\alpha'<\sqrt\kappa$ and use step 3.3 at rate $\alpha'$. On each unit ball centered at large $z$, both $w$ and $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ are $O(e^{-\alpha'|z|})$. By [F3] and [F5], $w$ has a $C^{1,\beta}$ norm of that order on the concentric half-ball for some $\beta>0$. Thus the right-hand side has a $C^{0,\beta}$ norm of the same order, and [F4] gives $C^{2,\beta}$ decay on a smaller ball. Inductively, for each multi-index $\gamma$, differentiating $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ gives $\Delta D^\gamma w=\kappa e^{-w}D^\gamma w+G_\gamma$, where $G_\gamma$ is a finite sum of products of lower derivatives of $w$ and is exponentially small by the induction hypothesis. Applying [F3] and [F4] on nested unit balls gives the same $e^{-\alpha'|z|}$ bound for two more derivatives. Since $e^{-\alpha'|z|}\le e^{-\alpha|z|}$ outside a fixed disk, every finite derivative has the stated rate.

proof_steps.claim: There is exactly one partition of $k=1$ for $N=1$, namely $Y_1=\{(0,0)\}$, so [F2] gives the unique fixed point. Here $\mathbf V_{\vec Y}=e_1$ and $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}$, whence $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V=1$, $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee=1$, and $t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V=t_1t_2$. proof_steps.claim: A two-tuple of partitions with total size one places its single box in exactly one of the two colors, so the only possibilities are $(\{(0,0)\},\varnothing)$ and $(\varnothing,\{(0,0)\})$. Their quotient representatives have $V$-characters $e_1$ and $e_2$, respectively.

Substitution in [F2] gives $$t_1+t_2+\frac{e_2}{e_1}+t_1t_2\frac{e_1}{e_2}.$$ The corresponding additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,a_2-a_1,\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2+a_1-a_2$, so their product is $E_1$. Interchanging the two colors gives the second displayed character and $E_2$.

Each fixed-point contribution is the reciprocal of its Euler product, so the degree-one coefficient is $E_1^{-1}+E_2^{-1}$. The TikZ drawing only records the two one-box colorings and is not used in this calculation.

Both outside groups vanish by step 3.1, so $i_*$ is an isomorphism. If $F=\varnothing$, the same argument gives zero localized Borel–Moore homology for $X$; if $F=X$, $i_*$ is the identity. The proof used only the finite invariant affine cover and not Sumihiro's theorem or compactness.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] The preceding lemma supplies the exact P² diagonal monad and its framed vanishings under the stated cohomology/base-change assumptions; its algebraic/analytic family comparison uses the exact projective GAGA interface and the stated base-change hypotheses. [[lem-qftx-p2-beilinson-diagonal-and-framed-vanishing]]

proof_steps.claim: Conversely, let $\mathcal E$ be a framed torsion-free sheaf with the stated Hilbert polynomial. The preceding Beilinson lemma constructs its monad, with terms $V_1\mathcal O(-1)$, $M\mathcal O$, and $V_2\mathcal O(1)$ of ranks $k,2k+N,k$. Its restriction to $L_\infty$ remains exact at the ends because $\mathcal E$ is locally free there. Put $K=\ker\beta|_{L_\infty}$. The sequence $0\to V_1\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to W\mathcal O\to0$ splits since $\operatorname{Ext}^1(W\mathcal O,V_1\mathcal O(-1))=V_1\otimes W^*\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$.

The remaining line extension $0\to V_1\mathcal O(-1)\oplus W\mathcal O\to M\mathcal O\to V_2\mathcal O(1)\to0$ has class in $\operatorname{Hom}(V_2,V_1)\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$, since $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$. Twist by $\mathcal O(-1)$ and take cohomology. The connecting map $V_2\to V_1\otimes H^1(\mathcal O(-2))$ is an isomorphism: the adjacent groups $H^0(\mathcal O(-1))$ and $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))$ vanish, while $H^1(\mathcal O(-2))\cong\mathbb C$. Thus $V_2$ is identified with $V_1$ by this canonical extension class. Choosing a basis of $V_1$ and using the fixed framed basis of $W$ identifies $M=V\oplus V\oplus W$ and the line maps with the two Euler blocks in the Statement. Any other such choice differs by one simultaneous element of $GL(V)$.

The remaining coefficients of the two linear maps are their $z_0$ coefficients, so write $\alpha=(z_0B_1-z_1,z_0B_2-z_2,z_0J)^T$ and $\beta=(-z_0C_1+z_2,z_0C_2-z_1,z_0I)$. The coefficients of $z_0z_1$ and $z_0z_2$ in $\beta\alpha=0$ force $C_1=B_2$ and $C_2=B_1$; the $z_0^2$ coefficient is then $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$. This recovers the stated ADHM form. The surjectivity of $\beta$ implies stability: if $U=\operatorname{span}\{B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(W)\}$ were proper, it is invariant and the induced $B_1,B_2$ on $V/U$ commute because $[B_1,B_2]=-IJ$ has image in $U$. Their dual actions on the nonzero annihilator $U^\perp\subset V^*$ commute, so [F6] gives a common eigen-covector $\lambda\ne0$ with $\lambda I=0$. At the corresponding affine point, $\lambda\beta=0$, contradicting surjectivity.

The Beilinson construction is natural under framed sheaf isomorphisms, so an isomorphism of framed sheaves induces maps on the cohomology vector spaces used in steps 1.2–6.2 and hence a single change of basis $g\in GL(V)$; the normalized Euler blocks force the recovered tuples to differ by $g\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)$. Conversely such a $g$ is an isomorphism of monads acting trivially on $W$, and therefore induces a framed sheaf isomorphism. This proves the pointwise inverse equivalence modulo $GL(V)$. For a finite-type data family, step 2.1 makes $\beta$ surjective on the total space, so $K=\ker\beta$ is locally free. The sequence $0\to V\mathcal O(-1)\to K\to\mathcal E\to0$ is exact and its terms before $\mathcal E$ are flat over the base. After tensoring with any residue field of the base, the first map remains sheaf-injective by step 1.1; hence $\operatorname{Tor}_1(k(s),\mathcal E)=0$. Since $\mathcal E$ is finite over each local ring of $\mathbb P^2\times S$ and its residue fiber is a vector space over the residue field, [F8] gives flatness over $S$. Under the stated relative cohomology and base-change hypotheses, the same constructions use vector bundles and are inverse for families.

Apply the family equivalence to $S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$. A first-order deformation of the ADHM data is $(\dot B_1,\dot B_2,\dot I,\dot J)$ satisfying $d\mu_{\mathbb C}=0$; infinitesimal changes of basis are $d_0(\xi)=([\xi,B_1],[\xi,B_2],\xi I,-J\xi)$. Differentiating the monad gives the chain perturbation $(\dot\alpha,\dot\beta)$ with $\beta\dot\alpha+\dot\beta\alpha=0$, and a change by $d_0(\xi)$ is the corresponding chain homotopy. Since the family construction and its inverse commute with this dual-number base change, they induce inverse linear maps on first-order framed deformations and on the quotient tangent spaces $\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_0$.

If $k=0$, $V=0$, all four maps and both equations are the unique zero-dimensional maps, stability and costability are vacuous, and the monad is $0\to W\mathcal O\to0$. Its middle cohomology is the framed bundle $W\mathcal O$ with Hilbert polynomial $N\binom{m+2}{2}$. Conversely, [F3] constructs this same zero-term monad from every framed sheaf with that polynomial, so the framing identifies each such sheaf with $W\mathcal O$. Thus both moduli spaces are points, and all empty-matrix and Euler-block conventions are satisfied.

final_edge_fact_uses.text:
[F7] The finite algebraic resolution gives
$\operatorname{ch}(F)=N-kH^2$, $c_1(F)=0$, $c_2(F)=kH^2$,
$\chi(F)=N-2k$; its line cycle class is the topological hyperplane class, and
the positive incidence fiber calculation gives $\pi^*u=H^2$.
[[lem-qftx-positive-real-monad-charge-normalization]]

proof_steps.claim: The finite monad resolution and its locally free cohomology give the algebraic Chern character and Chern classes in [F7]. Its same finite line resolution yields the topological classes after the hyperplane cycle class is identified with the Euler class of the complex normal line. The positive incidence-fiber Thom calculation in [F7] gives $\pi^*u=H_{\rm top}^2$. If the topological bundle is $\pi^*E$, naturality gives $\pi^*c_2(E)=kH_{\rm top}^2=k\pi^*u$; since $\pi^*u$ is a generator, $c_2(E)=ku$. This is conditional on the pullback hypothesis and asserts no Ward correspondence.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] Proper pushforward is functorial, closed inclusions are proper, and cap product with an equivariant cohomology class sends $[X]_T$ to Borel–Moore degree $2d-q$. [[def-qftx-localized-equivariant-borel-moore-data]]

proof_steps.claim: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a proper $T$-equivariant map between smooth separated finite-type varieties with finite invariant affine covers and proper fixed loci $F_X,F_Y$. Its restriction $f^T:F_X\to F_Y$ is proper, and the square formed by $i_X,i_Y,f^T,f$ commutes because $f$ sends fixed points to fixed points. Functoriality of proper Borel–Moore pushforward gives $f_*i_{X*}=i_{Y*}f^T_*$. After localization both $i_{X*}$ and $i_{Y*}$ are isomorphisms by [F2], so applying their inverses and then the proper traces proves $p_{Y*}^{\mathrm{loc}}f_*=p_{X*}^{\mathrm{loc}}$. If $X\to\mathrm{pt}$ itself is proper, then $p_{F*}=p_{X*}i_*$; composing with $i_*^{-1}$ proves $p_*^{\mathrm{loc}}=p_{X*}$.

Let $ eta=(i_*)^{-1}(\alpha\cap[X]_T)$. On each component, the complex orientation and refined Gysin map give $i_a^!(\alpha\cap[X]_T)=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Since $\alpha\cap[X]_T=i_* eta$, the self-intersection formula [F3] gives $e_T(
u_a)\cap eta_a=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Properness of $F_a$ makes $e_T(
u_a)$ invertible after localization by [F3], hence $ eta_a=(i_a^*\alpha/e_T(
u_a))\cap[F_a]_T$. Applying $p_{a*}$ and summing the finitely many components yields the displayed formula. The degree is $2d-q$: division by the degree-$2c_a$ Euler class lowers the localized cohomological degree of the insertion from $q$ to $q-2c_a$, and capping with the degree-$2d_a$ fundamental class gives $2d_a-(q-2c_a)=2d-q$.

reviewed_items.compatibility: Public mathematical Statement/Definition and hypotheses preserved. Six title changes need no mathematical propagation; Gysin added Remarks re-express existing proof, not a new relied-on result. Riesz label-only Statement/F6 change reviewed explicitly below.

fact_uses.text: [F2] $C^1$ change of variables: for a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T:U'\to V'$ of open sets and every nonnegative measurable $f$, $\int_{V'}f(y)\,dy=\int_{U'}f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,dx$ ([[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]).

proof_steps.claim: Since $\Psi$ has bounded first derivatives on $\overline{V_0}$, [F2] gives, for every nonnegative measurable $f$ on $V_0$ and $1\le p<\infty$, $$\int_{U_0}|f(\Phi(x))|^p\,dx=\int_{\Phi(U_0)}|f(y)|^p|\det D\Psi(y)|\,dy\le C\int_{V_0}|f(y)|^p\,dy.$$ For $p=\infty$, [F3] makes composition well defined on a.e. classes and gives $\|f\circ\Phi\|_{L^\infty(U_0)}\le\|f\|_{L^\infty(V_0)}$. Thus pullback by $\Phi$ is bounded on the stated $L^p$ spaces. The analogous estimate for $\Psi$ holds when $\Psi(V_0)\subseteq U_0$.

fact_uses.text: [F2] Assume Countable Choice. If $T:U\to V$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ and $f:V\to[0,\infty]$ is Lebesgue measurable, then $\int_Vf\,d\lambda_m=\int_Uf(T(x))|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_m(x)$. ([[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]])

proof_steps.claim: Diffeomorphism invariance (i). Let $u$ be measurable on $V'$ and apply the bi-Lipschitz upper bound of step 1.1: $|x-y|^{-d-sp}\le L^{d+sp}|\Psi(x)-\Psi(y)|^{-d-sp}$, so $[u\circ\Psi]_{s,p}^p\le L^{d+sp}\int_V\int_V|u(\Psi x)-u(\Psi y)|^p|\Psi(x)-\Psi(y)|^{-d-sp}dx\,dy$. The map $\Theta:=\Psi\times\Psi:V\times V\to V'\times V'$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of open subsets of $\mathbb R^{2d}$ with $|\det D\Theta(x,y)|=|\det D\Psi(x)||\det D\Psi(y)|$ and $\det D\Theta^{-1}(\xi,\eta)=\det D\Psi^{-1}(\xi)\det D\Psi^{-1}(\eta)$; the change-of-variables theorem [F2] applied to the nonnegative measurable integrand $f(\xi,\eta):=|u(\xi)-u(\eta)|^p|\xi-\eta|^{-d-sp}$ yields $\int_{V\times V}f(\Theta(x,y))\,dx\,dy=\int_{V'\times V'}f(\xi,\eta)|\det D\Psi^{-1}(\xi)|\,|\det D\Psi^{-1}(\eta)|\,d\xi\,d\eta\le M^{2d}\int_{V'\times V'}f$, where $M$ also bounds $|\det D\Psi^{-1}|\le M^d$ after enlarging the constant. For the $L^p$ term, [F2] applied in the form $\int_V|u(\Psi x)|^pdx\le M^d\int_{V'}|u|^p$ gives $\|u\circ\Psi\|_{L^p(V)}\le M^{d/p}\|u\|_{L^p(V')}$. Adding the two bounds, $\|u\circ\Psi\|_{W^{s,p}(V)}\le C(\Psi,s,p)\|u\|_{W^{s,p}(V')}$; exchanging $\Psi$ and $\Psi^{-1}$ gives the symmetric inequality.

Chart independence (ii). Let two atlases and partitions be as in [F5]. For each pair $j,k$, the support of $\chi_j\chi'_k$ on the boundary is compact inside the chart overlap. Cover it by finitely many small coordinate balls whose slightly larger closures remain in that overlap. Step 1.1 makes each transition bi-Lipschitz on those larger balls; its Jacobians and inverse Jacobians are bounded there by [F4]. Choose a finite smooth coordinate partition equal to one near this compact support. On each piece, the identity $(\chi_j\chi'_kg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}=((\chi'_kg)\circ(\Psi'_k)^{-1})\circ(\Psi'_k\circ\Psi_j^{-1})\, (\chi_j\circ\Psi_j^{-1})$ and steps 1.2 and 2.1 control the norm restricted to the ball. All multiplier factors are bounded Lipschitz there; multiplying by the coordinate cutoff extends them by zero to bounded Lipschitz functions on $\mathbb R^d$. The localised function is supported a positive distance $\delta$ from the ball's complement, so the extra cross term in its zero-extension seminorm is at most $C\delta^{-sp}\|v\|_p^p$, obtained by integrating $|h|^{-d-sp}$ over $|h|\ge\delta$. Thus its whole-space norm is bounded by the second atlas norm. Sum over the finite pieces and use $\sum_k\chi'_k=1$ to obtain the first atlas norm bounded by the second. Exchange the atlases for the reverse inequality.

fact_uses.text: [F7] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism satisfies the change-of-variables formula for nonnegative Lebesgue measurable functions. ([[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]).

proof_steps.claim: Choose the finite pole value $0$ in [F3]. Since $T_x^{-1}=T_x$, [F21] shows that preimages under $T_x$ of Lebesgue measurable sets are Lebesgue measurable; hence $y\mapsto\Phi(x-y)$ is measurable. The set $x-K$ is Borel by step 1.2, so [F20] and [F16] make $h_x(z):=\mathbf 1_{x-K}(z)|\Phi(z)|$ nonnegative Lebesgue measurable. Applying [F7] to $h_x$ and $T_x$, with $|\det DT_x|=1$, gives $$\int_{x-K}|\Phi(z)|\,dz=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h_x(z)\,dz=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h_x(T_x(y))\,dy=\int_K|\Phi(x-y)|\,dy,$$ because $x-y\in x-K$ exactly when $y\in K$. By [F13], [F11] and step 1.2, $$\int_K|\Phi(x-y)|\,dy\le\int_{B(0,R)}|\Phi(z)|\,dz<\infty,$$ where finiteness follows from [F5]–[F6]. This holds uniformly for $x\in C$.

If $M=0$, step 1.1 gives $\widehat f=0$ and step 4.1 gives zero potential for every representative. The case $n=1$ is excluded by the hypothesis $n\ge2$. Countable Choice is used exactly through the kernel convention, local-integrability, Borel-measurability, measurable-set, and change-of-variables interfaces [F3–F7, F20–F21]; no full Axiom of Choice is used. There are no endpoint claims or biconditional cases.

fact_uses.text: [F7] Local $C^{1,1}$ flattening. Here $C^{1,1}$ means that each local boundary graph is $C^1$ and its first derivatives are Lipschitz on compact patches. The flattening map is a shear with determinant one; its first derivative and inverse are bounded, and its second weak derivatives are essentially bounded: apply the real-valued converse of [[thm-w-one-infinity-functions-have-lipschitz-representatives]] to each Lipschitz graph-gradient component on a smaller convex base box. For smooth $w$, mollify the graph on a slightly larger base box. The graph functions and gradients converge uniformly; their uniformly bounded second derivatives converge locally in each finite $L^p$ to the weak second derivatives. Apply the ordinary chain rule to the smooth shears, then pass to the weak derivative identities using change of variables and these convergences. This gives $D(w\circ\Phi)=(Dw\circ\Phi)D\Phi$ and $D^2(w\circ\Phi)=(D^2w\circ\Phi)[D\Phi,D\Phi]+(Dw\circ\Phi)D^2\Phi$. The change-of-variables formula and the bound $\|gh\|_{L^p}\le\|g\|_{L^\infty}\|h\|_{L^p}$ therefore bound the local $W^{1,p}$ and $W^{2,p}$ norms of the pullback by the corresponding original norms, with constants controlled by the chart bounds. For general $w\in W^{2,p}$, smooth approximation on the open chart patch ([[thm-meyers-serrin-density-on-an-arbitrary-open-set]]) and weak stability of derivatives ([[lem-weak-stability-of-sobolev-derivatives]]) give the same weak chain rule and estimate. The Jacobian and chart derivatives are controlled on the finite atlas of the bounded $C^{1,1}$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]], [[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]). The transformed lower-order coefficients are bounded by the original bounds and the chart's $C^{1,1}$ bounds. ([[def-uniformly-elliptic-nondivergence-operator]])

proof_steps.claim: Uniform charts, transformed-coefficient modulus, and bounded overlap. Start with a finite $C^{1,1}$ boundary atlas and a finite interior atlas. In a boundary chart $x=\Phi(y)$ the transformed principal matrix is $\widetilde A(y)=D\Phi(y)^{-1}A(\Phi(y))D\Phi(y)^{-T}$. The chart maps and their first derivatives are uniformly bounded on the finite atlas, and $D\Phi$ is Lipschitz; therefore, for a modulus $\omega_A$ of $A$ on $\bar\Omega$, $$\omega_{\widetilde A}(s)\le C_0\bigl(\omega_A(C_0s)+s\bigr)$$ on every chart, with one $C_0$ for the finite atlas. Choose a small scale $r$ so the half-space estimate constant times $\omega_{\widetilde A}(C_0r)$ is as small as required below. A grid in each chart and in the interior gives inner patches covering $\Omega$: boundary half-patches cover a collar of width comparable to $r$, and the remaining interior balls have doubled balls contained in $\Omega$. Choose fixed larger patches for cutoffs and the doubled-ball interpolation inequality, still inside the chart or $\Omega$. The expanded patches have overlap at most $N_0$, independent of $r$; smooth cutoffs equal to one on inner patches and supported on the expanded patches have first and second derivatives bounded by $Cr^{-1}$ and $Cr^{-2}$. The grid overlap and finite atlas fix $N_0$ before we choose the local Hessian error.

Boundary patches and a prescribed local error. In a boundary chart flatten the graph, write $\widetilde u=u\circ\Phi$, let $\widetilde L$ be the transformed operator, and take a cutoff $\chi$ equal to one on an inner half-patch and supported on a larger half-patch. Set $v=\chi\widetilde u$. To see $v\in W^{1,p}_0(\mathbb R^n_+)$, choose $u_k\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ converging to $u$ in $W^{1,p}$ by [F1]. Their pullbacks, multiplied by $\chi$, are compactly supported in the open half-space and lie in $W^{1,p}_0(\mathbb R^n_+)$ by mollification. The smooth W^{1,p} chart estimate [F7] makes these pullbacks Cauchy in $W^{1,p}$; the change-of-variables $L^p$ estimate identifies their limit with $v$, so closedness of $W^{1,p}_0$ gives $v\in W^{1,p}_0(\mathbb R^n_+)$. Since $u\in W^{2,p}$, the same chart rule gives $v\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^n_+)$; extend it by zero away from the patch. Freeze the transformed principal matrix at the chart centre to get $\widetilde L_0$. The half-space estimate [F4], whose odd-reflection proof applies the whole-space estimate [F3], and the product identity [F5] bound $\|D^2v\|_{L^p}$ by the transformed $\|Lu\|_{L^p}$, the principal error $\|\chi(\widetilde A_0-\widetilde A):D^2\widetilde u\|_{L^p}$, lower-order products, and cutoff commutators bounded by $C(r^{-1}\|D\widetilde u\|_{L^p}+r^{-2}\|\widetilde u\|_{L^p})$ on the expanded patch. The identity $$\chi D^2\widetilde u=D^2v-D\chi\otimes D\widetilde u-D\widetilde u\otimes D\chi-(D^2\chi)\widetilde u$$ puts the principal error on the left with coefficient at most $C\omega_{\widetilde A}(C_0r)$, which is made small in step 1.1. For the term $\chi D\widetilde u$, write it as $Dv-(D\chi)\widetilde u$ and apply the whole-space interpolation inequality [F6] to the odd extension of $v$; choose its parameter small enough to absorb the resulting $\|D^2v\|_{L^p}$ term. For the cutoff commutator, odd-extend $\widetilde u$ across the flat face on the larger half-ball and apply the doubled-ball form of [F6], giving for every $\varepsilon>0$ $$r^{-1}\|D\widetilde u\|_{L^p(P^+)}\le\varepsilon\|D^2\widetilde u\|_{L^p(P^{++})}+C_\varepsilon r^{-2}\|\widetilde u\|_{L^p(P^{++})}.$$ The chart chain rule [F7] also contributes bounded first-order terms when comparing second derivatives; the same interpolation absorbs them into an arbitrarily small multiple of the outer Hessian norm. Thus, after first fixing the transformed-coefficient oscillation and then choosing the interpolation parameters, for any prescribed $\eta>0$ the boundary patch satisfies $$\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(P)}\le C_1\bigl(\|Lu\|_{L^p(P^{++})}+r^{-2}\|u\|_{L^p(P^{++})}\bigr)+\eta\|D^2u\|_{L^p(P^{++})},$$ where $P$ is the inner patch and $P^+$, $P^{++}$ are fixed expanded patches from step 1.1. All chart Jacobians and lower-order coefficient bounds enter $C_1$, which is independent of $u$.

fact_uses.text: [F2] If $A_0$ is a symmetric positive-definite matrix with spectrum in $[\lambda,\Lambda]$ and $w\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^n)$, put $S=A_0^{1/2}$, $\Phi(y)=x_0+Sy$, and $v=w\circ\Phi$. Testing the weak-derivative identities and changing variables by $\Phi$ gives $D_{y_i}v=\sum_k S_{ki}(D_{x_k}w)\circ\Phi$ and $D_{y_i y_j}^2v=\sum_{k,\ell}S_{ki}S_{\ell j}(D_{x_kx_\ell}^2w)\circ\Phi$ as $L^p$ classes; thus $v\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^n)$. The change-of-variables formula gives $\|g\circ\Phi\|_{L^p(dy)}=|\det S|^{-1/p}\|g\|_{L^p(dx)}$, so the Hessian norms before and after pullback are equivalent with constants depending only on $n,p,\lambda,\Lambda$, since $\|S\|\le\sqrt\Lambda$ and $\|S^{-1}\|\le\lambda^{-1/2}$. Finally $\Delta_yv=(A_0:D_x^2w)\circ\Phi$. Therefore the global Laplacian estimate [F1] gives $\|D^2w\|_{L^p}\le C(n,p,\lambda,\Lambda)\|A_0:D^2w\|_{L^p}$. ([[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-uniformly-elliptic-nondivergence-operator]])

proof_steps.claim: Frozen estimate on nested balls. Fix $x\in B_R(x_0)$ and $0<\rho<R/4$ with $B_{2\rho}(x)\subset B_R(x_0)$. Freeze $A$ at $A_0=A(x)$ and choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty(B_\rho(x))$ with $0\le\eta\le1$ and $\eta=1$ on $B_{\rho/2}(x)$, with $|D\eta|\le C_n\rho^{-1}$ and $|D^2\eta|\le C_n\rho^{-2}$. Set $w=\eta u$, extended by zero. The constant-coefficient estimate [F2] and the product identity [F4] give $\|D^2u\|_{L^p(B_{\rho/2}(x))}\le\|D^2w\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|A_0:D^2w\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\Bigl(\|f\|_{L^p(B_\rho(x))}+\omega_A(\rho)\|D^2u\|_{L^p(B_\rho(x))}+\bigl(M_b+\Lambda\rho^{-1}\bigr)\|Du\|_{L^p(B_\rho(x))}+\bigl(M_c+\Lambda\rho^{-2}\bigr)\|u\|_{L^p(B_\rho(x))}\Bigr),$ where $\omega_A(\rho):=\sup\{|A(y)-A(z)|:y,z\in\bar B_R(x_0),\ |y-z|\le\rho\}$ and the constant $C$ depends only on $n,p,\lambda,\Lambda$. Apply the doubled-ball interpolation inequality [F3] to $u$ on $B_{2\rho}(x)$: $\|Du\|_{L^p(B_\rho(x))}\le\varepsilon\rho\|D^2u\|_{L^p(B_{2\rho}(x))}+C_{n,p,\varepsilon}\rho^{-1}\|u\|_{L^p(B_{2\rho}(x))}.$ Since $\|D^2u\|_{L^p(B_\rho)}\le\|D^2u\|_{L^p(B_{2\rho})}$, choose $\varepsilon>0$ small and then $\rho_* >0$ so that for every $0<\rho\le\rho_*$ the coefficient of $\|D^2u\|_{L^p(B_{2\rho}(x))}$ after substitution is at most any prescribed $\theta_0>0$; this is possible because $\omega_A(\rho)\to0$ and $\rho M_b\le R M_b$. Absorbing constants in the lower-order term yields the local estimate $\|D^2u\|_{L^p(B_{\rho/2}(x))}\le C_0\|f\|_{L^p(B_\rho(x))}+C_0\rho^{-2}\|u\|_{L^p(B_{2\rho}(x))}+\theta_0\|D^2u\|_{L^p(B_{2\rho}(x))},$ where $C_0$ depends on $n,p,\lambda,\Lambda,RM_b,R^2M_c$ and the modulus of continuity of $A$, but not on $x$ or $\rho\le\rho_*$. The cutoff is identically one on the smaller ball, so the left side is the unweighted Hessian norm there; no division by a vanishing cutoff is used.

fact_uses.text: [F4] Under countable choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism satisfies the change-of-variables formula for every nonnegative Lebesgue-measurable integrand; continuous maps have Borel preimages of Borel sets. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]], [[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]].

proof_steps.claim: Let $T(z)=m+Lz$. It is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with Jacobian determinant $\det L>0$. For any Borel set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, define the nonnegative Borel function $g(x)=\mathbf1_E(x)f_Z(L^{-1}(x-m))/\det L$. By [F4] and the countable choice supplied by [A1], $\int_E f_Z(L^{-1}(x-m))(\det L)^{-1}\,dx =\int_{T^{-1}(E)} f_Z(z)\,dz =\mathbb P(TZ\in E).$ Thus the density in step 2.1 is $f_Z(L^{-1}(x-m))(\det L)^{-1}$. The determinant is positive because $L$ is triangular with positive diagonal.

fact_uses.text: [F9] Under Countable Choice, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T:U\to V$ between open subsets of $\mathbb R^n$ satisfies $\int_V f(y)\,dy=\int_U f(T(z))|\det DT(z)|\,dz$ for every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable $f$ ([[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]).

proof_steps.claim: The smooth case: integration. If $n=1$, then $|\Omega|\le b-a$, so integrating step 1.1 gives $\int_\Omega|\varphi|^p\le(b-a)^p\int_a^b|D\varphi(se)|^p\,ds=(b-a)^p\int_\Omega|D\varphi|^p$ by [F9] for the global linear diffeomorphism $s\mapsto se$ of $\mathbb R$ (where $e=1$ or $e=-1$ and the absolute Jacobian is $1$), and the support of $D\varphi$ in $\Omega$. Now suppose $n\ge2$. Choose orthonormal coordinates with last vector $e$ and write $x=x_\perp+x_ne$; the corresponding orthogonal map $T:\mathbb R^{n-1}\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ is a global $C^1$ diffeomorphism with $|\det DT|=1$. By [F9], nonnegative integrands have the same integral after composing with $T$; this applies both to $\mathbf1_\Omega|\varphi|^p$ and to $|D\varphi|^p$, which are Borel measurable since the zero extension is smooth and $\Omega$ is open. For each $x_\perp$, the slice $S_{x_\perp}:=\{x_n:(x_\perp,x_n)\in\Omega\}$ is a measurable subset of $(a,b)$, so $|S_{x_\perp}|\le b-a$. Integrating step 1.1 over $\Omega$ and applying Tonelli [F4] gives $\int_\Omega|\varphi|^p\,dx\le(b-a)^{p-1}\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}\int_{S_{x_\perp}}\int_a^b|D\varphi(x_\perp+se)|^p\,ds\,dx_n\,dx_\perp\le(b-a)^p\int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}\int_a^b|D\varphi(x_\perp+se)|^p\,ds\,dx_\perp$. The last integral equals $\int_{\mathbb R^n}|D\varphi|^p\,dx=\int_\Omega|D\varphi|^p$, since $\varphi$ and its gradient vanish outside $\Omega$ and $\Omega$ lies in the slab. Therefore $\|\varphi\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\le(b-a)^p\|D\varphi\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p$.

proof_steps.claim: There is exactly one partition of $k=1$ for $N=1$, namely $Y_1=\{(0,0)\}$, so [F2] gives the unique fixed point. Here $\mathbf V_{\vec Y}=e_1$ and $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}$, whence $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V=1$, $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee=1$, and $t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V=t_1t_2$. Substitution in the tangent character gives $t_1+t_2$; the two additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2$, so the Euler class is $\epsilon_1\epsilon_2$.

The degree-one coefficient is the sum over the single fixed point, so it equals $(\epsilon_1\epsilon_2)^{-1}$. This is a formal equivariant fixed-point contribution, not an asserted continuum path-integral value.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-adhm-fixed-point-instanton-count]]: fixed points are indexed by two-tuples of partitions of total size one, and the tangent character is $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V(t_1+t_2-1-t_1t_2)+\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee+t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V$.

proof_steps.claim: A two-tuple of partitions with total size one places its single box in exactly one of the two colors, so the only possibilities are $(\{(0,0)\},\varnothing)$ and $(\varnothing,\{(0,0)\})$. Their quotient representatives have $V$-characters $e_1$ and $e_2$, respectively.

For the first point, the ADHM convention [F1] gives $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}+e_2^{-1}$ and $\mathbf W^\vee=e_1+e_2$, while $\mathbf V=e_1$. Substitution in [F2] gives $$t_1+t_2+\frac{e_2}{e_1}+t_1t_2\frac{e_1}{e_2}.$$ The corresponding additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,a_2-a_1,\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2+a_1-a_2$, so their product is $E_1$. Interchanging the two colors gives the second displayed character and $E_2$.

Each fixed-point contribution is the reciprocal of its Euler product, so the degree-one coefficient is $E_1^{-1}+E_2^{-1}$. The TikZ drawing only records the two one-box colorings and is not used in this calculation.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] [[lem-qftx-round-s4-spin-twist-index-one]] proves the actual round positive-spin twist has kernel dimension one, cokernel zero and Chern number $-1$.

These identify the vertical problem exactly with the fixed $SU(2)$-invariant Hermitian $\mathcal O(-2)$ problem on $\mathbb CP^1$, componentwise in $E_x$. The estimates [F4] and the first-order nature of $\bar\partial^*$ give $B:H^m\to H^{m+1}$ bounded for each $m$. For jointly smooth $f(x,t)$, base difference quotients converge in every fibre $H^m$ uniformly on compact base sets, by the Taylor formula and compactness of the fibre. Applying the fixed bounded $B$ shows $\partial_x^\beta(Bf)=B(\partial_x^\beta f)$ at every order in every $H^{m+1}$. Sobolev embedding on the fixed two-dimensional compact fibre, with arbitrarily large $m$, gives joint smoothness in $(x,t)$. For the horizontal coefficient problem, choose also a smooth unit quaternionic frame of $Q_x^\perp$. Together the two quaternionic frames give a smooth $Sp(2)$ transformation from a fixed pair of planes to $(Q_x,Q_x^\perp)$. Its complex-linear action on $\mathbb CP^3$ is holomorphic and preserves the Fubini–Study and tautological metrics. It therefore transports the horizontal quotient, its vertical Bott operator and its induced metric to the fixed $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}$ problem identified below. That inverse is likewise one fixed bounded operator componentwise, so the same derivative argument applies. Thus no moving-cokernel inverse or unproved parametric Green assertion is used.

proof_steps.claim: For the global metric splitting, the mixed component of $\bar\partial(s\sigma)$ is a vertical degree-one form with coefficient $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$. On a fibre it has a unique vertical primitive by [F4]. The fixed-fibre $B=\bar\partial^*G$ construction and smooth-parameter difference-quotient argument in [F2], with the estimates [F5], make that primitive smooth over the base. The same fibrewise uniqueness makes it agree across frame and chart changes. Denote the horizontal correction by $\phi(s)$; then $\psi(s)=s\sigma+\phi(s)$ has zero mixed differential. If $s$ is the image of a closed representative $\alpha$, [F2]'s decomposition and closedness say that its horizontal remainder solves this same mixed equation. The difference is fibrewise holomorphic in $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$, hence zero by [F4]. Thus $\psi(s)=\alpha-\bar\partial_F\gamma$ is closed for a class image. The differential can still have a horizontal degree-two component for arbitrary $s$; the curvature component of the metric splitting is retained.

[[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]], [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]]

proof_steps.claim: Apply [F3] with $r=k-1\ge0$ to $\Delta_{A_0}:H^{k+1}\to H^{k-1}$. Its kernel is finite dimensional, and the Hodge theorem gives the topological direct decomposition $H^{k-1}=\ker\Delta_{A_0}\oplus\Delta_{A_0}(H^{k+1})$. Thus its range is closed with codimension equal to the kernel dimension, so $\Delta_{A_0}$ is Fredholm of index zero. By [F6] and the compactness of $K_A$ from step 1.1, $\Delta_A=\Delta_{A_0}+K_A$ is Fredholm of index zero.

[[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]], [[thm-elliptic-differential-operators-on-compact-vector-bundles-have-parametrices-and-regularity]]

proof_steps.claim:
Fix the smooth reference connection $A_0$ from the configuration data and set $h=A-A_0\in H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$. In a local orthonormal frame, $d_A=d_{A_0}+[h,\cdot]$ on zero-forms and $d_A^*=d_{A_0}^*-\iota_h$ on one-forms, where $\iota_h(a)=g^{ij}[h_i,a_j]$. Therefore $K_A:=\Delta_A-\Delta_{A_0}$ is a finite sum of terms of the forms $(
abla_{A_0}h)\xi$, $h
abla_{A_0}\xi$, and $h^2\xi$. These terms define a bounded map $H^{k+1}	o H^{k-1}$. They are compact: $(
abla_{A_0}h)\xi$ factors through the compact inclusion $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^{k-1}$ followed by multiplication in the algebra $H^{k-1}$; $h
abla_{A_0}\xi$ and $h^2\xi$ first map boundedly into $H^k$ and then use the compact inclusion $H^k\hookrightarrow H^{k-1}$. Here $k-1>d/2$, so the needed multiplication bounds follow from [F8].

The Sobolev interpolation estimate $\|\xi\|_{H^k}\le\varepsilon\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}+C_\varepsilon\|\xi\|_{L^2}$ follows by finite-atlas localization and the estimate in [F5]. Choose $\varepsilon$ so that the resulting $H^{k+1}$ term is absorbed into the left side. This yields $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C_A'(\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}+\|\xi\|_{L^2})$.

If no constant bounded $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}$ by $\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}$, choose $\|\xi_j\|_{H^{k+1}}=1$ with $\Delta_A\xi_j\to0$. By [F4], a subsequence converges in $L^2$; applying the estimate of step 2.2 to differences shows it is Cauchy in $H^{k+1}$. Its limit has $H^{k+1}$ norm one and lies in $\ker\Delta_A$, contradicting step 3.1. Thus $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C_A''\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}$. Together with bijectivity this proves the inverse $G_A$ is bounded.

proof_steps.claim: Localize by the fixed finite partition and extend each compactly supported coefficient by zero into a bounded Euclidean ball. For $p=2$, $2k>d$; [F2] makes each localized $H^k$ coefficient a Banach algebra and gives its $C^1$ representative when $k>d/2+1$. The finite sum of these estimates proves the same algebra and embedding bounds for sections, matrix-valued functions, and forms in the chosen bundle atlas.

The finite-dimensional matrix exponential is smooth, has derivative the identity at zero on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$, and maps $\mathfrak{su}(N)$ into $SU(N)$. In the Banach algebra from step 2.1 its power series and every termwise derivative converge in $H^{k+1}$ on a sufficiently small ball, since the algebra norm is submultiplicative after an equivalent rescaling. The matrix logarithm series converges on a neighborhood of the identity; for a unitary matrix sufficiently close to identity its logarithm is anti-Hermitian, and its trace is zero because the determinant is one and the sum of the small eigenvalue angles lies in $2\pi\mathbb Z$. Hence pointwise $\exp$ and $\log$ give inverse smooth maps between neighborhoods of zero in $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the identity in $\mathcal G_{k+1}$. Their translated charts cover the group; changes of chart are smooth because the transition functions of $\operatorname{Ad}P$ act by smooth conjugation and the multiplication is a bounded bilinear Sobolev map. The pointwise product and inverse therefore close on $\mathcal G_{k+1}$ and are smooth, giving the asserted Hilbert Lie group.

If $G$ and $H$ are two such frames, $D''G=D''H=0$ gives $\bar\partial(G^{-1}H)=0$. Thus the boundary-current limit in the disk identity is unchanged and the flux is unchanged by Stokes applied to $d a$. The energy along this variation is the constant $2\pi\xi|n|$ plus the squared $L^2$ norms of the two first-order residuals in step 1.1. Both residuals vanish at $t=0$; differentiating the squared norms gives $E'(0)=0$ and
$$E''(0)=2\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(|\delta(D_{A,1}\pm iD_{A,2})q|^2+\frac{|\delta(B\mp e^2(\xi-|q|^2))|^2}{2e^2}\right)dx_1dx_2\ge0,$$
with the upper signs for $n\ge0$ and lower signs for $n\le0$ (either choice when $n=0$). Therefore the first variation vanishes and no smooth compactly supported same-sector perturbation lowers the energy. Distinct divisors give distinct possible minimizing fields, so no cross-divisor uniqueness follows.

proof_steps.claim: In the chart w=λ₂/λ₁ on a real incidence fiber, the projected horizontal (0,1) directions are H₁=∂bar_z₁−w∂z₂ and H₂=∂bar_z₂+w∂z₁. For a unitary connection A define the pulled-back (0,1) operator by the vertical ordinary derivative and ∇_A along H₁,H₂. Its mixed squares vanish by the displayed commuting generators and holomorphic w coefficients. Its horizontal square is F_A(H₁,H₂)=F_bar1bar2−w(F_1bar1+F_2bar2)+w²F_12, which vanishes for an ASD two-form in the positive orientation: the three coefficients are precisely its self-dual component. Thus the operator squares to zero on this chart, and on the other projective chart by the same tensorial calculation. Apply [F2] to obtain a genuine holomorphic bundle. Its restriction to every real line is the constant bundle E_x, with positive reality pairing induced by the unitary metric and framing at infinity. This pairing is holomorphic: its vertical derivative vanishes on the constant fibres, and differentiating horizontally gives zero by the original identity ∇_A h=0, with the conjugate pullback at σ interchanging the conjugate horizontal directions.

Restrict H and ∇ to the totally real graph locus M=HP¹. Its smooth real incidence is diffeomorphic to Z by (P,[v])↦[v], with inverse [v]↦(span(v,jv),[v]); the explicit charts in [F3] verify smoothness. Under this identification dp(D) is exactly the span of H₁,H₂ in step 1.1: write X_z=((z₁,-bar_z₂),(z₂,bar_z₁)) and solve v(1,w)^T=0. Therefore the restricted smooth connection has F(H₁,H₂)=0 for every w, so all three self-dual coefficients in step 1.1 vanish. Hence it is ASD. Evaluation intertwines the original holomorphic operator on E with the reconstructed vertical/horizontal Dolbeault operator: it is holomorphic vertically, and on D its derivative is exactly the canonical relative derivative δ by step 3.1. These directions generate the (0,1) tangent in step 1.1, proving equality of the full operators, not just of underlying bundles.

Starting from A in step 1.1, its constant real-line sections identify the reconstructed smooth H with E. Along every alpha-plane the recovered connection has the same derivative as A; the cotangent uniqueness in step 3.1 makes the full connections equal. The unitary reality pairing and framing also agree. Starting from a Ward bundle, step 4.1 proves evaluation is a holomorphic isomorphism from the reconstructed pullback to the original bundle, and step 5.2 preserves its reality pairing and metric. These constructions and identities apply to morphisms as well, so descend to inverse maps on based unitary gauge and framed holomorphic isomorphism classes. proof_steps.claim: The affine space $\mathcal A_\infty$ contains $A_0$. Apply [F2] to the constant map from a one-point polyhedron with empty subpolyhedron and value $A_0$. Its endpoint is an element of $\mathcal A_\infty^*$, proving nonemptiness.

Apply [F2] to $F$ with $K=D^{j+1}$ and $L=\partial D^{j+1}=S^j$. Its boundary is already irreducible, so the endpoint is a map $G:D^{j+1}\to\mathcal A_\infty^*$ agreeing with $u$ on the boundary. Choose the based point $x_0\in S^j$ with $u(x_0)=A$. Since the disk is convex, $C_t(x)=(1-t)x+tx_0$ remains in the disk and fixes $x_0$. Then $G(C_t(x))$ is a homotopy from $G$ to the constant map at $A$ that fixes $x_0$ and remains in $\mathcal A_\infty^*$. Restricting it to $S^j$ gives a based nullhomotopy of $u$; by [F3], its class in $\pi_j(\mathcal A_\infty^*,A)$ is zero. Since $j$ and $u$ were arbitrary, every stated homotopy group vanishes.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] For the stated Sobolev index, the smooth irreducible projection $\mathcal A_\infty^*\to\mathcal A_\infty^*/\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty$ is a locally trivial topological principal $\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty$-bundle with its actual $C^\infty$ quotient topology; the Sobolev irreducible locus $\mathcal A_k^*$ is open. proof_steps.claim: Choose the fixed integer $k>r/2+1$. The smooth clause of [F3], applied with the configuration data [F2], makes $q_*$ a locally trivial principal $\overline{\mathcal G}^\infty(P)$-bundle. By [F4], its total space is nonempty, path connected, and has $\pi_j=0$ for every $j\ge1$, so it is weakly contractible in the sense used in [F6]. For a constant central gauge section $u=\zeta I_N$, the local action formula gives $A^u=A$ because $u^{-1}Au=A$ and $du=0$; hence reduced and full gauge groups have the same orbits on $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$.

The locus $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$ is gauge invariant: in the chosen frame, the based holonomy subgroup of $A^u$ is $u(p_m)^{-1}\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)u(p_m)$, so it has the same invariant subspaces up to conjugation. It is open: by [F2], the inclusion $\mathcal A^\infty(P)\hookrightarrow\mathcal A_k(P)$ is continuous, as each fixed $H^k$ norm is bounded by finitely many smooth derivative seminorms on the finite compact atlas. The smooth irreducible locus is the inverse image of the Sobolev irreducible locus, which is open by [F3]. The full orbit projection $q$ is open because, for any open $U\subseteq\mathcal A^\infty(P)$, its saturation $q^{-1}(q(U))=\bigcup_{u\in\mathcal G^\infty(P)}U\cdot u$ is open. For fixed smooth $u$, the map $A\mapsto u^{-1}Au+u^{-1}du$ is continuous in every finite-atlas derivative seminorm by the Leibniz rule; its inverse is the same formula for $u^{-1}$, so each gauge translate is a homeomorphism. Therefore $q(\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P))$ is open and $q|_{\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)}$ is an open quotient map onto this subset. The reduced and full actions have the same orbits there, so their quotient topologies identify the reduced orbit space homeomorphically with $q(\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P))$; this proves the claim about $\iota$ in the Statement. If $q$ had a continuous section, its restriction to this open subset would take each irreducible orbit to a point in that same orbit, hence into $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$. Via the stated homeomorphism, this would give a continuous section of $q_*$, contradicting step 3.1. Thus $q$ has no continuous section.

proof_steps.claim: For the smooth-space clause, fix now a smooth irreducible center $A\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and use the Banach slice and trivialization established in step 4.1. Put $U_A=\Phi_A(S_{A,\varepsilon}\times\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1})$ and $V_A=\pi_k(S_{A,\varepsilon})$. Since $U_A$ is open in $\mathcal A_k^*$, $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open in the stated $C^\infty$ topology; set $S_A^\infty=S_{A,\varepsilon}\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and $V_A^\infty=\pi_\infty(S_A^\infty)$. For a smooth $B\in U_A$, its unique reduced gauge class from step 4.1 has a representative $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$. It satisfies $d_A^*(B^{u^{-1}}-A)=0$. Locally in a bundle frame, write $C_j=uB_j u^{-1}-(\partial_j u)u^{-1}-A_j$. Substitution in $d_A^*C=0$, use of $\partial_i(u^{-1})=-u^{-1}(\partial_i u)u^{-1}$, and multiplication on the right by $u$ isolate the equation $g^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j u=R(A,B,g;u,u^{-1},du)$ on each chart. Every term in $R$ is a finite product of smooth coefficients (including first derivatives of $A,B$) and factors among $u,u^{-1},du$; hence the principal operator is the scalar smooth Laplacian on each matrix entry. If $u\in H^{r+1}$ for $r\ge k$, then this right-hand side lies in $H^r$ by [F7] and the smooth coefficient bounds. Elliptic regularity [F6] gives $u\in H^{r+2}$. Iteration proves $u$ smooth; changing its representative by an element of the finite center preserves smoothness. Thus every smooth point of the Banach saturation has a smooth trivialization representative, and $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*=\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$.

Suppose smooth $B_j\to B$ in $C^\infty$ within $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The Banach trivialization from step 4.1 gives convergence of their slice representatives in $H^k$ and of their reduced gauge classes in $H^{k+1}$. In a quotient chart around the limiting class from step 1.1, choose lifts $u_j,u$ that converge in $H^{k+1}$; this is possible because the finite center acts by disjoint translates. The equation in step 5.2 and elliptic estimates [F6] bootstrap convergence: if $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+1}$, then the assumed $C^\infty$ convergence gives $B_j\to B$ in $H^{r+1}$, and [F7] makes the right-hand sides converge in $H^r$. Apply the elliptic estimate to $u_j-u$, using also their already known $H^{k+1}$ convergence for the $L^2$ term, to get $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+2}$. Induction gives convergence in every Sobolev order, which on compact $M$ is the $C^\infty$ section topology. The slice representatives converge in $C^\infty$ by their action formula. Conversely the forward action is continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology by multiplication and differentiation of smooth sections. The saturation $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open, and $V_A^\infty$ is open in the quotient because the quotient map is open: the saturation of any open set is a union of its open gauge translates. The restricted map $S_A^\infty\times\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty\to\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$ is therefore a homeomorphism for the actual quotient topology, and it is equivariant. This proves the smooth-space topological principal bundle claim.

proof_steps.claim: To obtain derivative decay, fix $\alpha<\alpha'<\sqrt\kappa$ and use step 3.3 at rate $\alpha'$. Inductively, for each multi-index $\gamma$, differentiating $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ gives $\Delta D^\gamma w=\kappa e^{-w}D^\gamma w+G_\gamma$, where $G_\gamma$ is a finite sum of products of lower derivatives of $w$ and is exponentially small by the induction hypothesis. proof_steps.claim: The rational character formula is [F2]. proof_steps.claim: The first-factor action fixes exactly $p_0=[1:0]$ and $p_\infty=[0:1]$, while it fixes every point of the second factor. The normal complex line is the first factor and the fixed-component tangent space is the second. Moving the real two-dimensional first-factor orientation past the real two-dimensional second-factor orientation has sign $(-1)^{2\cdot2}=+1$, so the induced component orientations agree with the product orientations.

The dual tautological fiber at $p_0$ has weight $0$ and at $p_\infty$ has weight $-1$, so the first-factor class restricts to $0$ and $-u$. Thus the contribution from $F_0$ is $0/u=0$; on $F_\infty$, the restricted class is $(-u)\eta$ and the normal Euler class is $-u$, leaving $\eta$, whose integral is $1$. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] For \(r\geq1\), \(BT=(\mathbb{CP}^{\infty})^r\) has a countable CW structure whose CW topology is the ordinary product topology; the complete product-topology argument is given in the supplier's proof. [[lem-universal-complex-flag-bundle-is-bt-n]]

proof_steps.claim: If \(r=0\), \(BT\) is a point and the CW and paracompact assertions reduce to the compact manifold \(F\). For \(r\geq1\), [F1] gives \(BT\) its ordinary product CW topology, and [F3] makes it paracompact Hausdorff. By [F2], choose a finite CW complex \(K\) and a homotopy equivalence \(h:F\to K\). Since \(K\) is finite, its CW product with the CW complex \(BT\) has the ordinary product topology; hence \(BT\times K\) is a CW complex. The maps \(\mathrm{id}_{BT}\times h\) and the product of a homotopy inverse with \(\mathrm{id}_{BT}\) are homotopy inverses, since their coordinate homotopies are continuous in the product topology. Thus \(BT\times F\) has CW type. If \(F=\varnothing\), take \(K=\varnothing\).

If \(F=\varnothing\), the product is empty and paracompact Hausdorff, so assume \(F\ne\varnothing\). To prove paracompactness of \(BT\times F\), let \(\mathcal U\) be an open cover. For each \(x\in BT\) and \(y\in F\), choose a product neighborhood \(O_{x,y}\times V_{x,y}\) of \((x,y)\) contained in some member \(U_{x,y}\in\mathcal U\). Compactness of \(F\) selects finitely many \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\) whose \(V_{x,y_j}\) cover \(F\). Then \(O_x=\bigcap_{j=1}^m O_{x,y_j}\) is an open neighborhood of \(x\), and \(O_x\times F\) is covered by \(U_{x,y_1},\ldots,U_{x,y_m}\). Paracompactness of \(BT\) gives a locally finite open refinement \(\{W_\alpha\}\) of \(\{O_x\}\). For each \(\alpha\), choose \(x_\alpha\) with \(W_\alpha\subseteq O_{x_\alpha}\); the finitely many sets \((W_\alpha\times F)\cap U_{x_\alpha,y_j}\) cover \(W_\alpha\times F\), are open, and refine \(\mathcal U\). They are locally finite because a neighborhood \(N\times F\) meets sets indexed by only those \(\alpha\) for which \(W_\alpha\) meets \(N\), a finite set. Hence \(BT\times F\) is paracompact. It is Hausdorff as a product of Hausdorff spaces. The point and rank-zero cases satisfy the same conclusions.

On each finite Borel approximation, the first Chern class of the trivialized line is zero. proof_steps.claim: Let $a,b\in H^2(S^2\times S^2;\mathbb Z)$ be the positive generators from the two projections. By [F2], $a^2=b^2=0$ and $ab$ is the positive top generator. The map $\nabla:W\to S^2$ extends over the cone on $\beta$ by the definition $\beta=\nabla\alpha$; hence it extends to a map $q:S^2\times S^2=W\cup_\alpha D^4\to C_\beta$. On $W$, $q$ is the fold into the bottom $S^2$ of $C_\beta$, so $q^*x=a+b$. On the open $4$-cell, the extension is the characteristic disk of $C_\beta$ with degree $+1$ by [A1], so $q^*y=ab$.

In the cone $C_\beta$, $x^2=H(\beta)y$ by [F1]. Pulling back with step 1.1 yields $(a+b)^2=H(\beta)ab$. Since $a^2=b^2=0$ and degree-two classes commute, the left side is $2ab$. The class $ab$ is a generator, so $H(\beta)=2$.

Let $i:W\hookrightarrow S^2\times S^2$ be the $2$-skeleton inclusion. The characteristic disk extends $i\alpha$ over $D^4$, so $\Sigma i\circ\Sigma\alpha$ is null. Define
$$r=(\Sigma p_1\vee\Sigma p_2)\circ\operatorname{pinch}:\Sigma(S^2\times S^2)\longrightarrow\Sigma S^2\vee\Sigma S^2,$$
where $p_1,p_2$ are the projections and the pinch is [F3]. On the first suspended wedge summand, the first projection branch is the identity up to linear rescaling of the suspension coordinate and the second branch is constant; on the second summand the roles reverse. Thus $r\circ\Sigma i\simeq\operatorname{id}_{\Sigma W}$. Applying $r$ to the nullhomotopy in the first sentence gives $\Sigma\alpha\simeq *$. Composing with $\Sigma\nabla$ gives $\Sigma\beta\simeq *$. By the definition of the suspension homomorphism, this is $2[\Sigma h]=0$ because $[\beta]=2[h]$ from step 2.1 and [F1] identifies $[h]$ as the generator.

Its characteristic disk can be taken as the unit ball in $\mathbb C^2$ via $w\mapsto[w_0:w_1:\sqrt{1-|w|^2}]$; the interior parametrizes the complement of $\mathbb{CP}^1$, and on $|w|=1$ the boundary map is $[w_0:w_1]=h(w)$. Thus $\mathbb{CP}^2$ is the mapping cone $C_h$. By [F4], the degree-two generator squares to the degree-four generator, so [F5] gives $H(h)=1$.

Let $d_m:S^3\to S^3$ have degree $m$. The radial cone extension $D^4\to D^4$, $ru\mapsto r d_m(u)$, has relative degree $m$ and boundary $d_m$: on collapsing the disk boundary its map is $\Sigma d_m$, whose degree is $m$ by the natural homology suspension in [F6]. Together with the identity on $S^2$, it defines a map $C_{h\circ d_m}\to C_h$, since the boundary attaching maps agree. It pulls the degree-two generator of $C_h$ back to that of $C_{h\circ d_m}$ and the degree-four generator back to $m$ times the latter. Pulling back $x_h^2=y_h$ therefore gives $x_{h\circ d_m}^2=m y_{h\circ d_m}$, which is exactly $H(h\circ d_m)=m$ by [F5].

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[lem-qftx-round-s4-spin-twist-index-one]] gives the explicit quaternionic Clifford model, parallel chirality, unitary spin-twist connections, chiral kernel dimension one and cokernel zero, and selfadjoint full Dirac domain $H^1$.

proof_steps.claim: For any given spin four-manifold the local quaternionic model glues by its specified Spin(4) lift. In that quaternionic spin model, right multiplication by a quaternionic unit $j$ is an antiunitary map $J_0$ on $S^+\oplus S^-$, with $J_0^2=-1$. It commutes with the four Clifford matrices and $\Gamma$ and is parallel: the transition and connection matrices act from the left and hence commute with right multiplication. The same operation $J_E$ on the $SU(2)$ twist is parallel, antiunitary and has square $-1$. Define $J_5=\Gamma J_0$ on the spin factor. Then $J_5^2=-1$, it anticommutes with each of the four tangent Clifford matrices, and it anticommutes with $c_5=i\Gamma$ because anti-linearity changes $i$ to $-i$. Thus it is the pseudoreal Spin(5) structure, since even products of Clifford matrices commute with it. On the complex tensor product set $J=J_5\otimes J_E$; it is well-defined and antiunitary, $J^2=1$, and $JD_5=-D_5J$. Hence $J$ preserves the kernel and $iD_5$ commutes with $J$.

Chirality anticommutes with $D_4$ and is parallel, so $D_5^2=D_4^2-\partial_t^2$. It has scalar positive principal symbol and smooth coefficients. Formal symmetry follows from unitary connection compatibility and periodic integration by parts. The same shifted-resolvent argument applies to $D_4$ and $D_5$ on a general compact background: each square has scalar positive principal symbol, and [F2] gives the inverse of its positive shift from $L^2$ to $H^2$; multiplying by $D_j\mp i$ gives surjectivity of $D_j\pm i$ and the $H^1$ selfadjoint domain exactly as in [F1]. An $L^2$ weak chiral cokernel vector also has square zero distributionally; testing against smooth sections and using their $H^2$ density puts it in the adjoint domain of the selfadjoint square, hence in $H^2$, and [F2] then makes it smooth. This justifies identifying the cokernel with the negative-chirality kernel. Weak kernels are smooth by the same argument. For a zero mode $\psi$, integration by parts gives $0=\|D_5\psi\|^2=\|D_4\psi\|^2+\|\partial_t\psi\|^2$. Thus $\psi$ is independent of $t$ and lies in $\ker D_4$; conversely every such spinor gives a periodic product zero mode. In general its complex dimension is $n_++n_-$, identifying the smooth negative-chirality kernel with the cokernel by the formal $L^2$ adjoint. For the concrete round twist this dimension is $1$ by [F1]. This avoids any unproved general spectral-flow identity.

The constant central automorphism acts by $-1$ on both chiral spinor kernels and cokernels, and fixes the background connection. Its scalar on the inverse determinant line is $(-1)^{-n_+}(-1)^{n_-}=(-1)^{n_+-n_-}$. For the actual round twist [F1] gives dimensions one and zero, hence scalar $-1$. Parallel transport along a constant path is the identity for any connection. Closing by the inverse endpoint identification gives $z_*^{-1}\circ\mathrm{PT}=-1$; tensor powers give $(-1)^N$. This is an actual finite-dimensional exterior-power action, not an assumption equating a periodic eta invariant with holonomy.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A2] For $N\ge2$, the zero-FI correspondence supplier identifies the stable-and-costable real quotient with the framed ordinary ASD sector having $q_N=-k$, preserving the specified orientation, unitary framing, compact torus action and exact first-order family qualifications. For $N=1$, the rank-one boundary lemma proves that both ordinary spaces are empty at $k>0$ and are the framed flat point at $k=0$, with compatible compact actions and an explicit first-order groupoid equivalence. Its stabilization proof retains the rank-two supplier's actual GAGA, coupled-vanishing and intrinsic normal-form prerequisites; it introduces no extra rank-one dictionary premise. The two suppliers therefore cover the ordinary dictionary for every $N\ge1$ under exactly those inherited hypotheses. Neither identifies the positive-FI resolution or its rank-one formal coefficients with ordinary ASD moduli. [[thm-qftx-zero-fi-regular-adhm-asd-correspondence]], [[lem-qftx-rank-one-regular-adhm-and-ordinary-asd-boundary]]

proof_steps.claim: For $N\ge2$, the source and target of [A2]'s rank-two-and-higher supplier agree with the zero-FI regular quotient and the framed ASD sector in the conditional dictionary, with $q_N=-k$ and identical framing and orientation. For $N=1$, stabilize by adding one unused framed line as in the boundary lemma: its moment equations, word stability and costability are unchanged. Its proved boundary identifies the two empty spaces at $k>0$ and the unique framed flat points at $k=0$, and its direct first-order gauge argument supplies the corresponding family identification rather than inferring it from an orbit-set bijection. Thus the ordinary dictionary has no uncovered rank-one case; its exact rank-two analytic and normal-form hypotheses remain inherited. This does not place any positive-FI partition fixed point in the open regular ordinary locus. In particular, the positive-FI one-box rank-one contribution is still the formal coefficient of step 1.1 and is not an ordinary positive-charge abelian instanton.

For $k>0$, use the tuple $Y_1=\{(i,0):0\leq i<k\}$ and $Y_\alpha=\varnothing$ for $\alpha>1$; step 1.1 constructs a stable datum. Replacing $B_1$ by $B_1+c\,\mathrm{id}_V$ preserves the complex equation and stability while changing $\operatorname{tr}(B_1)$ by $kc$ for every $c\in\mathbb C$. Trace is invariant under conjugation, so the descended trace function on the geometric quotient has image $\mathbb C$, which is not compact. Thus the quotient is noncompact. The completed Borel carrier matches the compact real-Borel interface in [L1]. The ADHM/monad comparisons in [A1]–[A2] retain their exact analytic and family hypotheses, while step 2.3 has supplied the precise intrinsic localized Borel–Moore pushforward covered by [F6].

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[def-abbv-equivariant-integration-conventions]]: $H_T^*(X;\mathbb R)$ is Borel cohomology, $\mathcal R=H^*(BT;\mathbb R)$ is a polynomial domain under AC, $S$ is generated by nonzero character classes, and $\int_X$ is the oriented Borel-fiber pushforward.

proof_steps.claim:
The $\mathcal R$-linear pushforwards in [F1] and the identity $\int_M i_{j*}^T(\delta)=\int_{F_j}\delta$ in [F2] extend $S^{-1}\mathcal R$-linearly, so they apply to $\delta= eta_j/e_T(
u_j)$. Applying $\int_M$ to step 3.1 gives $\int_M\alpha=\sum_j\int_Mi_{j*}^T( eta_j/e_T(
u_j))=\sum_j\int_{F_j} eta_j/e_T(
u_j)$, which is the fixed-component formula in the localized coefficient ring. If $F=\varnothing$, [L2] says $S^{-1}H_T^*(M)=0$, so $\int_M\alpha$ localizes to zero; because $\mathcal R$ is a domain and every element of $S$ is nonzero, $\mathcal R\hookrightarrow S^{-1}\mathcal R$ is injective and the empty sum is indeed zero. If a normal rank is zero, its Euler denominator is $1$ by [F3], so that term is the ordinary integral over that fixed component.

If $F$ is nonempty and each fixed component is a point $p$, then $\nu_p=T_pM$ has no trivial weight and hence $n=2m$. With the stated ambient normal and positive point orientations, its complex character-line decomposition has Euler class $e_T(T_pM)=\epsilon_p\prod_{a=1}^m u_{\chi_{p,a}}$ by [F1]. Substituting into step 4.1 and using $\epsilon_p^{-1}=\epsilon_p$ yields the isolated-fixed-point formula. If $n=0$, the product is empty and the same calculation reads as the sum of the oriented point evaluations. For empty $F$, step 4.1 already gives zero in every dimension, without introducing $m$.

proof_steps.claim: Suppose \(\alpha\in\mathscr S_T(k)^{-1}H_T^n(M;k)\) satisfies \(i^*\alpha=0\). Step 1.1 writes \(\alpha=i_*^T(\beta)\) for a relative class \(\beta=(\beta_j)\). proof_steps.claim: The closed/open localization sequence for $i:F\hookrightarrow X$ and $X\setminus F$ contains $S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_{j+1}(X\setminus F)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X\setminus F)$. For a finite invariant open cover of $X\setminus F$, the augmented Čech complex with terms $j_{I!}\mathbb Q_{D_I}$, where $D_I$ is an intersection and $j_I:D_I\hookrightarrow X\setminus F$ is open, resolves the constant equivariant sheaf. Those groups vanish after localization by [F2]. Since the Čech filtration is finite and localization is exact by [F4], the abutment $S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X\setminus F;\mathbb Q)$ is zero for every $j$.

The closed/open localization sequence for $i:F\hookrightarrow X$ and $X\setminus F$ contains $S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_{j+1}(X\setminus F)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X)\to S_T^{-1}H^{\mathrm{BM},T}_j(X\setminus F)$. The proof used only the finite invariant affine cover and not Sumihiro's theorem or compactness.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] The normal Thom class represents the oriented Poincaré dual, and integral projective cohomology is generated by the tautological Euler class; its negative is c₁(O(1)). [[lem-normal-thom-class-realizes-the-poincare-dual-of-a-submanifold]], [[lem-integral-cohomology-ring-of-complex-projective-space-by-splitting]]

proof_steps.claim: The explicit incidence chart fixes vertical complex orientation followed by the positive base orientation to be the complex orientation of Z. The pullback of the positive point Thom class on S⁴ is the positive normal Thom class of its fiber CP¹; [F5] identifies its absolute class as the Poincaré dual of that fiber. A linear CP¹ has dual H²: H restricts with integral one to the line, and the integral projective cohomology ring gives H² as its positive degree-four generator. Hence π*u=H² for the positive generator u of H⁴(S⁴). Smooth evaluation gives E_twistor≅π*H, so c₂(E_twistor)=kH² is equivalent to c₂(H)[S⁴]=k. By [F4] this is q_N=-k; the same calculation verifies the forward map's charge clause. Framing is transported by evaluation at infinity. All constructions use incidence, evaluation and unique relative connections, so commute with the specified projective rotations and framing transformations. They therefore give the claimed T-equivariant bijection and all stated invariants, conditional on the exact absolute GAGA comparison [A1].

[F7] The finite algebraic resolution gives
$\operatorname{ch}(F)=N-kH^2$, $c_1(F)=0$, $c_2(F)=kH^2$,

proof_steps.claim: The finite monad resolution and its locally free cohomology give the algebraic Chern character and Chern classes in [F7]. If the topological bundle is $\pi^*E$, naturality gives $\pi^*c_2(E)=kH_{\rm top}^2=k\pi^*u$; since $\pi^*u$ is a generator, $c_2(E)=ku$. This is conditional on the pullback hypothesis and asserts no Ward correspondence.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] Proper pushforward is functorial, closed inclusions are proper, and cap product with an equivariant cohomology class sends $[X]_T$ to Borel–Moore degree $2d-q$. [[def-qftx-localized-equivariant-borel-moore-data]]

proof_steps.claim: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a proper $T$-equivariant map between smooth separated finite-type varieties with finite invariant affine covers and proper fixed loci $F_X,F_Y$. Its restriction $f^T:F_X\to F_Y$ is proper, and the square formed by $i_X,i_Y,f^T,f$ commutes because $f$ sends fixed points to fixed points. Functoriality of proper Borel–Moore pushforward gives $f_*i_{X*}=i_{Y*}f^T_*$. After localization both $i_{X*}$ and $i_{Y*}$ are isomorphisms by [F2], so applying their inverses and then the proper traces proves $p_{Y*}^{\mathrm{loc}}f_*=p_{X*}^{\mathrm{loc}}$. If $X\to\mathrm{pt}$ itself is proper, then $p_{F*}=p_{X*}i_*$; composing with $i_*^{-1}$ proves $p_*^{\mathrm{loc}}=p_{X*}$.

Let $ eta=(i_*)^{-1}(\alpha\cap[X]_T)$. On each component, the complex orientation and refined Gysin map give $i_a^!(\alpha\cap[X]_T)=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Since $\alpha\cap[X]_T=i_* eta$, the self-intersection formula [F3] gives $e_T(
u_a)\cap eta_a=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Properness of $F_a$ makes $e_T(
u_a)$ invertible after localization by [F3], hence $ eta_a=(i_a^*\alpha/e_T(
u_a))\cap[F_a]_T$. Applying $p_{a*}$ and summing the finitely many components yields the displayed formula. The degree is $2d-q$: division by the degree-$2c_a$ Euler class lowers the localized cohomological degree of the insertion from $q$ to $q-2c_a$, and capping with the degree-$2d_a$ fundamental class gives $2d_a-(q-2c_a)=2d-q$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] $SU(N)$ is path connected, $\pi_1(SU(N))=\pi_2(SU(N))=0$, and $\pi_3(SU(N))\cong\mathbb Z$. [[lem-qftx-low-unitary-homotopy-inputs]]

proof_steps.claim:
Suppose $r=3$. By [F3, F4], $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))\cong\pi_3(SU(N))\cong\mathbb Z$. The evaluation LES [F2, F6] has the component segment
$$\pi_1(SU(N))\longrightarrow\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))\longrightarrow\pi_0(\mathcal G(P))\longrightarrow\pi_0(SU(N)).$$
The outer terms are one-point sets by [F4]. The induced map on components is surjective by exactness, and its fibers are the orbits of $\pi_1(SU(N))$ on $\pi_0(\mathcal G_m(P))$ in the action clause of [F6]. That acting group is trivial, so each fiber is a singleton and the middle map is a bijection. Thus $\mathcal G(P)$ has infinitely many components. Since $\mathcal G(P)\to\overline{\mathcal G}(P)$ is a covering with $N$ sheets, components downstairs correspond to orbits of the finite deck group on components upstairs: a path downstairs lifts by [F7] to a path whose endpoint differs from its starting lift by one deck transformation, and each deck orbit is therefore one quotient component. Each orbit has at most $N$ elements, so infinitely many components remain.

Suppose $r=4$. By [F3] and [F5], $\pi_1(\mathcal G_m(P))\cong\pi_5(SU(N))\ne0$. In the evaluation LES, the map $\pi_1(\mathcal G_m(P))\to\pi_1(\mathcal G(P))$ has preceding term $\pi_2(SU(N))=0$ by [F4]; exactness makes it injective. The finite covering in [F2] induces an injection $\pi_1(\mathcal G(P))\hookrightarrow\pi_1(\overline{\mathcal G}(P))$ by [F6]. Hence $\pi_1(\overline{\mathcal G}(P))$ contains a nonzero subgroup. The two cases establish the statement for every $r,N,P$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] For every $N\ge2$ and every bundle on $S^3$, the reduced smooth gauge group has infinitely many path components; for every bundle on $S^4$, its fundamental group at the identity is nontrivial. [[thm-qftx-reduced-gauge-group-sphere-nontriviality]]

proof_steps.claim: Suppose $q_*$ had a continuous section. Apply [F6] to the nonempty principal bundle in step 2.1. Its structure group $\overline{\mathcal G}^\infty(P)$ would be path connected and have $\pi_j=0$ for every $j\ge1$. If $r=3$, this contradicts the infinitely many components in [F5]. If $r=4$, it contradicts the nonzero fundamental group in [F5]. Thus $q_*$ has no continuous section.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] The global charge form is $\beta_B=\frac{1}{8\pi^2}B(F\wedge F)$, and $q_B=\int_X\beta_B$; the Hodge star and the self-dual/ASD decomposition are those fixed by the orientation and metric. [[def-qftx-instanton-number-and-asd-sector]]

proof_steps.claim: Write $F_i=F_i^++F_i^-$ with $*_{g_X}F_i^+=F_i^+$ and $*_{g_X}F_i^-=-F_i^-$. Let $a=\int_X B(F_i^+\wedge *_{g_X}F_i^+)$ and $b=\int_X B(F_i^-\wedge *_{g_X}F_i^-)$. Orthogonality of the two Hodge eigenspaces [F3] makes the cross terms vanish; positivity of $B$ [F2] gives $a,b\geq0$. Consequently $\int_XB(F_i\wedge *_{g_X}F_i)=a+b$, while $\int_XB(F_i\wedge F_i)=a-b$. By [F1], $S_B=(a+b)/g^2$ and $q_B=(a-b)/(8\pi^2)$.

For nonnegative $a,b$, $a+b\geq|a-b|$, so the claimed bound follows after division by $g^2>0$. If $q_B>0$, then $a>b$ and equality is equivalent to $b=0$. Its integrand is the continuous nonnegative squared norm of $F_i^-$; if $F_i^-$ were nonzero at a point, it would be bounded away from zero on a neighborhood of positive Riemannian volume, contradicting $b=0$. Thus $F_i^-=0$. If $q_B<0$, equality in $a+b\geq b-a$ is equivalent to $a=0$; the same continuity and positivity argument gives $F_i^+=0$. If $q_B=0$, equality forces $a+b=0$, so nonnegativity gives $a=b=0$ and both components vanish, hence $F_i=0$. Conversely each of the three stated conditions makes its corresponding norm vanish and gives equality.
