final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A4] The current framed Ward theorem proves the local integrable-Dolbeault frames, universal-line degree-zero base change/evaluation, unique incidence connection and compatibility of the pairing-induced positive metric. Its comparison input is absolute projective GAGA, not independently chosen parallel metrics or assumed base-change surjectivity. [[thm-qftx-framed-penrose-ward-correspondence-on-s4]]

proof_steps.claim: Starting with a framed ASD connection, [A4] constructs its holomorphic Ward bundle; the exact coupled cohomology-vanishing and diagonal argument [[lem-qftx-asd-twistor-vanishing-and-monad-reconstruction]] reconstructs the normalized three-term monad. Starting with regular ADHM data, [A5] identifies its normalized real monad and projection connection with this Ward bundle and connection. The equality of the two constructions is the first-order and inverse-extraction clause in [A5], so it is conditional on that exact real block proof, not on the P² citation alone.

By [A5], both composites on framed isomorphism classes are identities: ADHM data produce the Ward bundle whose monad extraction returns the same $U(k)$ orbit, and an ASD connection produces a Ward bundle whose matrix extraction returns an orbit reconstructing that framed connection. The charge of each resulting connection is $q_N=-k$ by [F2]–[F3]. Thus the claimed bijection and charge statement follow conditionally on [A4]–[A5].

The finite-dimensional quotient and $\mathbb P^2$ sheaf maps are $T$-equivariant by [A1]–[A2]. The Ward construction is natural under rotations and framing transformations by [A4]; the exact raw monad torus factors are directly calculated in the new block lemma cited by [A5], while the equivariance of inverse normalization remains part of [A5]. These exact interfaces make the composite $T$-equivariant. The same composition on first-order families is valid only under the base-change hypotheses of [A2]–[A4] and the deformation compatibility of [A5]. This proves the stated conditional torus and tangent clauses and leaves the positive-FI boundary separate.

fact_uses.text: [F3] For measurable $g$ and $0<q<\infty$, $\int_X|g|^q\,d\mu=q\int_0^\infty t^{q-1}A_g(t)\,dt$, both sides possibly $+\infty$ ([[thm-layer-cake-formula-for-l-p-powers]]).

proof_steps.claim: Tonelli's theorem applied to the nonnegative product-measurable function $(x,t)\mapsto t^{p-2}|f(x)|\mathbf1_{\{|f(x)|>t\}}$ on the $\sigma$-finite product $X\times(0,\infty)$ converts the first term of the layer-cake integral into an $X$-integral: $$\int_0^\infty t^{p-1}\frac{2A}{t}\Bigl(\int_{\{|f|>t\}}|f|\,d\mu\Bigr)dt=2A\int_X|f|\Bigl(\int_0^{|f|}t^{p-2}\,dt\Bigr)d\mu=\frac{2A}{p-1}\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu,$$ where the inner integral was evaluated as $|f|^{p-1}/(p-1)$, legitimate because $p-1>0$, and the case $f(x)=0$ contributes $0$.

Likewise, Tonelli applied to $(x,t)\mapsto t^{p-3}|f(x)|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f(x)|\le t\}}$ gives, since $p-2<0$, $$\int_0^\infty t^{p-1}\frac{4B^2}{t^2}\Bigl(\int_{\{|f|\le t\}}|f|^2\,d\mu\Bigr)dt=4B^2\int_X|f|^2\Bigl(\int_{|f|}^\infty t^{p-3}\,dt\Bigr)d\mu=\frac{4B^2}{2-p}\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu,$$ the inner integral being $|f|^{p-2}/(2-p)$ and the case $f(x)=0$ contributing $0$.

Combining the layer-cake identity [F3] for $g=Tf$ with step 2.1 and steps 3.1 and 3.2 gives $$\|Tf\|_p^p=p\int_0^\infty t^{p-1}A_{Tf}(t)\,dt\le p\Bigl(\frac{2A}{p-1}+\frac{4B^2}{2-p}\Bigr)\|f\|_p^p,$$ because $t^{p-1}A_{Tf}(t)\le t^{p-1}$ times the two integrands integrated in steps 3.1 and 3.2; taking $p$-th roots gives the asserted strong $(p,p)$ bound. Since $Tf$ is determined a.e. by the class of $f$, the bound descends to $L^p(X)$ by [F5].

fact_uses.text: [F3] Chebyshev: $|\{|u|>t\}|\le t^{-2}\int|u|^2$ for measurable $u$; layer cake: $\|g\|_q^q=q\int_0^\infty t^{q-1}|\{|g|>t\}|dt$; Fubini applies to absolutely integrable complex kernels ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); Tonelli applies to nonnegative product-measurable integrands on $\sigma$-finite products ([[thm-chebyshev-markov-inequality-for-the-integral]], [[thm-layer-cake-formula-for-l-p-powers]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); the $L^p$ and $L^{p'}$ norms are the quotient norms of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], Hölder's inequality is [[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]], and $C_c^\infty$ is dense in $L^p$ for finite $p$ ([[thm-complex-finite-simple-and-smooth-compact-support-density-for-finite-p]]).

proof_steps.claim: Sharp two-level interpolation. Let $S$ be any linear operator defined on $L^1+L^2$, weak $(1,1)$ with constant $A$ and $L^2$-bounded with constant $B$, and let $1<q<2$. For $f\in L^q$ and any $\delta>0$ put $f_0:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|>\delta t\}}$ and $f_1:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le\delta t\}}$ at height $t>0$; then $f_0\in L^1$ and $f_1\in L^2$, since $\|f_0\|_1\le(\delta t)^{1-q}\|f\|_q^q$ and $\|f_1\|_2^2\le(\delta t)^{2-q}\|f\|_q^q$. Hence $\{|Sf|>t\}\subseteq\{|Sf_0|>t/2\}\cup\{|Sf_1|>t/2\}$ and the weak $(1,1)$ bound for $Sf_0$ together with Chebyshev and the $L^2$ bound for $Sf_1$ give $|\{|Sf|>t\}|\le\frac{2A}{t}\int_{\{|f|>\delta t\}}|f|+\frac{4B^2}{t^2}\int_{\{|f|\le\delta t\}}|f|^2$. Integrating $t^{q-1}|\{|Sf|>t\}|$ over $(0,\infty)$ and exchanging the integrals by Tonelli gives $\|Sf\|_q^q\le q\bigl[\frac{2A\delta^{1-q}}{q-1}+\frac{4B^2\delta^{2-q}}{2-q}\bigr]\|f\|_q^q$, because $\int_0^{|f|/\delta}t^{q-2}dt=\frac{(|f|/\delta)^{q-1}}{q-1}$ and $\int_{|f|/\delta}^\infty t^{q-3}dt=\frac{(|f|/\delta)^{q-2}}{2-q}$; choosing $\delta:=A/(2B^2)$ when $A,B>0$ balances the two terms at a constant multiple of $A^{2-q}B^{2q-2}$, so that $$\bigl\|Sf\bigr\|_q\le C_q\,A^{\frac2q-1}B^{2-\frac2q}\|f\|_q\le C_q(A+B)\|f\|_q,$$ the last inequality because the exponents $\frac2q-1$ and $2-\frac2q$ are nonnegative and sum to one, so the weighted geometric mean is at most the sum; if $A=0$, let $\delta\downarrow0$, and if $B=0$, let $\delta\to\infty$ in the preceding inequality, obtaining $Sf=0$ in either case.

The case $2<p<\infty$: apply step 1.2 with $q=p'$ to the adjoint $T^*$, which by step 1.1 has weak $(1,1)$ constant $A$ and $L^2$ norm $B$: for every $g\in L^{p'}$, $\|T^*g\|_{p'}\le C_{p'}(A_2+B)\|g\|_{p'}$. Then for $f\in L^p\cap L^2$ and $g\in L^{p'}\cap L^2$ with $\|g\|_{p'}\le1$, the adjoint identity and Hölder's inequality give $|\int(Tf)g|=|\langle f,T^*\overline g\rangle|\le\|f\|_p\|T^*\overline g\|_{p'}\le C_{p'}(A_2+B)\|f\|_p$, To establish $Tf\in L^p$ before using norm recovery, put $u=Tf\in L^2$, $E_N=B(0,N)\cap\{|u|\le N\}$ and $a_N=(\int_{E_N}|u|^p)^{1/p}$. If $a_N>0$, take $g_N=\mathbf1_{E_N}|u|^{p-1}\theta_u/a_N^{p-1}$, with $\theta_u=\overline u/|u|$ on $u\ne0$ and zero otherwise. This test is bounded on a finite-measure set, hence lies in $L^{p'}\cap L^2$, and satisfies $\|g_N\|_{p'}=1$, $\int ug_N=a_N$. The preceding pairing bound gives $a_N\le C_{p'}(A_2+B)\|f\|_p$; if $a_N=0$ the same inequality is immediate. Since $E_N$ increases to a full-measure set, monotone convergence gives $\|Tf\|_p\le C_{p'}(A_2+B)\|f\|_p$; since $C_c^\infty\subseteq L^p\cap L^2$ is dense in $L^p$, this bound extends uniquely to all of $L^p$, and $C_{p'}(A_2+B)\le C_{n,p}(A_2+B)\max(p,(p-1)^{-1})$.

The exponent dependence can be made dimension-only. Put $D=A_2+B$. If $D=0$, then $B=0$ and $T=0$. Otherwise normalize $S=T/D$. Step 1.1 and the weak endpoint give weak $(1,1)$ constants at most $a_n=C_n$ for both $S$ and $S^*$, and their $L^2$ norms are at most one. The interpolation-and-duality lemma [F4] at $q=3/2$ and its conjugate $3$ gives $\|S\|_{3\to3},\|S^*\|_{3\to3}\le d_n$ with $d_n$ depending only on $n$. For $1<p\le2$, split $f=f\mathbf1_{\{|f|>t\}}+f\mathbf1_{\{|f|\le t\}}$. Weak $(1,1)$ on the first part and Chebyshev with the strong $(3,3)$ bound on the second yield $|\{|Sf|>t\}|\le2a_nt^{-1}\int_{|f|>t}|f|+8d_n^3t^{-3}\int_{|f|\le t}|f|^3$. Layer cake and Tonelli, as in step 1.2, give $\|Sf\|_p^p\le p[2a_n/(p-1)+8d_n^3/(3-p)]\|f\|_p^p\le K_n(p-1)^{-1}\|f\|_p^p$, with $K_n\ge1$ independent of $p$. The compatible $L^1$ and $L^3$ actions agree on their intersection by approximation with bounded compact-support functions in both norms. Thus $\|S\|_{p\to p}\le K_n/(p-1)$ for $1<p\le2$. Apply this estimate to $S^*$ at $p'=p/(p-1)$ and use the finite-support tests and density argument of step 2.2 to get $\|S\|_{p\to p}\le K_n(p-1)\le K_np$ for $p>2$. Consequently $\|T\|_{p\to p}\le K_nD\max(p,(p-1)^{-1})$ throughout the strict range.

Steps 2.1 and 2.2 prove boundedness and uniqueness in the two open ranges; the given $L^2$ bound handles $p=2$. Step 3.1 also proves the stronger bound with a dimensional constant independent of $p$, and hence the stated estimate.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-qftx-taubes-arbitrary-divisor-plane-vortex]]: for each effective divisor there is a unique scalar $h$ with the stated logarithmic subtractions and decay; the reconstruction is smooth, solves the positive first-order equations, has finite energy, and has flux $2\pi$ times the degree. proof_steps.claim: Its multiplicities give degree $N=2+1=3$ and distributional source $4\pi(2\delta_{z_0}+\delta_{z_1})=8\pi\delta_{z_0}+4\pi\delta_{z_1}$. The center subtraction coefficients are $2m_0=4$ and $2m_1=2$. Applying [F2] gives the unique scalar $h$, its smooth subtractions, $h\to0$, and strict negativity away from the divisor.
Apply [F2] to the explicit effective divisor $|n|[0]$ of degree $|n|$ (the empty divisor if $n=0$) and conjugate when $n<0$. Its signed flux is $2\pi n$, and [F3] gives $T_n=2\pi\xi|n|$.

Here $P=(z-z_0)^2(z-z_1)$ and $s=2\log|P|$. The reconstruction in [F2] extends smoothly over both centers, solves the positive critical equations, and has flux $2\pi N=6\pi$. Since it is a fixed-divisor reconstructed solution, [F3] gives its attained absolute transverse energy $2\pi\xi N=6\pi\xi$. The argument determines the profile by the unique scalar boundary-value problem and supplies no elementary closed form.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F8] [[thm-interior-w-two-p-estimate-for-uniformly-elliptic-equations]]: for $p>2$ and $\Delta w=f\in L^p$ on a ball in $\mathbb R^2$, the $W^{2,p}$ norm on the concentric half-ball is bounded by the local $L^p$ norms of $f$ and $w$.

proof_steps.claim: On any smaller compact disk $K\Subset U$, [F8] applied on finitely many nested balls and the uniform $L^\infty$ bound of step 7.1 yields uniform $W^{2,p}$ bounds for $w_R$ for every finite $p>2$, since its Laplacian is bounded. As $e^s$ is smooth and $\Delta w_R=\kappa(e^s e^{w_R}-1)$, the right-hand side has a uniform $C^{0,\alpha}$ bound there; [F9] then yields a uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bound on $K$. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] For every effective divisor, the scalar Taubes problem has its unique smooth desingularized solution and reconstructs a smooth finite-energy critical connection/Higgs field with the prescribed zeros, flux, and exponential gauge-invariant decay; negative winding uses conjugation. [[thm-qftx-taubes-arbitrary-divisor-plane-vortex]]

proof_steps.claim: For each chosen effective divisor of degree $|n|$, apply [F3] with $e=g$ and $\xi=2v^2$, using its conjugate for negative n. [F4] fixes its finite energy and flux normalization. The polynomial phase correction relative to $n\theta$ is degree zero and tends to zero; the cutoff cleanup used in [F5] removes only this correction globally, preserving the divisor. The resulting embedded fields have a=p=0 and satisfy the appropriate critical equations, so all residuals in step 2.1 vanish and the full-model energy is exactly $T_n$. The same identity bounds every competing full-model profile below by $T_n$, proving absolute minimality. Compactly supported smooth variations preserve the flux/vacuum class, so differentiability of their energy at the minimum gives vanishing first variation. This proves actual existence and stationarity for every divisor, without a radial or unit-winding restriction.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] [[pthm-qftx-n2-linear-monopole-bps-vortex-bound]]: in the frozen-metric linear truncation, actual mathematical arbitrary-divisor vortices embed as stationary absolute full-model minima with $T_n=4\pi v^2|n|$; actual canonical full-model collars give $T_nL+O(1)$ for fixed-flux cylinder infima. Its nonlinear stationarity obstruction and screened dual-electric response keep this exact critical result separate from generic nonlinear confinement.

proof_steps.claim:
Under the additional vortex/minimization hypothesis in the Statement,
[F4] gives nonzero quantized original electric flux and a tension
$\sigma>0$. The interior of a translation-invariant tube of length $L$
contains the same transverse profile at each longitudinal coordinate, so
its bulk energy is $\sigma L$. The uniformly bounded endcap contribution
therefore gives $V(L)=\sigma L+O(1)$, which is linear confinement in this
effective model. This last conclusion is conditional: no preceding step establishes existence or minimization of the required profile. Original electric probes correspond to dual magnetic flux; the condensed original magnetic charges are dual electric charges and are screened in the linear response about the dual Higgs vacuum described by [F5]. This conclusion concerns classical effective energy, not a quantum Wilson-loop area law.

In the explicitly linear truncation, assume [A3] and apply [F5] with $\xi=2v^2$ to each chosen effective divisor of degree $|n|$. It supplies an actual smooth stationary full-model minimum of tension $T_n=2\pi\xi|n|=4\pi v^2|n|$, and actual finite collars from every fixed canonical full-model end trace in the stated valid neutral disk. Thus $T_nL\le I_L\le T_n(L-2\ell)+C_0+C_1$, proving $I_L=T_nL+O(1)$; matching minimizing traces attain $T_nL$ exactly. No solution or endcap existence is assumed for this critical boundary problem. The nonlinear obstruction in [F5] prevents extending its exact BPS assertion to generic u.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-qftx-taubes-arbitrary-divisor-plane-vortex]]: for every effective finite divisor of degree $|n|$ there is a smooth finite-energy planar critical pair with flux $2\pi n$ (using conjugation for $n<0$); for the empty divisor it is the vacuum. The local unwound exterior gauge has $q=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}$ and $A=-\tfrac12*dh$; that degree-changing exterior gauge is not asserted to extend globally. Separately, removing only the smooth degree-zero polynomial phase correction relative to $n\theta$ by a global cutoff gauge yields the canonical winding representative $q=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}e^{in\theta}$, $A=n\,d\theta-\tfrac12*dh$.

proof_steps.claim: For an end trace with exterior phase $n\theta+\phi$, choose a smooth radial cutoff $\eta$ which is zero on a disk containing the noncanonical region and one outside a larger disk. The real function $\chi=-\eta\phi$ extends smoothly by zero to the whole plane; the allowed gauge transformation $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ therefore makes the exterior phase exactly $n\theta$. This constructs the asserted degree-zero exterior phase cleanup without attempting to extend a degree-$n$ angular map across the disk. For the planar minimizer in [F2], write $P=|P|e^{i\vartheta}$ on the exterior; $\vartheta-n\theta$ is single-valued, smooth and tends to zero because $P(z)=z^n(1+O(|z|^{-1}))$ for $n\ge0$ (use the conjugate construction for $n<0$). Applying the same cutoff extension to $-(\vartheta-n\theta)$ changes its exterior fields to $q^*=\rho_*e^{in\theta}$ and $A^*=n\,d\theta-\tfrac12*dh$; hence $A^*-n\,d\theta$ decays exponentially.

In canonical exterior gauge write $q=\rho e^{in\theta}$ and $\alpha=A-n\,d\theta$. Directly, $D_Aq=e^{in\theta}(d\rho-i\rho\alpha)$, so the real and imaginary terms are orthogonal and $|D_Aq|^2=|d\rho|^2+\rho^2|\alpha|^2$. Uniform convergence gives $\rho\ge\sqrt\xi/2$ outside a disk; thus finite kinetic energy implies $\alpha\in L^2$ there. Also $|\rho-\sqrt\xi|\le |\rho^2-\xi|/\sqrt\xi$, so finite potential energy gives $\rho-\sqrt\xi\in L^2$ there. On compact disks all fields are smooth and bounded. Consequently, for any two cleaned end traces and the cleaned minimizer, differences of connections and Higgs fields are globally in $L^2$; each Higgs field is bounded.

Apply step 3.1 first to $p_0$ and $p_*$, defining its finite energy to be $C_0$, and then to $p_*$ and $p_1$, defining its finite energy to be $C_1$. For $L\ge2\ell$, place the first collar on $[0,\ell]$, the constant planar minimizer on $[\ell,L-\ell]$, and the second collar on $[L-\ell,L]$. The profiles match smoothly because the collar cutoff is constant near its ends. The middle has no longitudinal energy and contributes exactly $T_n(L-2\ell)$ by [F2]–[F3]. At $L=2\ell$ this middle interval has zero length; the two collars meet at the constant value $p_*$, so the same upper bound holds. This admissible concatenation proves $\inf\mathcal E_L\le C_0+T_n(L-2\ell)+C_1$.

Combining steps 1.1 and 4.1 gives $0\le\inf\mathcal E_L-T_nL\le C_0+C_1-2\ell T_n$ for every $L\ge2\ell$; the right side is a finite constant independent of $L$, proving the bounded-remainder conclusion. If $p_0=p_1=p_*$, the constant extension $(A_1,A_2,q)=(A^*,q^*)$, $A_3=0$, has energy $T_nL$ and satisfies the angular and no-leakage conditions. The lower bound from step 1.1 then proves it is an exact translation-invariant minimum.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-qftx-taubes-arbitrary-divisor-plane-vortex]]: for each effective finite divisor of degree $|n|$, the reconstructed smooth critical fields satisfy the corresponding first-order equations, have finite energy, and have flux $2\pi n$ with sign set by the orientation.

proof_steps.claim: For each fixed divisor, [F2] supplies a smooth pair satisfying the relevant first-order equations. Its square terms in step 1.1 vanish identically; the sequence estimates of steps 1.2–2.1 apply because [F2] gives finite energy and the same boundary sector. Hence its energy is exactly $2\pi\xi|n|$. The lower bound of step 3.1 applies to every admissible same-winding configuration, so this pair is an absolute transverse energy minimum, without radial or unit-winding assumptions.

Let $(a,\eta)$ be a smooth compactly supported variation of a minimizing pair, and set $A_t=A+ta$, $q_t=q+t\eta$; for any field expression $F$, define $\delta F:=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}F(A_t,q_t)$. For sufficiently small $t$, the fields remain in the same boundary sector; outside the compact support they equal the original fields. Thus the boundary-current limit in the disk identity is unchanged and the flux is unchanged by Stokes applied to $d a$. The energy along this variation is the constant $2\pi\xi|n|$ plus the squared $L^2$ norms of the two first-order residuals in step 1.1. Both residuals vanish at $t=0$; differentiating the squared norms gives $E'(0)=0$ and
$$E''(0)=2\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(|\delta(D_{A,1}\pm iD_{A,2})q|^2+\frac{|\delta(B\mp e^2(\xi-|q|^2))|^2}{2e^2}\right)dx_1dx_2\ge0,$$
with the upper signs for $n\ge0$ and lower signs for $n\le0$ (either choice when $n=0$). Therefore the first variation vanishes and no smooth compactly supported same-sector perturbation lowers the energy. Distinct divisors give distinct possible minimizing fields, so no cross-divisor uniqueness follows.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] [[thm-interior-w-two-p-estimate-for-uniformly-elliptic-equations]]: for $p>2$ on a two-dimensional ball, the interior $W^{2,p}$ norm is bounded by the local $L^p$ norms of the solution and its Laplacian.

proof_steps.claim: To obtain derivative decay, fix $\alpha<\alpha'<\sqrt\kappa$ and use step 3.3 at rate $\alpha'$. On each unit ball centered at large $z$, both $w$ and $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ are $O(e^{-\alpha'|z|})$. By [F3] and [F5], $w$ has a $C^{1,\beta}$ norm of that order on the concentric half-ball for some $\beta>0$. Thus the right-hand side has a $C^{0,\beta}$ norm of the same order, and [F4] gives $C^{2,\beta}$ decay on a smaller ball. Inductively, for each multi-index $\gamma$, differentiating $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ gives $\Delta D^\gamma w=\kappa e^{-w}D^\gamma w+G_\gamma$, where $G_\gamma$ is a finite sum of products of lower derivatives of $w$ and is exponentially small by the induction hypothesis. Applying [F3] and [F4] on nested unit balls gives the same $e^{-\alpha'|z|}$ bound for two more derivatives. Since $e^{-\alpha'|z|}\le e^{-\alpha|z|}$ outside a fixed disk, every finite derivative has the stated rate.

fact_uses.text: [F2] Under countable choice, $\lambda_m\times\lambda_k$ agrees with $\lambda_{m+k}$ on Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^{m+k}$ for positive integers $m,k$ ([[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]]).

proof_steps.claim: Put $W(x)=\prod_{j<n}(1+x_j^2)$ and $A=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^n}p_{\alpha+2\epsilon,\beta}(f)$. Expanding the product and taking absolute values gives $W(x)|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|\le A$. Also $|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|\le B:=p_{\alpha\beta}(f)\le A$. Each factor $(1+t^2)^{-1}$ has integral at most $6$: its integral on $[-1,1]$ is at most $2$, while on $2^k\le|t|<2^{k+1}$ it contributes at most $2\cdot2^k2^{-2k}$; the sum for $k\ge0$ is $4$. All functions are continuous and hence Borel measurable. For $n=1$ this proves $\int W^{-1}\le6$. For $n>1$, [F2] identifies integration of this Borel function against $\lambda_n$ with integration against $\lambda_{n-1}\times\lambda_1$; induction on $n$ and [F1] therefore give $\int W^{-1}\le6^n$.

fact_uses.text: [L1] On Borel sets, $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ agrees with $\lambda_{m+n}$. ([[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]])

proof_steps.claim: Let $A\in\mathcal L(\mathbb R^m)$ and $B\in\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$. By [L2], choose Borel cores $A_0,B_0$ and Borel null hulls $Z,W$ such that $A\mathbin\triangle A_0\subseteq Z$ and $B\mathbin\triangle B_0\subseteq W$. The slabs $Z\times\mathbb R^n$ and $\mathbb R^m\times W$ are Euclidean null: for example, $Z\times\mathbb R^n=\bigcup_{k\ge1}Z\times[-k,k]^n$, and [L1], [L3], and [L4] give Euclidean measure $0$ to each Borel rectangle in this union. Since $$(A\times B)\mathbin\triangle(A_0\times B_0)\subseteq(Z\times\mathbb R^n)\cup(\mathbb R^m\times W),$$ [L2] makes $A\times B$ Euclidean Lebesgue measurable.

Step 1.1 puts every measurable rectangle in $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^{m+n})$, so $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathcal L(\mathbb R^{m+n})$. Let $\rho$ be the restriction of $\lambda_{m+n}$ to this product sigma-algebra. For the rectangle in step 1.1, completeness [L5] and the null symmetric difference give $\rho(A\times B)=\lambda_{m+n}(A_0\times B_0)$; [L1] and [L2] identify this with $\lambda_m(A)\lambda_n(B)$. Thus $\rho$ has the product rectangle formula. By [L4] the factors are sigma-finite, so uniqueness in [L3] gives $\rho=\lambda_m\times\lambda_n$.

Because the product sigma-algebra is contained in the complete Euclidean Lebesgue sigma-algebra and the measures agree there by step 2.1, its completion is contained in $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^{m+n})$. Conversely, if $E\in\mathcal L(\mathbb R^{m+n})$, [L2] gives a Borel $C$ and a Borel null set $Z$ with $E\mathbin\triangle C\subseteq Z$. The Borel sets $C,Z$ belong to the product sigma-algebra, and [L1] and step 2.1 give $(\lambda_m\times\lambda_n)(Z)=\lambda_{m+n}(Z)=0$. Hence $E$ belongs to the completion of the product measure. The domains and measures therefore coincide, which is exactly the completion claim of [L6].

fact_uses.text: [F3] In finite Euclidean dimension, product Lebesgue measure agrees with Euclidean Lebesgue measure on Borel sets; nonnegative product integrals obey Tonelli. [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]].

proof_steps.claim: By [A1], take $d$ independent standard-normal coordinates $Z_1,\ldots,Z_d$. Their joint law is the product of the coordinate laws by [F2]. Thus, using [F1] and [F3], the vector $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)^T$ has Lebesgue density $f_Z(z)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\exp(-z^Tz/2).$

proof_steps.claim: The rational character formula is [F2]. For the real formula, restrict a smooth character to the coordinate circles; the rational supplier [F2] gives its integer vector \(\mathbf n\). The associated one-dimensional representation \(\mathbb C_{\chi_{\mathbf n}}\) is the tensor product of the coordinate representations \(\mathbb C_{\chi_i}^{\otimes n_i}\), interpreting negative powers as duals; taking associated bundles preserves this tensor-product isomorphism. Additivity and duality in [F3] give \(c_1(L_{\chi_{\mathbf n}})=\sum_i n_i u_i\) over \(\mathbb R\) as well, since the real generators in [F1] are the coefficient images of the same tautological Euler classes. The formula is unique because restriction to each coordinate circle recovers \(n_i\).

The empty product is \(1\), concatenation of two finite character lists multiplies their products, so \(1\in\mathscr S_T(k)\) and \(\mathscr S_T(k)\) is multiplicatively closed. For each nontrivial character \(\mathbf n\ne0\), step 1.1 gives the nonzero linear polynomial \(\sum_i n_i u_i\); a polynomial ring over a field is an integral domain, so every finite product of these classes remains nonzero. If \(r=0\), the generating list is empty and the set is \(\{1\}\). Hence \(0\notin\mathscr S_T(k)\) in all cases.

For a continuous left \(T\)-action on \(X\), the projection \(ET\times_T X\to BT\) makes singular cohomology a module over \(A_T(k)\) by pullback and cup product; pulling back first Chern classes defines the character actions used in the localization. The Borel space and module are defined for empty \(X\) as zero, and for \(r=0\) the localization changes no module because \(\mathscr S_T(k)=\{1\}\). This verifies the constructions in the Definition.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is the quotient topological group, each class has a representative in $[0,1)$, it is compact Hausdorff and second-countable, and its quotient map is open. proof_steps.claim:
By [A1], for any sequence $(A_n)$ of nonempty sets the family
$\mathcal F=\{A_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ has a choice function $g$. The composite
$n\mapsto g(A_n)$ is an indexed selector, even if some sets $A_n$ repeat.
Thus [F1] holds and supplies the countable-choice premise in the quotient
circle definition [F2].

For one factor, [F2] makes each quotient interval $q(I)$ open because
$q$ is open, and $q|_I$ is injective because $I$ has length less than $1$.
Its inverse chart is continuous: $q|_I$ is a continuous open bijection onto
$q(I)$. These charts cover the circle. If two charts overlap, local lifts
differ by an integer; this integer is locally constant, so each transition
map is locally a translation and hence smooth. The charts therefore define a
smooth one-manifold without boundary compatible with the quotient topology.

Addition and inversion on one factor are smooth in these charts. Near any
pair of points, choose local real lifts $x,y$ and an output chart around their
sum; after shrinking the input intervals, the coordinate expression for
addition is $x+y$ plus one fixed integer. Near any point, choose local lifts
for it and its inverse; the coordinate expression for inversion is $-x$ plus
one fixed integer. Both expressions are smooth. With the group law already
given by [F2], this is a Lie group by [F6]. Its underlying circle is compact,
Hausdorff and connected by [F2] and [F3], and it is abelian by the quotient
addition law.

The circle has a finite CW structure with one vertex $[0]$ and one open
$1$-cell, the image of $(0,1)$; its characteristic interval has both
endpoints attached to that vertex. For $T$, index product cells by subsets
$J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}$: coordinates in $J$ lie in the open $1$-cell and
all other coordinates equal $[0]$. Each cell is an open cube of dimension
$|J|$, its closure meets only cells indexed by subsets of $J$, and its
characteristic cube is the product of the factor characteristic intervals;
identify each closed cube with a closed disk of the same dimension. The map
$q^r:[0,1]^r\to T$ is a continuous surjection because every coordinate class
has a representative in $[0,1]$ by [F2]. If $K$ is closed in the cube,
then $K$ is compact, $q^r(K)$ is compact, and $q^r(K)$ is closed because $T$
is Hausdorff by [F2] and [F3]. Thus $q^r$ is a quotient map. It is the
characteristic map for the top cell. Every lower-cell characteristic cube is
obtained by precomposing $q^r$ with the continuous coordinate insertion that
fixes omitted coordinates at $0$, so the quotient topology of $q^r$ already
makes every characteristic map continuous; conversely $q^r$ is itself one of
those maps. Hence this quotient topology is exactly the weak topology
determined by the finitely many characteristic cubes. This gives a finite CW
structure with the identity as a $0$-cell. The singleton
identity is a subcomplex, so [F7] gives the homotopy extension property for
its inclusion.

proof_steps.claim: Pullback naturality [F13] shows that $d$ preserves the $T$-fixed forms. The normal representation is the direct sum of the complex character lines in step 3.1; the Euler class of a direct sum is the product because the product of the normalized Thom classes restricts to the positive generator on each direct-sum fiber and hence is its normalized Thom class. final_edge_fact_uses.text: [L1] Positive matrix-symbol second-order operators with the stated spectral heat data have the locally uniform rescaled tangent kernel, normalized tangent integral $\int k_x(w)\,dw=I$, and, for every $L>n$, the estimate $\|K_t(y,z)\|\le C_Lt^{-n/2}(1+d(y,z)/\sqrt t)^{-L}$. The proof constructs a frozen-coefficient kernel and its convergent Volterra correction; no scalar-principal-symbol assumption is used. [[lem-equivariant-rescaled-heat-kernel-extension]]

proof_steps.claim: Put $B_j=\sigma(d_j)(x,\xi)$, with $B_{-1}=B_N=0$. The principal symbol on $E^j$ of $\Delta$ is $p_j=B_j^*B_j+B_{j-1}B_{j-1}^*$. If its quadratic form vanishes on $v$, then $B_jv=0$ and $B_{j-1}^*v=0$; exactness gives $v\in\operatorname{im}B_{j-1}$ and also orthogonality to that image, hence $v=0$. Compactness of the unit cotangent sphere bundle gives $p_j(x,\xi)\ge c|\xi|^2I$ uniformly. Thus [L1] applies to $\Delta$, using exactly the given spectral heat data. Its principal symbol may be matrix-valued.

Write $n=\dim M$ and $J_x$ for the normal-coordinate volume density. For $y=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,v)$ in the chosen neighborhood, [L1] and step 1.1 imply that $t^{n/2}J_x(\sqrt t\,v)\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g^j K_t^j(g^{-1}y,y))$ tends pointwise to $\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g^j|_{E_x^j}\,k_{x,1}^j(dg_x^{-1}v,v))$. Simplicity makes $dg_x^{-1}-I$ invertible. Local distance comparison in the normal chart therefore gives $d(g^{-1}y,y)\ge c_x\sqrt t\,|v|$. Choose $L>n$; bounded density, unitary $\rho_g$ and [L1] bound the extended-by-zero rescaled density by $C(1+c_x|v|)^{-L}$, integrable on $T_xM$. Outside these neighborhoods compactness gives $d(g^{-1}y,y)\ge\delta>0$, so [L1] bounds the full complementary trace integral by $C t^{(L-n)/2}\to0$. By [F2], the heat-supertrace limit is consequently the sum of these tangent integrals. No uniform-integral-bound-to-convergence implication is used.

Since $dg_x$ is orthogonal, $|\det(dg_x^{-1}-I)|=|\det(I-dg_x)|$. The change of variables $w=(dg_x^{-1}-I)v$ therefore contributes $|\det_{\mathbb R}(I-dg_x)|^{-1}$. By [L1], the constant-coefficient tangent heat kernel has integral $I_{E_x^\bullet}$. Its graded fiber trace after composition with $\rho_g$ is $\sum_j(-1)^j\operatorname{tr}(\rho_g|_{E_x^j})$. For $n=0$, the tangent integral and determinant are both the empty-dimensional values $1$, so the same expression holds. Summing the finitely many contributions proves the stated limit.

proof_steps.claim: Work in one precompact bundle chart and write $p(y,\xi)=\sum A^{ij}(y)\xi_i\xi_j$. The matrices need not commute. For a parameter derivative, the matrix exponential satisfies $\partial e^{-p}=-\int_0^1e^{-(1-s)p}(\partial p)e^{-sp}\,ds$, obtained by differentiating the matrix ODE defining the exponential. Iterating this identity and differentiating in $\xi$ expresses every derivative in $y,\xi$ as finitely many simplex integrals of products of polynomial derivatives of $p$ and exponential factors whose time lengths sum to one. Since $p\ge c'|\xi|^2I$ uniformly on the chart closure, the product norm is at most a polynomial in $|\xi|$ times $e^{-c'|\xi|^2}$. Thus $e^{-p(y,\cdot)}$ is a uniformly bounded smooth Schwartz family. By [F1] its inverse transform $k_y(w)$ has all uniformly bounded Schwartz seminorms, and $\int k_y(w)\,dw=e^{-p(y,0)}=I$. This uses Fourier inversion on Schwartz functions, not an exchange of an undamped double Fourier integral.

Let $\kappa_i$ be finitely many charts with smooth unitary frames, and let $\phi_i$ be a partition subordinate to compact subsets of those charts. Choose smooth cutoffs $\chi_i(y,z)$ supported where both points lie in chart $i$, equal to one near $y=z$ whenever $z\in\operatorname{supp}\phi_i$. Write volume as $w_i(z)\,d\kappa_i(z)$. Define $Z_t(y,z)$ in these frames by the finite sum of $\phi_i(z)\chi_i(y,z)w_i(z)^{-1}t^{-n/2}k_{i,z}((\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z))/\sqrt t)$, interpreting each summand as a bundle map. In each summand the principal coefficients are frozen at the source $z$. Step 1.1, local equivalence of chart distance and $d$, and cutoff support give $\|Z_t(y,z)\|\le C_LH_{t,L}(y,z)$, where $H_{t,L}=t^{-n/2}(1+d(y,z)/\sqrt t)^{-L}$. Moreover $Z_tf\to f$ in $L^2$ for smooth $f$: put $\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z)=\sqrt t\,v$, use the uniform integrable Schwartz bound, and use $\sum_i\phi_i=1$ and $\int k_{i,y}=I$. For $R_t=(\partial_t+P_y)Z_t$, the frozen principal part cancels $\partial_t$. The remaining principal term contains $A(y)-A(z)=O(d(y,z))$ and two derivatives of the frozen kernel; lower terms contain at most one derivative. The bound $d(y,z)t^{-1}H_{t,L+1}\le t^{-1/2}H_{t,L}$ therefore gives $\|R_t(y,z)\|\le C_Lt^{-1/2}H_{t,L}(y,z)$. Derivatives of cutoffs are supported away from the diagonal and obey the same bound by choosing additional Schwartz decay.

Fix $x$ and put $y=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,a)$, $z=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,b)$. In a chart, Taylor expansion gives $(\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z))/\sqrt t\to d\kappa_i|_x(a-b)$, the frozen symbol tends to $p_i(x,\xi)$, and all frame maps, partition weights and density factors tend to their values at $x$. Linear change of cotangent variables in the absolutely convergent Fourier integral transforms each limiting chart expression into $\phi_i(x)k_x(a-b)$: the coordinate Jacobian cancels $w_i(x)$ because normal-coordinate volume density at $x$ is one. Summing gives $k_x(a-b)$. All convergences are uniform on bounded $a,b$ by step 1.1. By step 4.1, $t^{n/2}\|K_t-Z_t\|\le C\sqrt t$, so it has zero limit. This proves the rescaled limit and all assertions for $n>0$. If $M$ is empty the claims are vacuous; for $n=0$, compact $M$ is finite and differential operators act separately on its fibers, so ordinary matrix exponentiation gives exactly the asserted finite-dimensional limit.

\[

for \(p\in M\) and \(v,w\in T_pM\).

Every character is nontrivial because the fixed eigenspace has been removed. If \(\psi=\chi\), this integral is \(1\). If \(\psi
e\chi\), then \(	heta=\overline\chi\psi\) is a nontrivial character; choose \(t_0\in T\) with \(	heta(t_0)
e1\). Translation invariance gives \(I=\int_T	heta(t)\,d\mu(t)=\int_T	heta(t_0t)\,d\mu(t)=	heta(t_0)I\), so \(I=0\). The character averages are therefore exactly the eigenspace projections. If \(r=0\), the action is trivial, \(F=M\), and \(\nu_F=0\), so the weight assertion is vacuous. If \(M\) is empty, all asserted submanifolds and bundles are empty. Otherwise the construction applies componentwise and uses no assumption on connectedness of \(M\).

proof_steps.claim: Smoothness of the needed primitive does not require a theorem about varying complex structures. Choose smooth unit quaternionic frames of $Q_x$ on a base neighborhood and a smooth unitary frame of $E$. These identify the vertical problem exactly with the fixed $SU(2)$-invariant Hermitian $\mathcal O(-2)$ problem on $\mathbb CP^1$, componentwise in $E_x$. Set $B=\bar\partial^*G$ on vertical degree one. By [F3], $\bar\partial B=I-\Pi$, and by [F2] its degree-zero kernel is zero. The estimates [F4] and the first-order nature of $\bar\partial^*$ give $B:H^m\to H^{m+1}$ bounded for each $m$. For jointly smooth $f(x,t)$, base difference quotients converge in every fibre $H^m$ uniformly on compact base sets, by the Taylor formula and compactness of the fibre. Applying the fixed bounded $B$ shows $\partial_x^\beta(Bf)=B(\partial_x^\beta f)$ at every order in every $H^{m+1}$. Sobolev embedding on the fixed two-dimensional compact fibre, with arbitrarily large $m$, gives joint smoothness in $(x,t)$. For the horizontal coefficient problem, choose also a smooth unit quaternionic frame of $Q_x^\perp$. Together the two quaternionic frames give a smooth $Sp(2)$ transformation from a fixed pair of planes to $(Q_x,Q_x^\perp)$. Its complex-linear action on $\mathbb CP^3$ is holomorphic and preserves the Fubini–Study and tautological metrics. It therefore transports the horizontal quotient, its vertical Bott operator and its induced metric to the fixed $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}$ problem identified below. That inverse is likewise one fixed bounded operator componentwise, so the same derivative argument applies. Thus no moving-cokernel inverse or unproved parametric Green assertion is used.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] The fixed compact fibre Green inverse is bounded $H^m\to H^{m+2}$ for every integer $m\ge0$. [[thm-sobolev-compactness-and-elliptic-estimates-give-fredholm-hodge-decomposition]]

proof_steps.claim: For the global metric splitting, the mixed component of $\bar\partial(s\sigma)$ is a vertical degree-one form with coefficient $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$. On a fibre it has a unique vertical primitive by [F4]. The fixed-fibre $B=\bar\partial^*G$ construction and smooth-parameter difference-quotient argument in [F2], with the estimates [F5], make that primitive smooth over the base. The same fibrewise uniqueness makes it agree across frame and chart changes. Denote the horizontal correction by $\phi(s)$; then $\psi(s)=s\sigma+\phi(s)$ has zero mixed differential. If $s$ is the image of a closed representative $\alpha$, [F2]'s decomposition and closedness say that its horizontal remainder solves this same mixed equation. The difference is fibrewise holomorphic in $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}\otimes E_x$, hence zero by [F4]. Thus $\psi(s)=\alpha-\bar\partial_F\gamma$ is closed for a class image. The differential can still have a horizontal degree-two component for arbitrary $s$; the curvature component of the metric splitting is retained.

proof_steps.claim:
Fix the smooth reference connection $A_0$ from the configuration data and set $h=A-A_0\in H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$. Therefore $K_A:=\Delta_A-\Delta_{A_0}$ is a finite sum of terms of the forms $(
abla_{A_0}h)\xi$, $h
abla_{A_0}\xi$, and $h^2\xi$. These terms define a bounded map $H^{k+1}	o H^{k-1}$. They are compact: $(
abla_{A_0}h)\xi$ factors through the compact inclusion $H^{k+1}\hookrightarrow H^{k-1}$ followed by multiplication in the algebra $H^{k-1}$; $h
abla_{A_0}\xi$ and $h^2\xi$ first map boundedly into $H^k$ and then use the compact inclusion $H^k\hookrightarrow H^{k-1}$. Here $k-1>d/2$, so the needed multiplication bounds follow from [F8].

Choose $\varepsilon$ so that the resulting $H^{k+1}$ term is absorbed into the left side. This yields $\|\xi\|_{H^{k+1}}\le C_A'(\|\Delta_A\xi\|_{H^{k-1}}+\|\xi\|_{L^2})$.

On each finite Borel approximation, the first Chern class of the trivialized line is zero. Since $\chi$ is nontrivial, $u_\chi\in S_T$ is invertible after localization. For any class $\beta$, its localized image satisfies $\beta/1=(u_\chi\cap\beta)/u_\chi=0$ by step 2.1. There are finitely many components by [F1], so \(H_T^*(F;k)\) and its localization split into the finite product of the component rings treated in step 3.1. A finite tuple of units is a unit componentwise. If \(F=\varnothing\), its cohomology is the zero ring and its unique element is a unit; if a normal component has rank zero, its product in step 2.1 is \(1\). These cases include \(r=0\), trivial actions, and empty \(M\).

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] On a bounded extension domain, $W^{k,2}$ is a Banach algebra when $2k>d$, and the higher-order embedding gives $H^k\hookrightarrow C^1$ when $k>d/2+1$. proof_steps.claim: Localize by the fixed finite partition and extend each compactly supported coefficient by zero into a bounded Euclidean ball. For $p=2$, $2k>d$; [F2] makes each localized $H^k$ coefficient a Banach algebra and gives its $C^1$ representative when $k>d/2+1$. The finite sum of these estimates proves the same algebra and embedding bounds for sections, matrix-valued functions, and forms in the chosen bundle atlas.

The finite-dimensional matrix exponential is smooth, has derivative the identity at zero on $\mathfrak{su}(N)$, and maps $\mathfrak{su}(N)$ into $SU(N)$. In the Banach algebra from step 2.1 its power series and every termwise derivative converge in $H^{k+1}$ on a sufficiently small ball, since the algebra norm is submultiplicative after an equivalent rescaling. The matrix logarithm series converges on a neighborhood of the identity; for a unitary matrix sufficiently close to identity its logarithm is anti-Hermitian, and its trace is zero because the determinant is one and the sum of the small eigenvalue angles lies in $2\pi\mathbb Z$. Hence pointwise $\exp$ and $\log$ give inverse smooth maps between neighborhoods of zero in $H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ and the identity in $\mathcal G_{k+1}$. The inverse-function theorem [F3] also supplies these local Banach charts. Their translated charts cover the group; changes of chart are smooth because the transition functions of $\operatorname{Ad}P$ act by smooth conjugation and the multiplication is a bounded bilinear Sobolev map. The pointwise product and inverse therefore close on $\mathcal G_{k+1}$ and are smooth, giving the asserted Hilbert Lie group.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F6] The finite-atlas Sobolev product bounds hold in every integer order $0\le r\le k$: $\|fg\|_{H^r}\le C\|f\|_{H^k}\|g\|_{H^r}$. [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]], [[cor-sobolev-algebra-above-the-critical-index]], [[lem-qftx-gauge-sobolev-calculus]]

proof_steps.claim: Let $B_j=A_j^{u_j}$ and work in the fixed finite atlas. The local action formula gives $du_j=u_jB_j-A_ju_j$. Since $u_j$ is unitary, its pointwise matrix norm is bounded uniformly. If a uniform $H^r$ bound holds for some $0\le r\le k$, [F6] bounds both products on the right in $H^r$; hence $du_j$ is bounded in $H^r$ and $u_j$ is bounded in $H^{r+1}$. Induction through $r=k$ gives a uniform $H^{k+1}$ bound.

Conversely, let $g\in SU(N)$ commute with every element of $\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)$. Two paths give the same value because their concatenation has holonomy commuting with $g$. In local coordinates this gives a parallel section $u$ with $u(p_m)=g$. It is $C^1$ since $A\in H^k\hookrightarrow C^1$ and the parameter-dependent parallel-transport ODE is $C^1$ in the endpoint. The equation $du=uA-Au$, the bounds [F6], and induction on $r=0,1,\ldots,k$ show $u\in H^{k+1}$: starting with its $C^1$ local coefficients, if $u\in H^r$ then the right side is in $H^r$, so all first derivatives are in $H^r$ and $u\in H^{r+1}$. The coefficients depend smoothly on parameters as maps into $C^\alpha_w$, since all their parameter derivatives have uniform bounds on compact subsets. The inverse $(1+K(p))^{-1}$ is the uniformly convergent Neumann series; the identity $L(p+h)-L(p)=-L(p+h)(K(p+h)-K(p))L(p)$ for $L=(1+K)^{-1}$ gives its first derivative in operator norm, and induction gives derivatives of every order. For each such derivative, the fixed-point equation and [F1] gain one $w$ derivative; induction gives all mixed $C^{m,\alpha}_w$ derivatives on the same radius, because only the inverse in the initial $C^\alpha$ space needs smallness. If $A_j$ is holomorphic in an untouched coordinate, $K$ has zero antiholomorphic parameter derivative by [F2], and differentiating the inverse identity gives the same for $g$.

Gauge by this $g$ on the smaller disk. The transformed coefficient is $A_i'=g^{-1}(\partial_{\bar z_i}g+A_i g)$, and $A_j'=0$. The square-zero condition in a smooth frame is $\partial_{\bar z_i}A_j-\partial_{\bar z_j}A_i+[A_i,A_j]=0$, and it is preserved by the gauge transformation by direct conjugation of $(D'')^2$. Therefore every remaining $A_i'$ is holomorphic in $z_j$. Kill the next coordinate by steps 1.1–2.1 with a cutoff only in that coordinate. Their holomorphic-parameter assertion preserves $A_j'=0$. Continue through the finitely many coordinates, shrinking the respective coordinate disks as needed. The product of the resulting smooth invertible gauges has all transformed coefficients zero, proving the required local frame.

If $G$ and $H$ are two such frames, $D''G=D''H=0$ gives $\bar\partial(G^{-1}H)=0$. For smooth scalar functions this implies holomorphy: the one-variable Cauchy formula applies with the other variables fixed, and its iterated integral on a product of small circles gives a locally convergent joint power series. Thus the transition matrices are holomorphic, giving [F4]'s bundle structure; any other structure with the same $D''$ has the same class of holomorphic frames, hence agrees. In these frames an intertwining smooth bundle map has matrix $M$ with $\bar\partial M=0$, so is holomorphic by the same calculation, and the converse follows by the Leibniz rule. Rank zero is immediate and the finite gauge induction covers every positive finite rank.

proof_steps.claim: Stabilize a rank-one raw datum by $W'=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C$, $I'=(I,0)$ and $J'=(J,0)^t$, retaining $V,B_1,B_2$. Then $I'J'=IJ$, $I'I'^\dagger=II^\dagger$ and $J'^\dagger J'=J^\dagger J$. The word span is unchanged and $\ker J'=\ker J$, so both moments and regularity are unchanged. On the finite stereographic chart the raw kernel matrix annihilates the added framing line, and its orthogonal projection is $P_1\oplus1$. Thus [A1] produces a smooth rank-two ASD connection whose restriction to that chart is a line connection plus the flat added line and whose charge is $q_2=-k$. By [F2] its determinant curvature vanishes. On that chart this curvature is exactly the first line's curvature, so the whole rank-two curvature is zero there. Smoothness makes it zero also at infinity, hence $q_2=0$ and $k=0$. Thus no regular rank-one zero-FI datum exists for $k>0$, conditional on the exact retained rank-two input. By [F6], a regular complex rank-one orbit would have such a zero-real-moment representative, so the same emptiness conclusion applies to the complex regular quotient.

A regular raw first-order family with $k>0$ would reduce to a prohibited datum from step 1.1, so none exists; the connection family for $k>0$ has no allowable special fiber by step 1.2. At $k=0$ the rank-zero internal $D$-module and all raw maps are uniquely zero, with trivial internal gauge group. Its forward monad is the constant framed line and its forward connection is $d$, also over $D$. Step 3.1 supplies a unique framed gauge from every first-order connection object to this one. Thus this explicit construction is an equivalence of the two first-order groupoids. Reduction and involution-preserving scalar maps commute with it, because the zero datum and the constant line pull back to themselves and the framed trivializing isomorphism is unique. The same argument after complexifying the real tangent spaces gives zero complexified tangent spaces; it does not assert a correspondence for arbitrary complex connections without the Hermitian real condition.

Stabilization intertwines $T$ with the rank-two compact action having framing weights $(h,1)$. In the zero-charge classification, inverse rotations and framing changes send a flat framed object to a flat framed object; the unique framed parallel trivialization identifies it with the same point. Its uniqueness also makes the first-order identifications equivariant. They hold for every first-order Hermitian family defined above, hence also for the subset satisfying the exact locally-free/cohomology-base-change hypotheses retained in [A1]; no extra family statement is obtained from an orbit-set bijection. Positive-FI rank-one stable data and their non-locally-free sheaves and formal fixed-point series were not used in any step.

proof_steps.claim: If $K=\varnothing$ or $f(K)\subseteq\mathcal A_\infty^*$, the constant homotopy suffices. Otherwise realize the given finite simplicial complex by its barycentric coordinates as a compact subset of $\mathbb R^q$, taking $q\ge1$. Let $U=f^{-1}(\mathcal A_\infty^*)$, an open neighborhood of $L$ by [F2]. Choose nested relatively open neighborhoods $U_0,U_1,U_2$ of $L$ in $K$ with $\overline U_0\subset U_1$, $\overline U_1\subset U_2$, and $\overline U_2\subset U$; if $L=\varnothing$ take them empty. The compact family $f(\overline U_2)$ is uniformly stable under a sufficiently small $C^1$ perturbation: each member has the finite-loop positive margin in [F2], and a finite subcover gives one positive tolerance. Include this $C^1$ norm among the finitely many seminorms in which all forthcoming approximations are to be small.

Choose a smooth ambient cutoff $0\le\theta\le1$ which is zero on a neighborhood of $\overline U_0$ and one on a neighborhood of the disjoint compact set $K\setminus U_1$. Such a cutoff follows from finitely many ambient bumps separating the two compact sets. Define on $K$ the continuous family $h(s)=f(s)+\theta(s)(g(s)-f(s))$. The straight interpolation from $f$ to $h$ is fixed near $L$ and is $\delta$-small in every selected seminorm. By the uniform $C^1$ margin in step 1.1, choosing $\delta$ small ensures it is irreducible on $\overline U_2$. Its closed reducible-parameter set $R=\{s\in K:h(s)\notin\mathcal A_\infty^*\}$ is compact and contained in $K\setminus U_2$, hence in the ambient open region where $\theta=1$ and $h=g$ on $K$. If $R$ is empty the first interpolation already proves the result. Otherwise choose an ambient open $W$ with compact closure in $V\cap\{\theta=1\}$, containing $R$ and avoiding a neighborhood of $L$, and a smooth cutoff $0\le\chi\le1$ with compact support $T\subset W$, positive on $R$. All subsequent holonomy calculations use the ambient family $g$ on $W$; on the actual parameter subset $K\cap W$ this is exactly $h$.

Define on all of $K$ the final family $h_v(s)=h(s)+\chi(s)\sum_{j,a}v_{j,a}b_{j,a}(s)$, with the added term zero off $W$. The compact support $T$ and its spatial smoothness make this term continuous in every section seminorm, and its value uniformly small in any specified finite list by taking $v$ sufficiently small. If $\chi(s)>0$, then $s\in W$ and $h(s)=g(s)$, so $h_v(s)$ has the holonomy tuple $\Phi(s,v)$, which has no common invariant proper subspace by step 9.1. Therefore $h_v(s)$ is irreducible. If $\chi(s)=0$, then $s\notin R$ since $\chi$ is positive on $R$, so $h_v(s)=h(s)$ was already irreducible. The straight perturbation homotopy from $h$ to $h_v$ is fixed on an open neighborhood of $L$. Concatenate it with the interpolation in step 3.1. Choose $\delta$ and then $v$ within half of each requested seminorm tolerance; the triangle inequality gives the asserted bounds relative to the original $f$ for the entire concatenated homotopy. All formulas are global on $K$, so faces and cofaces agree automatically.

proof_steps.claim: If $T(f,\omega)=0$ with $(f,\omega)\in H^1$, step 3.1 and weak regularity [F3] make both entries smooth and harmonic. By [F2], $f$ is constant and the harmonic two-form is zero, giving a one-dimensional complex kernel. The same vanishing has an elementary check: $d^*\omega=0$ and $*\omega=\omega$ imply $d\omega=0$; since $H^2=0$, write $\omega=d\beta$, and [F4] gives $\|\omega\|_2^2=\int\omega\wedge\overline\omega=\int d(\beta\wedge\overline\omega)=0$. For $T^*\alpha=0$, one has $d^*\alpha=0$ and $d\alpha$ anti-self-dual; hence $\|d\alpha\|_2^2=-\int d\alpha\wedge d\overline\alpha=0$ by [F4]. Thus $\alpha$ is harmonic and is zero by $H^1=0$. The Green inverse $G_1:L^2\to H^2$ of $\Delta_1$, which exists without a kernel by [F2]–[F3], gives the bounded right inverse $T^*G_1:L^2\to H^1$ of $T$. The range is therefore all $L^2$, the kernel is finite, and $T$ is Fredholm with index $1$. The unitary maps in step 2.1 transfer this conclusion to $D^+_{A_+}$.

For the full Dirac operator use the block $\mathscr D=\begin{pmatrix}0&T^*\\T&0\end{pmatrix}$ under the unitary identifications. Its square is the direct sum of the Hodge Laplacians in step 3.1, with domain $H^2$ by [F3]. It is symmetric on $H^1$ by smooth density. For $P=\mathscr D^2$, [F3] applied to the positive operator $P+1$ gives its inverse $B:L^2\to H^2$: its kernel is zero by the identity $((P+1)u,u)=\|\mathscr D u\|^2+\|u\|^2$. Then $(\mathscr D\mp i)B$ maps $L^2$ to $H^1$ and is a right inverse of $\mathscr D\pm i$. If $v\in\operatorname{dom}\mathscr D^*$, choose $u\in H^1$ with $(\mathscr D+i)u=(\mathscr D^*+i)v$; then $v-u$ is in $\ker(\mathscr D^*+i)=\operatorname{ran}(\mathscr D-i)^\perp=0$. Thus the adjoint domain is $H^1$ and $\mathscr D$ is selfadjoint there. The same identities show its squared domain is $H^2$, using weak regularity when $u\in H^1$ and $\mathscr D u\in H^1$.
