Under this identification dp(D) is exactly the span of H₁,H₂ in step 1.1: write X_z=((z₁,-bar_z₂),(z₂,bar_z₁)) and solve v(1,w)^T=0. Therefore the restricted smooth connection has F(H₁,H₂)=0 for every w, so all three self-dual coefficients in step 1.1 vanish. Hence it is ASD. Evaluation intertwines the original holomorphic operator on E with the reconstructed vertical/horizontal Dolbeault operator: it is holomorphic vertically, and on D its derivative is exactly the canonical relative derivative δ by step 3.1. These directions generate the (0,1) tangent in step 1.1, proving equality of the full operators, not just of underlying bundles.

Starting from A in step 1.1, its constant real-line sections identify the reconstructed smooth H with E. Along every alpha-plane the recovered connection has the same derivative as A; the cotangent uniqueness in step 3.1 makes the full connections equal. The unitary reality pairing and framing also agree. Starting from a Ward bundle, step 4.1 proves evaluation is a holomorphic isomorphism from the reconstructed pullback to the original bundle, and step 5.2 preserves its reality pairing and metric. These constructions and identities apply to morphisms as well, so descend to inverse maps on based unitary gauge and framed holomorphic isomorphism classes. No irreducibility or absence of parallel sections was used.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] For every continuous map from a finite polyhedron into $\mathcal A_\infty$, with irreducible values on a subpolyhedron, the relative avoidance lemma supplies a homotopy fixed on that subpolyhedron and an open neighborhood of it whose endpoint is entirely irreducible. Its complete argument and exact batch-56 inputs were inspected; the configuration and stabilizer suppliers now have current ready Step 1 records ([[lem-qftx-relative-finite-parameter-irreducible-avoidance]]).

proof_steps.claim: The affine space $\mathcal A_\infty$ contains $A_0$. Apply [F2] to the constant map from a one-point polyhedron with empty subpolyhedron and value $A_0$. Its endpoint is an element of $\mathcal A_\infty^*$, proving nonemptiness.

Let $A,B\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The affine path $\gamma(t)=(1-t)A+tB$ is continuous in the Fréchet topology and has irreducible endpoints. Apply [F2] with $K=I$ and $L=\{0,1\}$. The resulting endpoint path remains in $\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and fixes both endpoints, so the locus is path-connected.

Apply [F2] to $F$ with $K=D^{j+1}$ and $L=\partial D^{j+1}=S^j$. Its boundary is already irreducible, so the endpoint is a map $G:D^{j+1}\to\mathcal A_\infty^*$ agreeing with $u$ on the boundary. Choose the based point $x_0\in S^j$ with $u(x_0)=A$. Since the disk is convex, $C_t(x)=(1-t)x+tx_0$ remains in the disk and fixes $x_0$. Then $G(C_t(x))$ is a homotopy from $G$ to the constant map at $A$ that fixes $x_0$ and remains in $\mathcal A_\infty^*$. Restricting it to $S^j$ gives a based nullhomotopy of $u$; by [F3], its class in $\pi_j(\mathcal A_\infty^*,A)$ is zero. Since $j$ and $u$ were arbitrary, every stated homotopy group vanishes.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F4] Proper pushforward is functorial, closed inclusions are proper, and cap product with an equivariant cohomology class sends $[X]_T$ to Borel–Moore degree $2d-q$. [[def-qftx-localized-equivariant-borel-moore-data]]

proof_steps.claim: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a proper $T$-equivariant map between smooth separated finite-type varieties with finite invariant affine covers and proper fixed loci $F_X,F_Y$. Its restriction $f^T:F_X\to F_Y$ is proper, and the square formed by $i_X,i_Y,f^T,f$ commutes because $f$ sends fixed points to fixed points. Functoriality of proper Borel–Moore pushforward gives $f_*i_{X*}=i_{Y*}f^T_*$. After localization both $i_{X*}$ and $i_{Y*}$ are isomorphisms by [F2], so applying their inverses and then the proper traces proves $p_{Y*}^{\mathrm{loc}}f_*=p_{X*}^{\mathrm{loc}}$. If $X\to\mathrm{pt}$ itself is proper, then $p_{F*}=p_{X*}i_*$; composing with $i_*^{-1}$ proves $p_*^{\mathrm{loc}}=p_{X*}$.

Let $ eta=(i_*)^{-1}(\alpha\cap[X]_T)$. On each component, the complex orientation and refined Gysin map give $i_a^!(\alpha\cap[X]_T)=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Since $\alpha\cap[X]_T=i_* eta$, the self-intersection formula [F3] gives $e_T(
u_a)\cap eta_a=i_a^*\alpha\cap[F_a]_T$. Properness of $F_a$ makes $e_T(
u_a)$ invertible after localization by [F3], hence $ eta_a=(i_a^*\alpha/e_T(
u_a))\cap[F_a]_T$. Applying $p_{a*}$ and summing the finitely many components yields the displayed formula. The degree is $2d-q$: division by the degree-$2c_a$ Euler class lowers the localized cohomological degree of the insertion from $q$ to $q-2c_a$, and capping with the degree-$2d_a$ fundamental class gives $2d_a-(q-2c_a)=2d-q$.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F3] For the stated Sobolev index, the smooth irreducible projection $\mathcal A_\infty^*\to\mathcal A_\infty^*/\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty$ is a locally trivial topological principal $\overline{\mathcal G}_\infty$-bundle with its actual $C^\infty$ quotient topology; the Sobolev irreducible locus $\mathcal A_k^*$ is open. [[thm-qftx-sobolev-smooth-irreducible-gauge-bundle]]

proof_steps.claim: Choose the fixed integer $k>r/2+1$. The smooth clause of [F3], applied with the configuration data [F2], makes $q_*$ a locally trivial principal $\overline{\mathcal G}^\infty(P)$-bundle. By [F4], its total space is nonempty, path connected, and has $\pi_j=0$ for every $j\ge1$, so it is weakly contractible in the sense used in [F6]. For a constant central gauge section $u=\zeta I_N$, the local action formula gives $A^u=A$ because $u^{-1}Au=A$ and $du=0$; hence reduced and full gauge groups have the same orbits on $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$.

The locus $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$ is gauge invariant: in the chosen frame, the based holonomy subgroup of $A^u$ is $u(p_m)^{-1}\operatorname{Hol}_{p_m}(A)u(p_m)$, so it has the same invariant subspaces up to conjugation. It is open: by [F2], the inclusion $\mathcal A^\infty(P)\hookrightarrow\mathcal A_k(P)$ is continuous, as each fixed $H^k$ norm is bounded by finitely many smooth derivative seminorms on the finite compact atlas. The smooth irreducible locus is the inverse image of the Sobolev irreducible locus, which is open by [F3]. The full orbit projection $q$ is open because, for any open $U\subseteq\mathcal A^\infty(P)$, its saturation $q^{-1}(q(U))=\bigcup_{u\in\mathcal G^\infty(P)}U\cdot u$ is open. For fixed smooth $u$, the map $A\mapsto u^{-1}Au+u^{-1}du$ is continuous in every finite-atlas derivative seminorm by the Leibniz rule; its inverse is the same formula for $u^{-1}$, so each gauge translate is a homeomorphism. Therefore $q(\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P))$ is open and $q|_{\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)}$ is an open quotient map onto this subset. The reduced and full actions have the same orbits there, so their quotient topologies identify the reduced orbit space homeomorphically with $q(\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P))$; this proves the claim about $\iota$ in the Statement. If $q$ had a continuous section, its restriction to this open subset would take each irreducible orbit to a point in that same orbit, hence into $\mathcal A^{\infty,*}(P)$. Via the stated homeomorphism, this would give a continuous section of $q_*$, contradicting step 3.1. Thus $q$ has no continuous section.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F7] For every integer $r>d/2$, multiplication is bounded on $H^r$, and the embeddings $H^s\hookrightarrow C^m$ hold when $s>d/2+m$; the finite-atlas estimates used in the smoothness bootstrap follow by localization and Hölder. [[cor-sobolev-algebra-above-the-critical-index]], [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]]

proof_steps.claim: Apply the inverse-function theorem [F4] to $\Phi_A(s,u):=s^u$ on the local Banach product $S_{A,\varepsilon}\times\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ near $(A,e)$; its derivative is $L_A$ from step 1.2. Shrink $\varepsilon$ so the slice remains in the open irreducible locus. At $(s,e)$, for $s=A+a$, the derivative is $L_s(b,\xi)=b+d_s\xi$ on $b\in\ker d_A^*$; this differs from $L_A$ only by $(b,\xi)\mapsto[a,\xi]$. Its operator norm is at most $C\|a\|_{H^k}$ by [F7]. Choose $\varepsilon$ so $C\varepsilon\|L_A^{-1}\|<1$; then [F5] makes $L_s$ an isomorphism for every $s$ in the slice. At an arbitrary $(s,u_0)$, write $u=u_0v$ near $u_0$ and use $s^{u_0v}=(s^{u_0})^v$. Applying the inverse action by $u_0$ to the target tangent and changing the gauge tangent by the invertible adjoint action identifies this derivative with $L_s$. Hence the derivative is an isomorphism at every point of the slice product, and the inverse-function theorem makes $\Phi_A$ a local diffeomorphism throughout.

For the smooth-space clause, fix now a smooth irreducible center $A\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and use the Banach slice and trivialization established in step 4.1. Put $U_A=\Phi_A(S_{A,\varepsilon}\times\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1})$ and $V_A=\pi_k(S_{A,\varepsilon})$. Since $U_A$ is open in $\mathcal A_k^*$, $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open in the stated $C^\infty$ topology; set $S_A^\infty=S_{A,\varepsilon}\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and $V_A^\infty=\pi_\infty(S_A^\infty)$. For a smooth $B\in U_A$, its unique reduced gauge class from step 4.1 has a representative $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$. It satisfies $d_A^*(B^{u^{-1}}-A)=0$. Locally in a bundle frame, write $C_j=uB_j u^{-1}-(\partial_j u)u^{-1}-A_j$. Substitution in $d_A^*C=0$, use of $\partial_i(u^{-1})=-u^{-1}(\partial_i u)u^{-1}$, and multiplication on the right by $u$ isolate the equation $g^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j u=R(A,B,g;u,u^{-1},du)$ on each chart. Every term in $R$ is a finite product of smooth coefficients (including first derivatives of $A,B$) and factors among $u,u^{-1},du$; hence the principal operator is the scalar smooth Laplacian on each matrix entry. If $u\in H^{r+1}$ for $r\ge k$, then this right-hand side lies in $H^r$ by [F7] and the smooth coefficient bounds. Elliptic regularity [F6] gives $u\in H^{r+2}$. Iteration proves $u$ smooth; changing its representative by an element of the finite center preserves smoothness. Thus every smooth point of the Banach saturation has a smooth trivialization representative, and $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*=\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$.

Suppose smooth $B_j\to B$ in $C^\infty$ within $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The Banach trivialization from step 4.1 gives convergence of their slice representatives in $H^k$ and of their reduced gauge classes in $H^{k+1}$. In a quotient chart around the limiting class from step 1.1, choose lifts $u_j,u$ that converge in $H^{k+1}$; this is possible because the finite center acts by disjoint translates. The equation in step 5.2 and elliptic estimates [F6] bootstrap convergence: if $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+1}$, then the assumed $C^\infty$ convergence gives $B_j\to B$ in $H^{r+1}$, and [F7] makes the right-hand sides converge in $H^r$. Apply the elliptic estimate to $u_j-u$, using also their already known $H^{k+1}$ convergence for the $L^2$ term, to get $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+2}$. Induction gives convergence in every Sobolev order, which on compact $M$ is the $C^\infty$ section topology. The slice representatives converge in $C^\infty$ by their action formula. Conversely the forward action is continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology by multiplication and differentiation of smooth sections. The saturation $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open, and $V_A^\infty$ is open in the quotient because the quotient map is open: the saturation of any open set is a union of its open gauge translates. The restricted map $S_A^\infty\times\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty\to\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$ is therefore a homeomorphism for the actual quotient topology, and it is equivariant. This proves the smooth-space topological principal bundle claim.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]] and [[thm-extension-theorem-for-bounded-smooth-domains]]: on each bounded disk, $W^{2,p}$ for $p>2$ supplies $C^{1,\beta}$ representatives for $0<\beta<1-2/p$.

proof_steps.claim: To obtain derivative decay, fix $\alpha<\alpha'<\sqrt\kappa$ and use step 3.3 at rate $\alpha'$. On each unit ball centered at large $z$, both $w$ and $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ are $O(e^{-\alpha'|z|})$. By [F3] and [F5], $w$ has a $C^{1,\beta}$ norm of that order on the concentric half-ball for some $\beta>0$. Thus the right-hand side has a $C^{0,\beta}$ norm of the same order, and [F4] gives $C^{2,\beta}$ decay on a smaller ball. Inductively, for each multi-index $\gamma$, differentiating $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ gives $\Delta D^\gamma w=\kappa e^{-w}D^\gamma w+G_\gamma$, where $G_\gamma$ is a finite sum of products of lower derivatives of $w$ and is exponentially small by the induction hypothesis. Applying [F3] and [F4] on nested unit balls gives the same $e^{-\alpha'|z|}$ bound for two more derivatives. Since $e^{-\alpha'|z|}\le e^{-\alpha|z|}$ outside a fixed disk, every finite derivative has the stated rate.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [A4] The current framed Ward theorem proves the local integrable-Dolbeault frames, universal-line degree-zero base change/evaluation, unique incidence connection and compatibility of the pairing-induced positive metric. Its comparison input is absolute projective GAGA, not independently chosen parallel metrics or assumed base-change surjectivity. [[thm-qftx-framed-penrose-ward-correspondence-on-s4]]

proof_steps.claim: Starting with a framed ASD connection, [A4] constructs its holomorphic Ward bundle; the exact coupled cohomology-vanishing and diagonal argument [[lem-qftx-asd-twistor-vanishing-and-monad-reconstruction]] reconstructs the normalized three-term monad. Starting with regular ADHM data, [A5] identifies its normalized real monad and projection connection with this Ward bundle and connection. The equality of the two constructions is the first-order and inverse-extraction clause in [A5], so it is conditional on that exact real block proof, not on the P² citation alone.

By [A5], both composites on framed isomorphism classes are identities: ADHM data produce the Ward bundle whose monad extraction returns the same $U(k)$ orbit, and an ASD connection produces a Ward bundle whose matrix extraction returns an orbit reconstructing that framed connection. The charge of each resulting connection is $q_N=-k$ by [F2]–[F3]. Thus the claimed bijection and charge statement follow conditionally on [A4]–[A5].

The finite-dimensional quotient and $\mathbb P^2$ sheaf maps are $T$-equivariant by [A1]–[A2]. The Ward construction is natural under rotations and framing transformations by [A4]; the exact raw monad torus factors are directly calculated in the new block lemma cited by [A5], while the equivariance of inverse normalization remains part of [A5]. These exact interfaces make the composite $T$-equivariant. The same composition on first-order families is valid only under the base-change hypotheses of [A2]–[A4] and the deformation compatibility of [A5]. This proves the stated conditional torus and tangent clauses and leaves the positive-FI boundary separate.

reviewed_items.compatibility: Public mathematical Statement/Definition and hypotheses preserved. Six title changes need no mathematical propagation; Gysin added Remarks re-express existing proof, not a new relied-on result. Riesz label-only Statement/F6 change reviewed explicitly below.

fact_uses.text: [F6] Under Countable Choice, for every nonnegative Borel function $g$, $\int_{\mathbb R^n}g(x)\,dx=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^{n-1}}g(r\omega)r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr$, with $\sigma$ a finite Borel measure. ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]])

proof_steps.claim: By [F6], the size bound gives $\int_{R\le|x|\le2R}|K_j(x)|\,dx\le c_n|S^{n-1}|\int_R^{2R}dr/r=c_n|S^{n-1}|\log2$. For every $h\ne0$, directly integrating the difference bound gives $\int_{|x|\ge2|h|}|K_j(x-h)-K_j(x)|\,dx\le C_n|h||S^{n-1}|\int_{2|h|}^\infty r^{-2}dr=|S^{n-1}|C_n/2$. Thus $K_j$ is a base Calderón–Zygmund kernel with $A_1=c_n|S^{n-1}|\log2$ and $A_2=|S^{n-1}|C_n/2$; its first-difference estimate now establishes standard $1$-Hölder status with $A_2'=C_n$.

fact_uses.text: [F4] For nonnegative Borel $q$, polar integration gives $\int_{\mathbb R^n}q(x)\,dx=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^{n-1}}q(r\omega)r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr$. ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

proof_steps.claim: Let $0<R\le1$. For $n\ge3$, [F4] gives $\int_{B_R}|\Phi_n(x)|\,dx=\frac1{n-2}\int_0^R r\,dr=\frac{R^2}{2(n-2)}<\infty$. For $n=2$, using $\omega_1=2\pi$ from step 1.1, it gives $\int_{B_R}|\Phi_2(x)|\,dx=\int_0^R r(-\log r)\,dr=-\frac{R^2}{2}\log R+\frac{R^2}{4}<\infty$. The polar integration use [F4] also assumes [A1].

The zero-dimensional case is outside the stated $n\ge2$ kernel and has no unit-sphere convention used here. The polar endpoint $r=0$ is included as an improper integral in step 2.1; away from zero the kernel is smooth. Countable Choice is used only through [F1], [F2], and [F4]; no full Axiom of Choice is used.

fact_uses.text: [F1] The polar surface measure is normalized by $\sigma(E)=n\lambda_n(\{t\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<t\le1\})$ on Borel $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$, and for nonnegative Borel $h$ one has $\int_{\mathbb R^n}h\,d\lambda_n=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^{n-1}}h(t\omega)t^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dt$ ([[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

proof_steps.claim: Spherical oscillation bound for a smooth function. Let $v\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$, $B:=B(x,r)$, and fix $z\in B$ and $\rho>0$. For $y\in B$ the chain rule and the fundamental theorem [F3] applied to $t\mapsto v(ty+(1-t)z)$ give $v(y)-v(z)=\int_0^1Dv(ty+(1-t)z)\cdot(y-z)\,dt$, hence $|v(y)-v(z)|\le|y-z|\int_0^1|Dv(ty+(1-t)z)|\,dt$. Writing $S_\rho:=\partial B(z,\rho)$ for the sphere equipped with its surface measure, and using that the homothety $y\mapsto ty+(1-t)z$ maps $S_\rho$ onto $S_{t\rho}$ with surface element scaled by $t^{n-1}$; its image of $B\cap S_\rho$ is contained in $B\cap S_{t\rho}$ by convexity, so enlargement gives the inequality below (the surface measures are the polar measures of cones, so this is the linear change-of-variables property of [F1] and [F4]), $\int_{B\cap S_\rho}|v(y)-v(z)|\,dS(y)\le\rho\int_0^1\int_{B\cap S_\rho}|Dv(ty+(1-t)z)|\,dS(y)\,dt\le\rho\int_0^1t^{1-n}\int_{B\cap S_{t\rho}}|Dv(w)|\,dS(w)\,dt$. Since $|w-z|=t\rho$ on $S_{t\rho}$, the inner integral equals $\rho^{n-1}t^{n-1}\int_{B\cap S_{t\rho}}|Dv(w)|\,|z-w|^{1-n}\,dS(w)$; substituting $s=t\rho$, so that $dt=ds/\rho$, the last display becomes $\rho^{n-1}\int_0^\rho\int_{B\cap S_s}|Dv(w)|\,|z-w|^{1-n}\,dS(w)\,ds=\rho^{n-1}\int_{B\cap B(z,\rho)}|Dv(w)|\,|z-w|^{1-n}\,dw$, the final equality being the polar-coordinate formula [F1] for the nonnegative function $w\mapsto|Dv(w)||z-w|^{1-n}$ on $B\cap B(z,\rho)$ (whose singularity at $w=z$ is integrable; a single point is null).

The oscillation bound for a smooth function. Let $v\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and keep $B=B(x,r)$. Since $u_{B}$ is the normalized integral, $|v(z)-v_B|=|B|^{-1}|\int_B(v(z)-v(y))\,dy|$; writing the integral over $B$ in polar coordinates around $z$ and using $B\subseteq B(z,2r)$, step 1.1 gives $|v(z)-v_B|\le|B|^{-1}\int_0^{2r}\int_{B\cap S_\rho}|v(y)-v(z)|\,dS(y)\,d\rho\le|B|^{-1}\int_0^{2r}\rho^{n-1}\,d\rho\int_B|Dv(y)|\,|z-y|^{1-n}\,dy$ for every $z\in B$. By [F2], $|B|=\sigma(S^{n-1})r^n/n$ and $\int_0^{2r}\rho^{n-1}d\rho=(2r)^n/n$, so $|B|^{-1}\int_0^{2r}\rho^{n-1}d\rho=2^n/\sigma(S^{n-1})=:c(n)$; hence $|v(z)-v_B|\le c(n)\int_B|Dv(y)||z-y|^{1-n}dy$ for every $z\in B$.

fact_uses.text: [F3] Polar coordinates: $\int_{\mathbb R^n}g\,d\lambda_n=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^{n-1}}g(r\theta)r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\theta)\,dr$; the surface measure $\sigma$ is preserved by orthogonal transformations and the map $\theta\mapsto a+R\theta$ multiplies it by $R^{n-1}$; $\sigma(S^{n-1})=\omega_{n-1}=n|B_1|$. ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]])

proof_steps.claim: Zero spherical means. On the unit sphere $k_{ij}(\theta)=-\omega_{n-1}^{-1}(\delta_{ij}-n\theta_i\theta_j)$. By [F3] the measure $\sigma$ is invariant under coordinate reflections, so $\int\theta_i\theta_j\,d\sigma=0$ for $i\ne j$; it is also invariant under coordinate permutations, so all $n$ numbers $\int\theta_i^2d\sigma$ are equal, and $\sum_i\theta_i^2=1$ gives $\int\theta_i^2d\sigma=\omega_{n-1}/n$. Hence $\int_{S^{n-1}}\theta_i\theta_j\,d\sigma=\delta_{ij}\omega_{n-1}/n$ and therefore $\int_{S^{n-1}}k_{ij}(\theta)\,d\sigma(\theta)=-\omega_{n-1}^{-1}(\delta_{ij}\omega_{n-1}-n\delta_{ij}\omega_{n-1}/n)=0$. By the homogeneity of step 1.1 the mean over every centred sphere vanishes: $\int_{S(0,\rho)}k_{ij}\,dS=\rho^{n-1}\rho^{-n}\int_{S^{n-1}}k_{ij}(\theta)d\sigma=0$.

$k_{ij}$ is a standard Hölder Calderón–Zygmund kernel. The annular size condition follows from step 2.1 and [F3]: $\int_{R\le|z|\le2R}|k_{ij}|\,dz=\int_R^{2R}\rho^{-1}d\rho\int_{S^{n-1}}|k_{ij}(\theta)|\,d\sigma\le (1+n)\log 2=:A_1$. Hörmander's condition follows from the difference estimate of step 2.1 and polar integration: for $y\ne0$, $\int_{|x|\ge2|y|}|k_{ij}(x-y)-k_{ij}(x)|\,dx\le C_n|y|\int_{2|y|}^\infty\rho^{-n-1}\omega_{n-1}\rho^{n-1}d\rho=C_n\omega_{n-1}/2=:A_2$. The pointwise estimate of step 2.1 is exactly condition (1) of [F9] with $\delta=1$ and constant $C_n2^{n+1}$, so $k_{ij}$ is standard $1$-Hölder in the sense of [[def-standard-holder-calderon-zygmund-kernel]].

The principal value exists. Let $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$. Using the vanishing spherical means of step 2.2 on the annulus, $$\int_{|z|\ge\varepsilon}k_{ij}(z)\varphi(z)\,dz=\int_{\varepsilon\le|z|<1}k_{ij}(z)\bigl(\varphi(z)-\varphi(0)\bigr)\,dz+\int_{|z|\ge1}k_{ij}(z)\varphi(z)\,dz.$$ The second integral is absolutely convergent because $|k_{ij}(z)\varphi(z)|\le C_n|z|^{-n}|\varphi(z)|$ and $\varphi$ is Schwartz, and the first integrand is dominated by $C_n\|\nabla\varphi\|_\infty|z|^{1-n}$, which is integrable on $|z|<1$ for $n\ge2$; hence the first integral converges as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ by dominated convergence. Therefore $W_{ij}(\varphi):=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{|z|\ge\varepsilon}k_{ij}(z)\varphi(z)\,dz$ exists for every Schwartz $\varphi$; the bound $|W_{ij}(\varphi)|\le C_n(\|\nabla\varphi\|_\infty+\sup_z(1+|z|)^2|\varphi(z)|)$ proves continuity in Schwartz seminorms, so the map is a tempered distribution agreeing with $k_{ij}$ off the origin, and taking $\delta_j=1/j$ exhibits it as a principal-value distribution for $k_{ij}$ in the sense of [F9].

The principal value and the two integrals. With $0<\varepsilon<1$, the vanishing of $\int_{\varepsilon\le|x-y|<1}k_{ij}(x-y)dy$ by step 2.2 gives $$\int_{|x-y|\ge\varepsilon}k_{ij}(x-y)f(y)dy=\int_{\varepsilon\le|x-y|<1}k_{ij}(x-y)\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr)dy+\int_{|x-y|\ge1}k_{ij}(x-y)f(y)\,dy.$$ The first integrand is bounded by $C_n[f]_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^n}|x-y|^{\alpha-n}$, whose integral over $|x-y|<1$ is finite because $\alpha-n>-n$, so dominated convergence lets $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ pass to the absolutely convergent first integral of the statement; the other integral is absolutely convergent because $|k_{ij}(x-y)f(y)|\le C_n|f(y)|$ on $|x-y|\ge1$ and $f$ is integrable. Hence the principal value $\mathrm{p.v.}\int k_{ij}(x-y)f(y)dy$ exists for every $x$ and equals the sum of the two integrals of the displayed formula.

Distributional identity. Let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ and choose $R$ with $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset B_{R/2}(0)$. For $0<\varepsilon<R/2$ apply the divergence theorem [F4] on the bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega_\varepsilon:=\{\varepsilon<|x|<R\}$ to the field $F:=\Phi\partial_j\varphi\,e_i-\varphi\,\partial_i\Phi\,e_j$. Since $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_i(\Phi\partial_j\varphi)-\partial_j(\varphi\partial_i\Phi)=\Phi\partial_i\partial_j\varphi-k_{ij}\varphi$ and $F=0$ near $|x|=R$, while $
u=-x/|x|$ on $|x|=\varepsilon$, $$\int_{\Omega_\varepsilon}\Phi\,\partial_i\partial_j\varphi\,dx=\int_{\Omega_\varepsilon}k_{ij}\varphi\,dx+\int_{|x|=\varepsilon}\Bigl(\Phi\,\partial_j\varphi\,
u_i-\varphi\,\partial_i\Phi\,
u_j\Bigr)dS.$$ On $|x|=\varepsilon$ the first boundary term tends to $0$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, because $\Phi=O(\varepsilon^{2-n})$ or $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ and $dS$ contributes $\varepsilon^{n-1}$; the second boundary term is $-\int_{|x|=\varepsilon}\varphi\,\partial_i\Phi\,
u_j\,dS$, and by step 1.1, the outward normal $
u=-x/\varepsilon$ and the scaling rule of [F3], $$\int_{|x|=\varepsilon}\varphi\,\partial_i\Phi\,
u_j\,dS= rac{1}{\omega_{n-1}\varepsilon^{n+1}}\int_{|x|=\varepsilon}\varphi(x)\,x_ix_j\,dS(x)\longrightarrow rac{\delta_{ij}}{n}\varphi(0),$$ because $\int_{|x|=\varepsilon}\varphi\,x_ix_j\,dS=\varepsilon^{n+1}\int_{S^{n-1}}\varphi(\varepsilon	heta)	heta_i	heta_j\,d\sigma(	heta)$ and $\varphi(\varepsilon	heta)=\varphi(0)+O(\varepsilon)$. Hence the boundary integral in the identity tends to $- rac{\delta_{ij}}{n}\varphi(0)$. Passing to the limit, using local integrability of $\Phi$ on the left and step 3.2 on the right, gives $\langle\partial_i\partial_j\Phi,\varphiangle=\langle\Phi,\partial_i\partial_j\varphiangle=W_{ij}(\varphi)- rac{\delta_{ij}}{n}\varphi(0)$; by [F5] this is the distributional identity $D_{ij}\Phi=\mathrm{p.v.}\,k_{ij}- rac{\delta_{ij}}{n}\delta_0$.

Assembly. Combining steps 3.3 and 3.4 gives, for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $\partial_i\partial_jNf(x)=\mathrm{p.v.}\int k_{ij}(x-y)f(y)dy-(\delta_{ij}/n)f(x)$, and the two ordinary integrals in the equivalent displayed form converge absolutely by step 3.4; step 3.3 supplies the classical second derivatives. The subtraction of $f(x)$ is made only on the unit ball: the globally subtracted integrand obeys $|k_{ij}(x-y)(f(y)-f(x))|\ge\frac12|f(x)|\,|k_{ij}(x-y)|$ for all $y$ outside a large ball when $f(x)\ne0$, and $\int_{|z|\ge1}|k_{ij}(z)|dz=\int_1^\infty\rho^{-1}d\rho\int_{S^{n-1}}|k_{ij}(\theta)|d\sigma=\infty$ by [F3] and step 1.1, so no absolutely convergent Lebesgue integral over $\mathbb R^n$ can replace the principal value; the annular cancellation of step 2.2 is what makes the truncations converge. The case $\alpha=1$ was reduced to $\beta=1/2<\alpha$ in step 3.3, where higher Hölder regularity than assumed is irrelevant to the formula; the positivity of $\alpha$ makes $|z|^{\alpha-n}$ integrable at the origin in step 3.4. All constructions are pointwise in $x$ and use only Countable Choice in the cited measure, polar, potential and distribution interfaces.

fact_uses.text: [F3] Under countable choice, polar coordinates integrate a nonnegative Borel function as its sphere integral followed by $t^{n-1}dt$. ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

proof_steps.claim: Polar coordinates give the ball average $\frac n{r^n}\int_0^r t^{n-1}m(t)\,dt\ge u(a)$. For signed $u$, apply the nonnegative polar formula to its positive and negative parts on the bounded ball; both are bounded and integrable. Replacing $u$ by $-u$ proves both reversed inequalities.

Integrating the expansion with the radial weights gives ball average $u(a)+r^2\Delta u(a)/(2(n+2))+o(r^2)$. Either assumed mean inequality, divided by $r^2>0$ and followed by $r\downarrow0$, forces $\Delta u(a)\ge0$. Negation gives the superharmonic converse.

fact_uses.text: [F4] Assume Countable Choice. For every Borel measurable $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty]$, $\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^{d-1}}f(r\omega)r^{d-1}d\sigma(\omega)dr$, where $\sigma$ is the finite Borel measure on $S^{d-1}$ given by the polar formula; a Borel measurable angular function composed with $z\mapsto z/|z|$ is Borel measurable off the origin, and the origin is a null set. ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]])

proof_steps.claim: The polar identity and the directional notation. Replace $g$ by a Borel function equal to it almost everywhere; such a function is obtained by replacing the measurable sets in simple approximations by Borel sets modulo null sets. For every fixed increment its difference integral is unchanged, and the double integral is unchanged by Tonelli. Work with that Borel representative below. Substitute $y=x+h$ in [F1] and use translation invariance [F3] to write, for a.e. fixed $h$, $\int_{\mathbb R^d}|g(x)-g(x+h)|^pdx=D_g(|h|,h/|h|)$; Tonelli [F2] then gives $[g]_{s,p}^p=\int_{\mathbb R^d}D_g(|h|,h/|h|)|h|^{-d-sp}dh$. The functions $(h,\omega)\mapsto D_g(h,\omega)$ and $F_g$ are Borel measurable: the first is an iterated integral of the nonnegative measurable function $(x,h,\omega)\mapsto|g(x+h\omega)-g(x)|^p$ over $x$, and the second is the section integral of $D_g(h,\omega)h^{-1-sp}$, both covered by Tonelli's measurability clause [F2]. Polar coordinates [F4] turn the display into $[g]_{s,p}^p=\int_{S^{d-1}}F_g(\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega)$, and $F_g(e_i)=\int_0^\infty h^{-1-sp}\int_{\mathbb R^d}|g(x+he_i)-g(x)|^pdx\,dh$ is the $i$-th summand in the statement; all quantities are nonnegative extended integrals, so no convergence hypothesis is needed.

The sphere comparison. For a bounded nonnegative compactly supported Borel function $\varphi$ and a nonnegative Borel measurable $F$ on $S^{d-1}$, Tonelli [F2] and polar coordinates [F4], applied to the nonnegative Borel function $z\mapsto\varphi(z)F(z/|z|)$ with the value $0$ prescribed at the origin, give $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\varphi(z)F(z/|z|)\,dz=\int_{S^{d-1}}F(\omega)\bigl(\int_0^\infty\varphi(r\omega)r^{d-1}dr\bigr)d\sigma(\omega)\le C_\varphi\int_{S^{d-1}}F\,d\sigma$, where $C_\varphi:=\sup_{\omega\in S^{d-1}}\int_0^\infty\varphi(r\omega)r^{d-1}dr$ satisfies $C_\varphi\le MR^d/d<\infty$ whenever $\varphi\le M$ and its support lies in $B(0,R)$; this applies in particular to $\varphi=\rho$ and to $\varphi=\psi$.

The upper comparison. Fix $\omega\in S^{d-1}$ and $r>0$ and put $p_k:=r\sum_{i\le k}\omega_ie_i$ for $k=0,\dots,d$, so that $p_0=0$ and $p_d=r\omega$. Telescoping along the polygonal path $p_0,\dots,p_d$ gives $g(x+r\omega)-g(x)=\sum_{k=1}^d\bigl(g(x+p_k)-g(x+p_{k-1})\bigr)$, and each summand is the translate by $p_{k-1}$ of the increment $g(\cdot+r\omega_ke_k)-g(\cdot)$; by convexity and [F3], $D_g(r,\omega)\le d^{p-1}\sum_{k=1}^dD_g(r|\omega_k|,\operatorname{sgn}(\omega_k)e_k)$, the term being zero when $\omega_k=0$. Multiplying by $r^{-1-sp}$, integrating in $r$, and substituting $h=r|\omega_k|$ in the $k$-th term (using $|\omega_k|^{sp}\le1$) and using $F_g(-e_k)=F_g(e_k)$ by translation invariance gives $F_g(\omega)\le d^{p-1}\sum_{k=1}^dF_g(e_k)$ for every $\omega$. Integrating over $S^{d-1}$ with [F4] and step 1.1 yields the upper comparison $[g]_{s,p}^p\le d^{p-1}\sigma(S^{d-1})\sum_{i=1}^dF_g(e_i)$.

fact_uses.text: [F2] The polar formula holds for every nonnegative Borel function. ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

proof_steps.claim: Applying F2 to the indicator of that same annular cone gives its volume as $C\sigma(A)$. Thus $Cm(A)=C\sigma(A)$ for every Borel A, and division by the strictly positive C gives $m=\sigma$. For an orthogonal O, $D(OX)^TD(OX)=DX^TX$, while $D(a+RX)^TD(a+RX)=R^2DX^TDX$. Applying F1 chartwise proves orthogonal invariance and the factor $R^{n-1}$, also for integrals by simple approximation.

Use F2 with $1_{B_1}$: $|B_1|=\int_0^1r^{n-1}\sigma(S^{n-1})\,dr=\sigma(S^{n-1})/n$. A possible contribution at the origin is absent because the polar formula already applies to this indicator. Step 3.1 now yields the asserted chart area $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

fact_uses.text: [F6] Polar coordinates compute the radial integrals used below. ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]])

proof_steps.claim: Multiplication by a bounded Lipschitz function is bounded on $W^{s,p}$. Let $a$ be bounded and Lipschitz on $\mathbb R^d$ and $v$ measurable. Then $|a(x)v(x)-a(y)v(y)|^p\le2^{p-1}\bigl(|a(x)|^p|v(x)-v(y)|^p+|a(x)-a(y)|^p|v(y)|^p\bigr)$, and with $\|a\|_\infty$ and $[a]_{\mathrm{Lip}}$ the two bounds, integrating against $|x-y|^{-d-sp}dx\,dy$ gives $[av]_{s,p}^p\le2^{p-1}\bigl(\|a\|_\infty^p[v]_{s,p}^p+[a]_{\mathrm{Lip}}^p\int_{|h|\le1}|h|^{p-d-sp}dh\int|v|^pd\xi+2^p\|a\|_\infty^p\int_{|h|>1}|h|^{-d-sp}dh\int|v|^p\bigr)$ by translating the second term in $x$ for fixed $y$. Both constants are finite because $p-sp>0$ for $s<1$ and $d+sp>d$; hence $[av]_{s,p}\le C(a,d,p,s)\bigl(\|v\|_{L^p}+[v]_{s,p}\bigr)$, and $\|av\|_{L^p}\le\|a\|_\infty\|v\|_{L^p}$, so $\|av\|_{W^{s,p}}\le C'(a,d,p,s)\|v\|_{W^{s,p}}$.

Chart independence (ii). Let two atlases and partitions be as in [F5]. For each pair $j,k$, the support of $\chi_j\chi'_k$ on the boundary is compact inside the chart overlap. Cover it by finitely many small coordinate balls whose slightly larger closures remain in that overlap. Step 1.1 makes each transition bi-Lipschitz on those larger balls; its Jacobians and inverse Jacobians are bounded there by [F4]. Choose a finite smooth coordinate partition equal to one near this compact support. On each piece, the identity $(\chi_j\chi'_kg)\circ\Psi_j^{-1}=((\chi'_kg)\circ(\Psi'_k)^{-1})\circ(\Psi'_k\circ\Psi_j^{-1})\, (\chi_j\circ\Psi_j^{-1})$ and steps 1.2 and 2.1 control the norm restricted to the ball. All multiplier factors are bounded Lipschitz there; multiplying by the coordinate cutoff extends them by zero to bounded Lipschitz functions on $\mathbb R^d$. The localised function is supported a positive distance $\delta$ from the ball's complement, so the extra cross term in its zero-extension seminorm is at most $C\delta^{-sp}\|v\|_p^p$, obtained by integrating $|h|^{-d-sp}$ over $|h|\ge\delta$. Thus its whole-space norm is bounded by the second atlas norm. Sum over the finite pieces and use $\sum_k\chi'_k=1$ to obtain the first atlas norm bounded by the second. Exchange the atlases for the reverse inequality.

fact_uses.text: [F2] Polar coordinates: for a Borel function $g\ge0$ on $\mathbb R^n$, $\int_{\mathbb R^n}g\,d\lambda=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^{n-1}}g(r\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega)\,r^{n-1}dr$, where $\sigma$ is the surface measure with $\sigma(S^{n-1})=|S^{n-1}|$ ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]); the integral over a smaller domain is at most the integral over a larger one ([[prop-measure-monotonicity]]).

proof_steps.claim: Fix $y\ne0$. By the pointwise Hölder bound of [F1] and monotonicity of the integral, $$\int_{|x|\ge2|y|}|k(x-y)-k(x)|\,dx\le A_2'|y|^\delta\int_{|x|\ge2|y|}|x|^{-n-\delta}dx.$$

Polar coordinates evaluate the radial integral: substituting $x=r\omega$ and using $|x|^{-n-\delta}r^{n-1}=r^{-1-\delta}$, $$\int_{|x|\ge2|y|}|x|^{-n-\delta}dx=|S^{n-1}|\int_{2|y|}^\infty r^{-1-\delta}dr=|S^{n-1}|\frac{(2|y|)^{-\delta}}{\delta},$$ the last step being the elementary integral $\int_a^\infty r^{-1-\delta}dr=a^{-\delta}/\delta$ for $a>0$ and $\delta>0$.

fact_uses.text:
[F2] Polar integration gives the integral of a nonnegative Borel function as
the radial integral against $r^{n-1}\,dr\,d\sigma$.
([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

proof_steps.claim: For $n\ge3$ and any $R>0$, assign the finite value $0$ to the kernel at the pole as permitted by [F11]; then $|\Phi|\mathbf 1_{B_R}$ is Borel. Apply [F2] and use [F1] and $\sigma(S^{n-1})=\omega_{n-1}$ from [F3] to obtain $$\int_{B_R}|\Phi(x)|\,dx=\frac{1}{(n-2)\omega_{n-1}}\int_0^R r^{n-1}r^{2-n}\,\omega_{n-1}\,dr=\frac{R^2}{2(n-2)}<\infty.$$

For $n=2$ and any $R>0$, again assign $\Phi(0)=0$ as permitted by [F11]. By [F1]–[F3] and step 1.1, $$\int_{B_R}|\Phi(x)|\,dx=\frac{\omega_1}{2\pi}\int_0^Rr|\log r|\,dr.$$ If $0<R\le1$, the radial integral is $-\frac{R^2}{2}\log R+\frac{R^2}{4}$; if $R\ge1$, splitting at $1$ gives $\frac{R^2}{2}\log R-\frac{R^2}{4}+\frac12$. Both values are finite, including at $R=1$, and the prefactor is finite by step 1.1.

The regular functional in [F8] is therefore well-defined; [F9], under [A1], proves it is a distribution. The pole value changes only a singleton, which is null by [F10], and the radial integrals prove finiteness at the improper endpoint $r=0$ and every finite outer radius $R>0$. The claim assumes $n\ge2$; it makes no global-integrability assertion at $R=\infty$, and Countable Choice is used only through the named polar, surface-measure, ball-measure, Borel-measurability, singleton-null, and embedding interfaces, not full AC.

fact_uses.text: [F9] Polar coordinates give $\int_{D_r}|z|^{-1}\,dA=2\pi r$ and make every $C|z|^{\alpha-2}$ singularity integrable near $0$ when $\alpha>0$ ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

proof_steps.claim: For $z\ne0$, direct differentiation of $\Gamma$ gives $a(z):=\partial_z\Gamma(z)=-1/(4\pi z)$; polar coordinates give $\int_{D_r}|a|\,dA=r/2$. Integrating by parts outside $D_\varepsilon$ against a compactly supported smooth test function leaves an inner boundary term bounded by $C\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|$, which tends to zero, so the distributional derivative of $\Gamma$ is the regular distribution of $a$.

For every compactly supported smooth test function $\varphi$, Fubini and the distributional derivative identity in step 1.1 give $\langle\partial_zNq,\varphi\rangle=\langle a*q,\varphi\rangle$, with $$(a*q)(z)=\int_{\mathbb C}a(z-\zeta)q(\zeta)\,dA(\zeta).$$ This integral is absolutely finite for each $z$, since $q$ is bounded, supported in $\overline D_2$, and $a$ is locally integrable. It is continuous: on a compact set of $z$-values let $\delta=|z-z'|<1$; the two disks of radius $2\delta$ around $z,z'$ contribute at most $C\|q\|_\infty\delta$, while on their complement $|\nabla a(w)|\le C|w|^{-2}$ and the mean value theorem bounds the difference by $C\|q\|_\infty\delta\log(C_0/\delta)$ for a fixed $C_0$. Since $Nq\in C^2$, both sides are continuous; [F6] makes them equal almost everywhere, and [F8] then makes them equal everywhere. Therefore $Tq=-4\partial_zNq=(1/\pi)\int q(\zeta)/(z-\zeta)\,dA(\zeta)$.

For the global Hölder seminorm when $k=0$, put $K(w)=-1/(\pi w^2)$ and $k_{ij}(w)=\partial_i\partial_j\Gamma(w)$. Let $\Omega$ be a disk with $\operatorname{supp}q\Subset\Omega$ and $x\in\Omega$, and choose a larger disk $D_s(x)\supset\overline\Omega$. On the outer circle the explicit derivative $\partial_i\Gamma(w)=-w_i/(2\pi|w|^2)$ and polar symmetry give $\int_{\partial D_s(x)}\partial_i\Gamma(x-y)\nu_j(y)\,dS(y)=\delta_{ij}/2$. Also $k_{ij}(x-y)=-\partial_{y_j}\partial_i\Gamma(x-y)$, so the divergence theorem gives $\int_{D_s(x)\setminus\Omega}k_{ij}(x-y)\,dA(y)=-\delta_{ij}/2+g_{ij,\Omega}(x)$, where $$g_{ij,\Omega}(x):=\int_{\partial\Omega}\partial_i\Gamma(x-y)\nu_j(y)\,dS(y).$$ Split the centered-disk cancellation formula [F5] into $\Omega$ and $D_s(x)\setminus\Omega$; on the latter $q(y)=0$, so the $\delta_{ij}/2$ terms cancel and $$\partial_i\partial_jNq(x)=\int_\Omega k_{ij}(x-y)(q(y)-q(x))\,dA(y)-q(x)g_{ij,\Omega}(x).$$ Taking the linear combination $-\partial_{xx}+2i\partial_{xy}+\partial_{yy}$ gives the corresponding formula for $Sq$ with kernel $K$ and boundary factor $G_\Omega=-g_{xx,\Omega}+2ig_{xy,\Omega}+g_{yy,\Omega}$.

Split the integral difference over $D_\delta(m)$ and $\Omega\setminus\overline D_\delta(m)$. On the inner disk, $|K(x-y)(q(y)-q(x))|\le C[q]_{0,\alpha}|x-y|^{\alpha-2}$ and likewise for $x'$, so polar integration bounds both contributions by $C_\alpha[q]_{0,\alpha}\delta^\alpha$. On the outer region, write the difference integrand as $$[K(x-y)-K(x'-y)](q(y)-q(x))-K(x'-y)(q(x)-q(x')).$$ With $\rho=|y-m|\ge\delta$, the segment between $x-y$ and $x'-y$ stays at distance at least $\rho/2$ from zero; $|\nabla K(w)|\le C|w|^{-3}$ and the mean value theorem bound the first term by $C[q]_{0,\alpha}\delta\rho^{\alpha-3}$. Its area integral is at most $C[q]_{0,\alpha}\delta\int_\delta^R\rho^{\alpha-2}d\rho\le C_\alpha[q]_{0,\alpha}\delta^\alpha$, using $\alpha<1$. For the second term, $|q(x)-q(x')|\le[q]_{0,\alpha}\delta^\alpha$ and each real component $\int_{\Omega\setminus\overline D_\delta(m)}k_{ij}(x'-y)\,dA(y)$ is bounded by the divergence theorem: its boundary fluxes are $\partial_i\Gamma$ on the outer circle and inner circle, each bounded by $C$ using $|x'-y|\ge3R/4$ on the outer circle and $|x'-y|\ge\delta/2$ on the inner one. This proves $[Sq]_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^2}\le C_\alpha[q]_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^2}$.

On $\overline D_4$, the local Hessian estimate [F4] bounds $|Sq|$ by $C_\alpha\|q\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}$. For $|z|\ge3$, the integral formula gives $$|Sq(z)|\le\frac{\|q\|_\infty}{\pi}\int_{\overline D_2}|z-\zeta|^{-2}\,dA(\zeta)\le4\|q\|_\infty,$$ since $|z-\zeta|\ge1$. Hence $\|Sq\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)}\le C_\alpha\|q\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)}$.

fact_uses.text: [F2] Polar coordinates: for every Borel measurable $f:\mathbb R^n\to[0,\infty]$, $\int_{\mathbb R^n}f\,d\lambda_n=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^{n-1}}f(r\omega)r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr$ ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

proof_steps.claim: Surface normalisation. By [F2] applied to $\mathbf1_{B(0,1)}$, $\lambda_n(B(0,1))=\sigma(S^{n-1})\int_0^1t^{n-1}dt=\sigma(S^{n-1})/n$. Thus [F6] gives $0<\sigma(S^{n-1})=n\lambda_n(B(0,1))<\infty$.

Translation to polar coordinates at $x$. Define $G(y):=|Du(y)|\,|x-y|^{1-n}$ for $y\ne x$ and $G(x):=0$; this is Borel measurable because $|Du|$ is continuous and $y\mapsto|x-y|^{1-n}$ is Borel. Applying [F2] to the nonnegative Borel function $z\mapsto G(x+z)$ and then [F3] gives $$\int_{S^{n-1}}\int_0^\infty|Du(x+t\omega)|\,dt\,d\sigma(\omega)=\int_{S^{n-1}}\int_0^\infty G(x+t\omega)t^{n-1}\,dt\,d\sigma(\omega)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}G(y)\,dy,$$ where the first equality uses $|x-(x+t\omega)|^{1-n}=t^{1-n}$ and the two integrations are the iterated polar integral of the nonnegative function $z\mapsto G(x+z)$; the singularity at $y=x$ is a single point and does not affect the value of the integral.

fact_uses.text: [F6] Polar coordinates: for $n\ge1$ and every Borel $h:\mathbb R^n\to[0,\infty]$, $\int_{\mathbb R^n}h\,d\lambda_n=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^{n-1}}h(r\omega)r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr$, and $\sigma$ is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$. [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]

proof_steps.claim: Let $A_n:=\int_{S^{n-1}}\omega_j\,d\sigma(\omega)$ and $H(x):=\mathbf 1_{\{1<|x|<2\}}\,x_j$. The function $H$ is Borel and $\int_{\mathbb R^n}|H|\,d\lambda_n<\infty$; the map $x\mapsto-x$ is a linear bijection with $|\det|=1$, so [F7] gives $\int_{\mathbb R^n}H(-x)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}H(x)\,d\lambda_n(x)$, while $H(-x)=-H(x)$ gives $\int H\,d\lambda_n=-\int H\,d\lambda_n$, that is, $\int_{\mathbb R^n}H\,d\lambda_n=0$. On the other hand [F6] applied to the nonnegative and the negative part of $H$ gives $\int_{\mathbb R^n}H\,d\lambda_n=\int_1^2 r^{n-1}\bigl(\int_{S^{n-1}}r\omega_j\,d\sigma(\omega)\bigr)dr=A_n\int_1^2r^n\,dr$ with $\int_1^2r^n\,dr>0$, so $A_n=0$. Hence for every $r>0$ the homogeneity [F1] gives $\int_{S^{n-1}}K_j(r\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega)=c_nr^{-n}\int_{S^{n-1}}\omega_j\,d\sigma(\omega)=c_nr^{-n}A_n=0$.

fact_uses.text: [F3] Polar coordinates: $\int_{\mathbb R^n}h\,d\lambda_n=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^{n-1}}h(r\omega)r^{n-1}d\sigma(\omega)\,dr$ for nonnegative Borel $h$ and, by splitting real and imaginary parts into their positive and negative parts, for integrable complex Borel $h$, and the finite Borel measure $\sigma$ is uniquely determined by this property. [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]

proof_steps.claim: For $0<\varepsilon<R$ and $\xi\ne0$ put $\Lambda_{\varepsilon,R}(\xi):=\int_{\varepsilon<|y|<R}K_j(y)e^{-2\pi iy\cdot\xi}dy$. The cosine part of the integrand is odd in $y$, so it integrates to zero on the symmetric annulus, and $K_j(y)=c_ny_j/|y|^{n+1}$ gives $\Lambda_{\varepsilon,R}(\xi)=-ic_n\int_{\varepsilon<|y|<R}\frac{y_j}{|y|^{n+1}}\sin(2\pi y\cdot\xi)\,dy$. Polar coordinates [F3] turn this into $\Lambda_{\varepsilon,R}(\xi)=-ic_n\int_\varepsilon^R\frac{dr}{r}\int_{S^{n-1}}\omega_j\sin(2\pi r\,\xi\cdot\omega)\,d\sigma(\omega)$.

For $\xi\ne0$ one has $\int_{S^{n-1}}\operatorname{sgn}(\xi\cdot\omega)\omega_j\,d\sigma(\omega)=A_n\frac{\xi_j}{|\xi|}$ with $A_n:=\int_{S^{n-1}}|\omega_1|\,d\sigma$: by [F3] the measure $\sigma$ is invariant under the orthogonal map $\omega\mapsto R\omega$, so substituting $\omega=R^{\mathsf T}u$ for an orthogonal map with $R(\xi/|\xi|)=e_1$ (take $R=I$ if $v:=\xi/|\xi|=e_1$, and otherwise take $R=I-2ww^{\mathsf T}/|w|^2$ with $w=v-e_1$) and reflecting $u_k\mapsto-u_k$ for $k\ne1$ (which preserves $\operatorname{sgn}(u_1)u_1$ and kills the other components by oddness) leaves only $A_n(R^{\mathsf T}e_1)_j=A_n\xi_j/|\xi|$.

$A_n=2\pi^{(n-1)/2}/\Gamma((n+1)/2)$: compute $C:=\int_{B_n}|x_1|\,dx$ twice. Polar coordinates [F3] give $C=\int_0^1r^ndr\cdot A_n=A_n/(n+1)$; for $n\ge2$, slicing at $x_1=t$ gives, by [F5], [F14] and [F4], $C=\int_{-1}^1|t|V_{n-1}(1)(1-t^2)^{(n-1)/2}dt=2V_{n-1}(1)/(n+1)=2\pi^{(n-1)/2}/((n+1)\Gamma((n+1)/2))$, hence $A_n=(n+1)C=2V_{n-1}(1)=2\pi^{(n-1)/2}/\Gamma((n+1)/2)$. For $n=1$ the sphere is $S^0=\{-1,1\}$: the defining identity of [F3], applied to functions supported in the annulus $1<|x|<2$, shows that the measure $\sigma$ is the counting measure $\delta_{-1}+\delta_1$, so $A_1=\int_{S^0}|\omega_1|\,d\sigma=1+1=2$, while $2\pi^{0}/\Gamma(1)=2$ by $\Gamma(1)=1$ of [F15]. Hence $A_n=2\pi^{(n-1)/2}/\Gamma((n+1)/2)$ for every $n\ge1$, and $c_nA_n\pi/2=1$ by cancellation of $\Gamma((n+1)/2)$ and $\pi^{(n+1)/2}$.

fact_uses.text: [F9] Polar coordinates evaluate radial nonnegative integrals; in particular $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\min(1,L|h|)^p|h|^{-d-sp}dh<\infty$ when $0<s<1$. ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]])

proof_steps.claim: Truncation. Choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ with $0\le\eta\le1$, equal to one on $B(0,1)$, and set $\eta_R(x)=\eta(x/R)$ and $A_R=(1-\eta_R)g$. Dominated convergence gives $\|A_R\|_p\to0$. Write $A_R(x)-A_R(y)=(1-\eta_R(x))(g(x)-g(y))+(\eta_R(y)-\eta_R(x))g(y)$. The weighted integral of the first term's $p$-th power tends to zero by dominated convergence, dominated by the defining seminorm integrand of $g$. For the second, $|\eta_R(x)-\eta_R(y)|\le\min(2,\|D\eta\|_\infty|x-y|/R)$; translating $h=x-y$ and scaling $h=Rz$ bounds its weighted integral by $C R^{-sp}\|g\|_p^p$, with $C<\infty$ by [F9]. The inequality $|a+b|^p\le2^{p-1}(|a|^p+|b|^p)$ now gives $[A_R]_{s,p}\to0$, so $\eta_Rg\to g$ in $W^{s,p}$.

fact_uses.text: [F2] Polar coordinates: $\int_{\mathbb R^n}h\,d\lambda_n=\int_0^\infty\int_{S^{n-1}}h(r\omega)r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr$ for nonnegative Borel $h$ ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

proof_steps.claim: The truncated kernel has finite mass. Put $k(z):=|z|^{1-n}\mathbf 1_{B(0,2\rho)}(z)$ for $z\ne0$ and $k(0):=0$. By [F2] applied to the nonnegative Borel function $k$ and by [F1], [F3], $\|k\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^n)}=\int_{S^{n-1}}\int_0^{2\rho}t^{1-n}t^{n-1}\,dt\,d\sigma(\omega)=2\rho\,\sigma(S^{n-1})=2\rho\, n\,\lambda_n(B(0,1))=:C_0(n)\rho$, so $\|k\|_1$ is finite and equals a dimension-only multiple of $\rho$.

John-domain volume control. Put $a:=\operatorname{dist}(x_0,\partial\Omega)>0$. The ball $B(x_0,a)$ lies in $\Omega$: a segment from $x_0$ to any point outside $\Omega$ first meets the boundary, so an outside point cannot be closer than $a$. Polar coordinates [F2] therefore give $|\Omega|\ge \sigma(S^{n-1})a^n/n$. Evaluating [F7] at the endpoint of the curve gives $|x-x_0|\le c_Ja$ for every $x\in\Omega$, hence $\operatorname{diam}\Omega\le2c_Ja\le2c_J(n/\sigma(S^{n-1}))^{1/n}|\Omega|^{1/n}$.

The convolution bound. For $g\in L^p(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$, choose a finite Borel representative $g_0$ by [F11] (replace any infinite values on a Borel null set by zero). The function $F_0(x,z)=k(z)g_0(x-z)$ is Borel, hence measurable for the product of the Lebesgue sigma-algebras. The two Lebesgue spaces are sigma-finite, being exhausted by bounded balls of finite measure [F2, F3]. Translation invariance [F5] and step 1.1 give $\int\|F_0(\cdot,z)\|_p\,dz=\int k(z)\|g_0(\cdot-z)\|_p\,dz=\|k\|_1\|g\|_p<\infty$. Minkowski [F4] therefore shows that the absolute integral is finite almost everywhere and $\|Tg_0\|_p\le\|k\|_1\|g\|_p$, where $Tg_0(x)=\int k(z)g_0(x-z)\,dz$. This also defines $Tg$ for any Lebesgue representative $g$: for each fixed $x$, the exceptional set of $z$ is the translate and reflection $x-N$ of the null set $N$ where $g\ne g_0$, and has measure zero by reflection invariance [F12] and translation invariance [F5]. Thus the section integrals agree wherever finite, and the measurable almost-everywhere representative $Tg_0$ supplies $\|Tg\|_p\le\|k\|_1\|g\|_p$.

fact_uses.text: [L1] Polar coordinates for nonnegative Borel functions hold under Countable Choice ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

proof_steps.claim: Fix $x\in\Omega$ and $R>0$ with $\overline{B_R(x)}\subseteq\Omega$. Polar coordinates and the ball-volume formula give, for $0<r\le R$, $\int_0^r t^{n-1}M_u(x,t)\,dt=\frac{r^n}{n}A_u(x,r)=\frac{r^n}{n}u(x)$. Here $M_u(x,t)$ is continuous in $t$: $u$ is uniformly continuous on the compact closed ball, and the sphere measure is finite. Differentiating the two sides for $0<r<R$ gives $r^{n-1}M_u(x,r)=r^{n-1}u(x)$, hence the spherical mean-value property.

Taylor's formula at any $x$ gives $u(x+h)=u(x)+\nabla u(x)\cdot h+\tfrac12 h^TH_u(x)h+o(|h|^2)$ uniformly as $|h|\le r\to0$. Averaging over $B_r(0)$ kills the linear and off-diagonal quadratic terms by reflection symmetry. Rotation symmetry makes every diagonal second moment equal; their sum is $|B_r|^{-1}\int_{B_r}|h|^2\,dh=nr^2/(n+2)$ by the polar formula and the ball-volume formula. Thus each diagonal moment is $r^2/(n+2)$, and $A_u(x,r)=u(x)+\frac{r^2}{2(n+2)}\Delta u(x)+o(r^2)$.

fact_uses.text: [F4] If $\overline{B(a,2R)}\subset\Omega$, there is $\eta\in C_c^\infty(B(a,2R))$ equal to $1$ on $B(a,R)$ ([[lem-euclidean-bump-for-a-compact-set-inside-an-open-set]]). Polar coordinates give the radial integral formula ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]), and weak derivatives are defined by integration by parts against compactly supported smooth tests ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]).

proof_steps.claim: Conclusion. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 cover $q\le n$ and $q>n$, so every finite $q$ is covered with a constant depending only on $n,q,\Omega$. To see that these constants cannot remain bounded as $q\to\infty$, choose $a\in\Omega$ and $R>0$ with $\overline{B(a,2R)}\subset\Omega$, and choose $\eta$ as in [F4]. Define $w(x)=\eta(x)\log\log(1+R/|x-a|)$ for $x\ne a$, assigning any finite value at $a$. If $r=|x-a|\le R/2$, then $$|D\log\log(1+R/r)|=\frac{R}{r(r+R)\log(1+R/r)}\le\frac1{r\log(R/r)}.$$ Thus polar coordinates [F4] give $\int_{B(a,R/2)}|Dw|^n\,dx\le C\int_0^{R/2}\frac{dr}{r(\log(R/r))^n}<\infty$ for $n\ge2$; also $w\in L^n$ near $a$ because $\log\log(1+R/r)=O(r^{-1/2})$ and the polar $L^n$ integral of $r^{-1/2}$ converges for $n\ge2$, and on the rest of its compact support $w$ is smooth with bounded derivatives. For every coordinate line with nonzero transverse displacement from $a$, $w$ is smooth and compactly supported on that line. Apply the fundamental theorem ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]]) to $w$ times a test function. The transverse singleton of excluded lines is null since $n\ge2$, and $w,Dw\in L^n\subseteq L^1$ on their bounded support. Fubini ([[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]) therefore integrates the section identities to the weak derivative identity, proving $w\in W^{1,n}(\Omega)$. It is essentially unbounded on every neighbourhood of $a$: for every $M>0$ it exceeds $M$ on a punctured ball about $a$, so $E_M$ has positive measure. If $q_j\to\infty$ and admissible constants satisfied $C(q_j)\le C_*$, then for each $M>0$, the set $E_M=\{x:|w(x)|>M\}$ has positive measure and $$C_*\|w\|_{W^{1,n}(\Omega)}\ge\|w\|_{L^{q_j}(\Omega)}\ge M|E_M|^{1/q_j}.$$ Letting $j\to\infty$ gives $C_*\|w\|_{W^{1,n}}\ge M$ for every $M$, a contradiction. Hence the best constants necessarily diverge as $q\to\infty$, and no $L^\infty$ endpoint is asserted.

fact_uses.text: [F2] Holder's inequality $\int|fg|\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_{p'}$ for conjugate exponents ([[thm-holder-inequality-for-integrals]]), and $\int_{B(z,R)}|z-y|^{(1-n)p'}dy=\omega_{n-1}R^{\,n-(n-1)p'}/(n-(n-1)p')$ with $n-(n-1)p'>0$ because $p>n$, while $(n-(n-1)p')/p'=1-n/p$ by polar coordinates ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]]).

proof_steps.claim: Oscillation on a ball. Fix a ball $B(x,\rho)\subseteq\Omega$. By [F1], for almost every $z\in B(x,\rho)$, $|u(z)-u_{B(x,\rho)}|\le C_0(n)\int_{B(x,\rho)}|Du(y)|\,|z-y|^{1-n}dy$. Holder [F2] with exponents $p$ and $p'$ bounds this by $C_0(n)\|Du\|_{L^p(B(x,\rho))}\bigl(\int_{B(z,2\rho)}|z-y|^{(1-n)p'}dy\bigr)^{1/p'}$, where the integration region has been enlarged from $B(x,\rho)\subseteq B(z,2\rho)$ to $B(z,2\rho)$. By [F2] the kernel integral equals $c(n,p)\rho^{\,n-(n-1)p'}$ with $n-(n-1)p'>0$ and exponent $(n-(n-1)p')/p'=1-n/p$, so $|u(z)-u_{B(x,\rho)}|\le C_1(n,p)\,\rho^{1-n/p}\|Du\|_{L^p(B(x,\rho))}$ for almost every $z\in B(x,\rho)$.

Convergence of the ball means and the representative. Fix a ball $B(x,r)$ with $B(x,2r)\Subset\Omega$ and let $0<\rho\le\sigma\le r$. For almost every $z\in B(x,\rho)$ step 1.1 applied on $B(x,\sigma)$ gives $|u(z)-u_{B(x,\sigma)}|\le C_1\sigma^{1-n/p}\|Du\|_{L^p(B(x,\sigma))}\le C_1\sigma^{1-n/p}\|Du\|_{L^p(B(x,r))}$; averaging in $z$ over $B(x,\rho)$ yields $|u_{B(x,\rho)}-u_{B(x,\sigma)}|\le C_1\sigma^{1-n/p}\|Du\|_{L^p(B(x,r))}$. Hence the net $(u_{B(x,\rho)})_{\rho\downarrow0}$ is Cauchy and we may define $u^{*}(x):=\lim_{\rho\downarrow0}u_{B(x,\rho)}$ for every $x$ such that some $B(x,2r)\Subset\Omega$, with $|u^{*}(x)-u_{B(x,\rho)}|\le C_1\rho^{1-n/p}\|Du\|_{L^p(B(x,r))}$ for $0<\rho\le r$. The zero extension of $u$ to $\mathbb R^n$ lies in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$ by Holder [F2] on bounded balls, since $u\in L^p(\Omega)$; its sufficiently small ball means at each interior point are those of $u$. Thus [F3] and [F4] give $u_{B(x,\rho)}\to u(x)$ for almost every $x$, so $u^{*}=u$ almost everywhere: $u^{*}$ is a representative of the class. The Countable-Choice interface used here is supplied by [F5].

fact_uses.text: [F3] The chart sphere measure agrees with polar measure, is invariant under orthogonal maps, and scales by $R^{n-1}$ on radius-$R$ spheres. Polar integration uses $r^{n-1}dr\,d\sigma$. In dimension two, $|B_1|=\pi$ and $\omega_1=2\pi$. ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[thm-real-gamma-functional-equation]])

proof_steps.claim: Put $r=|z|$. Differentiating the two profiles in [F1] using [F2] and [F11] gives, for every $z\ne0$ and all $i,j$, $$\partial_i\Phi(z)=-\frac{z_i}{\omega_{n-1}r^n},\qquad K_{ij}(z):=\partial_i\partial_j\Phi(z)= \frac{n z_i z_j r^{-n-2}-\delta_{ij}r^{-n}}{\omega_{n-1}}.$$ A further differentiation and the displayed formulas give $|D\Phi(z)|\le C_n r^{1-n}$, $|K_{ij}(z)|\le C_n r^{-n}$, and $|DK_{ij}(z)|\le C_n r^{-n-1}$. The trace of the Hessian formula is zero away from $0$. Thus the same estimates hold in the logarithmic and power cases; in $n=2$ [F3] gives the needed $\omega_1=2\pi$.

Orthogonal invariance in [F3] gives $\int_{S^{n-1}}	heta_i	heta_j\,d\sigma=0$ for $i
e j$ by coordinate reflection. Coordinate permutations make all diagonal integrals equal, and $\sum_i	heta_i^2=1$ makes each equal $\omega_{n-1}/n$. Therefore, on the sphere centered at $x$, $$\int_{\partial B_R(x)}\partial_i\Phi(x-y)
u_j(y)\,dS(y)= rac{\delta_{ij}}n,$$ where $
u(y)=(y-x)/R$ is its outward normal. This follows by substituting $y=x+R	heta$ and the first formula of step 1.1. The same calculation in the variable $z$ gives $\int_{\partial B_R(0)}\partial_i\Phi(z)z_j/R\,dS(z)=-\delta_{ij}/n$.

The difference $u_\varepsilon-Nf$ is supported in the kernel variable $|x-y|<2\varepsilon$, so [F7] and polar integration [F3] give a uniform-in-$x$ bound $\|f\|_\infty\int_{B_{2\varepsilon}}|\Phi(z)|dz$, which tends to zero like $O(\varepsilon^2)$ for $n\ge3$ and $O(\varepsilon^2(1+|\log\varepsilon|))$ for $n=2$. Also $$G_i(x):=\int\partial_i\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$$ is absolutely finite, since $D\Phi$ is locally integrable by step 1.1 and $f$ is bounded with compact support. From the product rule, the difference $\partial_i u_\varepsilon-G_i$ is bounded uniformly in $x$ by $$C_n\|f\|_\infty\left(\int_{B_{2\varepsilon}}|z|^{1-n}dz+ \varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{2\varepsilon}}|\Phi(z)|dz\right),$$ which tends to zero (the second term is $O(\varepsilon(1+|\log\varepsilon|))$ when $n=2$). Thus $u_\varepsilon\to Nf$ and $\partial_i u_\varepsilon\to G_i$ uniformly on compact sets. The limit $G_i$ is continuous as a locally uniform limit of continuous functions.

Set $$H_{ij}(x):=\int_{B_R(x)}K_{ij}(x-y)(f(y)-f(x))dy-\frac{\delta_{ij}}n f(x).$$ The singular integral is absolutely convergent: its absolute integrand is at most $C_n[f]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^n}|x-y|^{\alpha-n}$, whose polar radial integral at zero is a constant times $\int_0^Rr^{\alpha-1}dr<\infty$. In the omitted inner ball $|z|<\varepsilon$, $D^2q_\varepsilon=0$, so the error from replacing it by $K_{ij}$ after multiplication by $|f(x-z)-f(x)|$ is at most $$C_{n,\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^n}\int_0^\varepsilon r^{\alpha-1}\,dr\le C_{n,\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^n}\varepsilon^\alpha.$$ On the transition annulus $\varepsilon<|z|<2\varepsilon$, the product rule, [F4], and the kernel estimates of step 1.1 bound the same error by $$C_{n,\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^n} \bigl(\varepsilon^\alpha+\varepsilon^\alpha(1+|\log\varepsilon|)\mathbf1_{\{n=2\}}\bigr).$$ Outside $B_{2\varepsilon}$ the kernels agree. The total error tends to zero by [F2], uniformly for $x\in Q$. Therefore $\partial_jG_{i,\varepsilon}\to H_{ij}$ uniformly on $Q$. Each $H_{ij}$ is continuous as this uniform limit.

We prove the local Hölder estimate. Take distinct $x,x'$ in a compact box $Q$; the case $x=x'$ is trivial. Put $m=(x+x')/2$ and $d=|x-x'|>0$. Choose one radius $R$ so large that for every pair in $Q$, $\operatorname{supp}f\subset B_R(m)$, the ball $B_R(m)$ has positive distance from both poles to its boundary, and $R\ge2d$. For any bounded $C^1$ domain $\Omega$ with $\operatorname{supp}f\cup\{x\}\subset\Omega$, choose $\varepsilon$ so small that $B_{2\varepsilon}(x)\subset\Omega$ and $q_\varepsilon=\Phi$ near $\partial\Omega$. Since $f$ vanishes outside $\Omega$ and $u_\varepsilon$ is defined by convolution, $$\partial_j\partial_i u_\varepsilon(x)=\int_\Omega\partial_j\partial_iq_\varepsilon(x-y)f(y)dy=\int_\Omega\partial_j\partial_iq_\varepsilon(x-y)(f(y)-f(x))dy-f(x)\int_{\partial\Omega}\partial_iq_\varepsilon(x-y)\nu_j(y)dS(y),$$ where the last equality is the divergence theorem in $y$ and uses $\partial_{y_j}\partial_iq_\varepsilon(x-y)=-\partial_{x_j}\partial_iq_\varepsilon(x-y)$. By the inner-ball and transition-annulus estimates of step 4.1, the first integral tends to $\int_\Omega K_{ij}(x-y)(f(y)-f(x))dy$; the boundary integral equals $g_\Omega(x)$ for these small $\varepsilon$. The left side tends to $H_{ij}(x)$ by steps 3.2 and 4.1. Thus $$H_{ij}(x)=\int_\Omega K_{ij}(x-y)(f(y)-f(x))dy-f(x)g_\Omega(x),\quad g_\Omega(x)=\int_{\partial\Omega}\partial_i\Phi(x-y)\nu_j(y)dS(y).$$ We use this formula with the fixed domain $\Omega=B_R(m)$ for both $x$ and $x'$. Splitting the integral difference into $B_d(m)$ and its complement, the inner part is at most $$C_{n,\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^n} \int_{B_d(m)}(|x-y|^{\alpha-n}+|x'-y|^{\alpha-n})dy \le C_{n,\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^n}d^\alpha.$$ On $\Omega\setminus B_d(m)$ write the integrand difference as $$[K_{ij}(x-y)-K_{ij}(x'-y)](f(y)-f(x)) -(f(x)-f(x'))K_{ij}(x'-y).$$ The mean-value theorem [F12] and $|DK_{ij}(z)|\le C_n|z|^{-n-1}$ bound the first term by $C_n[f]_{\alpha}d|y-m|^{\alpha-n-1}$. Its integral is bounded by $C_{n,\alpha}[f]_{\alpha}d^\alpha$, because $d\int_d^\infty r^{\alpha-2}dr=d^\alpha/(1-\alpha)$. For the second term, apply the divergence theorem to the annulus $B_R(m)\setminus\overline B_d(m)$; the two boundary fluxes of $D\Phi$ are bounded by $C_n$ using $|D\Phi(z)|\le C_n|z|^{1-n}$ and $R\ge2d$. Its contribution is at most $C_n[f]_{\alpha}d^\alpha$. Finally, reflection through $m$ and the oddness of $D\Phi$ show $g_\Omega(x)=g_\Omega(x')$, while the same outer-sphere bound gives $|g_\Omega(x)|\le C_n$. Hence $|f(x)g_\Omega(x)-f(x')g_\Omega(x')|\le C_n[f]_{\alpha}d^\alpha$. Together these bounds give $$[H_{ij}]_{\alpha;Q}\le C_{n,\alpha}[f]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^n}.$$ The estimates use the real exponent strictly below $1$ in the convergent outer radial integral.

On a compact $K$, choose $R_0$ so $\operatorname{supp}f$ and $K$ lie in a fixed bounded ball. Then for all $x\in K$, the integrals for $Nf$ and $DNf$ are bounded by $\|f\|_\infty$ times the integrals of $|\Phi|$ and $|D\Phi|$ over a fixed ball, which are finite by polar integration [F3]. The formula of step 4.1 bounds $|D^2Nf(x)|$ by $$C_{n,\alpha,R_0}[f]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^n}+n^{-1}\|f\|_\infty.$$ Together with step 5.2 this is the displayed local $C^{2,\alpha}$ estimate.

If $f=0$ or $\operatorname{supp}f=\varnothing$, the integral and every term in the cancellation formula vanish. The proof covers $n=2$ by the logarithmic profile and $n\ge3$ by the power profile. Dimensions $n=1$ and $n=0$ are outside the theorem's explicit range; the estimates and Green normalization used here are stated for $n\ge2$. The strict endpoint restrictions $0<\alpha<1$ are used in local integrability of $r^{\alpha-1}$ and convergence of $\int_d^\infty r^{\alpha-2}dr$. All radii and boxes are chosen individually from bounded sets; the only stated choice axiom is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ in [A1]. The result is one-way and asserts no converse. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 4.1, step 5.2, step 6.2, cases] $\square$

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-adhm-fixed-point-instanton-count]]: the fixed points for $N=1,k=1$ are indexed by the one one-box partition, and their tangent character is computed from the ADHM deformation complex.

proof_steps.claim: There is exactly one partition of $k=1$ for $N=1$, namely $Y_1=\{(0,0)\}$, so [F2] gives the unique fixed point. Here $\mathbf V_{\vec Y}=e_1$ and $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}$, whence $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V=1$, $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee=1$, and $t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V=t_1t_2$. Substitution in the tangent character gives $t_1+t_2$; the two additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2$, so the Euler class is $\epsilon_1\epsilon_2$.

The degree-one coefficient is the sum over the single fixed point, so it equals $(\epsilon_1\epsilon_2)^{-1}$. This is a formal equivariant fixed-point contribution, not an asserted continuum path-integral value.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-adhm-fixed-point-instanton-count]]: fixed points are indexed by two-tuples of partitions of total size one, and the tangent character is $\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf V(t_1+t_2-1-t_1t_2)+\mathbf V^\vee\mathbf W^\vee+t_1t_2\mathbf W\mathbf V$.

proof_steps.claim: A two-tuple of partitions with total size one places its single box in exactly one of the two colors, so the only possibilities are $(\{(0,0)\},\varnothing)$ and $(\varnothing,\{(0,0)\})$. Their quotient representatives have $V$-characters $e_1$ and $e_2$, respectively.

For the first point, the ADHM convention [F1] gives $\mathbf W=e_1^{-1}+e_2^{-1}$ and $\mathbf W^\vee=e_1+e_2$, while $\mathbf V=e_1$. Substitution in [F2] gives $$t_1+t_2+\frac{e_2}{e_1}+t_1t_2\frac{e_1}{e_2}.$$ The corresponding additive weights are $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,a_2-a_1,\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2+a_1-a_2$, so their product is $E_1$. Interchanging the two colors gives the second displayed character and $E_2$.

Each fixed-point contribution is the reciprocal of its Euler product, so the degree-one coefficient is $E_1^{-1}+E_2^{-1}$. The TikZ drawing only records the two one-box colorings and is not used in this calculation.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F5] [[lem-qftx-round-s4-spin-twist-index-one]] proves the actual round positive-spin twist has kernel dimension one, cokernel zero and Chern number $-1$.

proof_steps.claim: By [A2], [F5] and [F6], the concrete background has index one, real product-kernel parity one and central line action $-1$, so the specified physical test [F1] applies. Since $z^2=1$ and $\chi(z)^2=(-1)^2=1$, the assignment $\chi(1)=1$, $\chi(z)=-1$ is a character of $C_2$. Its inverse equals itself, so the tensor product of the boundary and bulk lines has the trivial character.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F1] [[def-qftx-smooth-sobolev-gauge-configuration]] fixes the Sobolev spaces and right-action convention. [[lem-qftx-gauge-sobolev-calculus]] gives the differential $D\Phi_A(0,0)(a,\xi)=a+d_A\xi$.

proof_steps.claim: The calculus lemma [F1] differentiates the right-action formula at the identity, giving $D\Phi_A(0,0)(a,\xi)=a+d_A\xi$. Its domain is $\ker d_A^*\oplus H^{k+1}(\operatorname{ad}P)$ and its codomain is $H^k(T^*M\otimes\operatorname{ad}P)$. The gauge derivative $d_A:H^{k+1}\to H^k$ explains the one-derivative loss.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[lem-qftx-gauge-stabilizer-and-properness]] identifies the stabilizer by evaluation with the holonomy centralizer and gives centralizer $Z_N$ for irreducible $SU(N)$ holonomy.

proof_steps.claim: If $u$ is in the stabilizer, its value $u(p_m)$ is in the holonomy centralizer by [F2]. Conversely, [F2] says each centralizing value extends uniquely by parallel transport to a stabilizing gauge section. Thus evaluation is a bijection between the stabilizer and the centralizer. In particular, when $u(p_m)=e$, parallel transport gives $u=e$ everywhere, proving the based stabilizer is trivial without irreducibility.

If $A$ is irreducible, [F2] identifies the full stabilizer with $Z_N$. Every element of this center is divided out in $\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$, so the reduced stabilizer consists only of the identity coset.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] [[thm-qftx-taubes-arbitrary-divisor-plane-vortex]]: for each effective divisor there is a unique scalar $h$ with the stated logarithmic subtractions and decay; the reconstruction is smooth, solves the positive first-order equations, has finite energy, and has flux $2\pi$ times the degree. Negative winding follows by conjugation.

proof_steps.claim: Its multiplicities give degree $N=2+1=3$ and distributional source $4\pi(2\delta_{z_0}+\delta_{z_1})=8\pi\delta_{z_0}+4\pi\delta_{z_1}$. The center subtraction coefficients are $2m_0=4$ and $2m_1=2$. Applying [F2] gives the unique scalar $h$, its smooth subtractions, $h\to0$, and strict negativity away from the divisor.
Apply [F2] to the explicit effective divisor $|n|[0]$ of degree $|n|$ (the empty divisor if $n=0$) and conjugate when $n<0$. Its signed flux is $2\pi n$, and [F3] gives $T_n=2\pi\xi|n|$.

Here $P=(z-z_0)^2(z-z_1)$ and $s=2\log|P|$. The reconstruction in [F2] extends smoothly over both centers, solves the positive critical equations, and has flux $2\pi N=6\pi$. Since it is a fixed-divisor reconstructed solution, [F3] gives its attained absolute transverse energy $2\pi\xi N=6\pi\xi$. The argument determines the profile by the unique scalar boundary-value problem and supplies no elementary closed form.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] The transform is defined by fibrewise harmonic projection, and its correction is the unique solution of a fibrewise Dolbeault equation; the local operator is $\nabla_A^*\nabla_A+2$. [[lem-qftx-coupled-penrose-injective-edge]], [[lem-qftx-coupled-penrose-operator-coefficient]]

proof_steps.claim:
The global Dolbeault complex of a direct sum is the direct sum of its Dolbeault complexes. The fibre harmonic projection in [F2] is the orthogonal projection for the direct-sum metric, hence is block diagonal; the vertical correction is unique on every summand, so it is block diagonal too. Therefore $\mathcal P_{E\oplus\mathbb C^m}=\mathcal P_E\oplus\mathcal P_{\mathbb C^m}$, and the same identity holds after dualization. On the added flat summand the operator is $
abla^*
abla+2$; pairing with a section and integrating gives $\|
abla s\|^2+2\|s\|^2$, so its kernel is zero. This verifies preservation under adding any finite flat summand.

final_edge_fact_uses.text: [F2] The fibre-harmonic coefficient is independent of representative and the resulting global map is injective: its zero class has horizontal remainder in $\mathcal O(-1)^{\oplus2}$, which has no holomorphic sections. [[lem-qftx-coupled-penrose-injective-edge]]

proof_steps.claim: For $x\in U_N\cap U_S$, both chart computations restrict the same global closed form to the same fibre $L_x$. They use the same fibre Dolbeault operator and normalized harmonic projection, so both give the same value $s(x)$. If the global representative changes by $\bar\partial_F\beta$, its vertical restriction changes by $\bar\partial_V\beta$; harmonic forms are orthogonal to exact forms, so the harmonic projection is unchanged. Hence the chart sections agree and are independent of the representative, and they glue to a global section on $S^4$.

The operator-valued map $A\mapsto\Delta_A\in\mathcal B(H^{k+1},H^{k-1})$ is a continuous polynomial of degree at most two in the local coefficients of $A$, by step 1.1 and the product estimates [F8]. Apply step 3.1 first to $p_0$ and $p_*$, defining its finite energy to be $C_0$, and then to $p_*$ and $p_1$, defining its finite energy to be $C_1$. proof_steps.claim: Apply the inverse-function theorem [F4] to $\Phi_A(s,u):=s^u$ on the local Banach product $S_{A,\varepsilon}\times\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1}$ near $(A,e)$; its derivative is $L_A$ from step 1.2. Shrink $\varepsilon$ so the slice remains in the open irreducible locus. At $(s,e)$, for $s=A+a$, the derivative is $L_s(b,\xi)=b+d_s\xi$ on $b\in\ker d_A^*$; this differs from $L_A$ only by $(b,\xi)\mapsto[a,\xi]$. Its operator norm is at most $C\|a\|_{H^k}$ by [F7]. Choose $\varepsilon$ so $C\varepsilon\|L_A^{-1}\|<1$; then [F5] makes $L_s$ an isomorphism for every $s$ in the slice. At an arbitrary $(s,u_0)$, write $u=u_0v$ near $u_0$ and use $s^{u_0v}=(s^{u_0})^v$. Applying the inverse action by $u_0$ to the target tangent and changing the gauge tangent by the invertible adjoint action identifies this derivative with $L_s$. Hence the derivative is an isomorphism at every point of the slice product, and the inverse-function theorem makes $\Phi_A$ a local diffeomorphism throughout.

For the smooth-space clause, fix now a smooth irreducible center $A\in\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and use the Banach slice and trivialization established in step 4.1. Put $U_A=\Phi_A(S_{A,\varepsilon}\times\bar{\mathcal G}_{k+1})$ and $V_A=\pi_k(S_{A,\varepsilon})$. Since $U_A$ is open in $\mathcal A_k^*$, $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open in the stated $C^\infty$ topology; set $S_A^\infty=S_{A,\varepsilon}\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ and $V_A^\infty=\pi_\infty(S_A^\infty)$. For a smooth $B\in U_A$, its unique reduced gauge class from step 4.1 has a representative $u\in\mathcal G_{k+1}$. It satisfies $d_A^*(B^{u^{-1}}-A)=0$. Locally in a bundle frame, write $C_j=uB_j u^{-1}-(\partial_j u)u^{-1}-A_j$. Substitution in $d_A^*C=0$, use of $\partial_i(u^{-1})=-u^{-1}(\partial_i u)u^{-1}$, and multiplication on the right by $u$ isolate the equation $g^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j u=R(A,B,g;u,u^{-1},du)$ on each chart. Every term in $R$ is a finite product of smooth coefficients (including first derivatives of $A,B$) and factors among $u,u^{-1},du$; hence the principal operator is the scalar smooth Laplacian on each matrix entry. If $u\in H^{r+1}$ for $r\ge k$, then this right-hand side lies in $H^r$ by [F7] and the smooth coefficient bounds. Elliptic regularity [F6] gives $u\in H^{r+2}$. Iteration proves $u$ smooth; changing its representative by an element of the finite center preserves smoothness. Thus every smooth point of the Banach saturation has a smooth trivialization representative, and $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*=\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$.

Suppose smooth $B_j\to B$ in $C^\infty$ within $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$. The Banach trivialization from step 4.1 gives convergence of their slice representatives in $H^k$ and of their reduced gauge classes in $H^{k+1}$. In a quotient chart around the limiting class from step 1.1, choose lifts $u_j,u$ that converge in $H^{k+1}$; this is possible because the finite center acts by disjoint translates. The equation in step 5.2 and elliptic estimates [F6] bootstrap convergence: if $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+1}$, then the assumed $C^\infty$ convergence gives $B_j\to B$ in $H^{r+1}$, and [F7] makes the right-hand sides converge in $H^r$. Apply the elliptic estimate to $u_j-u$, using also their already known $H^{k+1}$ convergence for the $L^2$ term, to get $u_j\to u$ in $H^{r+2}$. Induction gives convergence in every Sobolev order, which on compact $M$ is the $C^\infty$ section topology. The slice representatives converge in $C^\infty$ by their action formula. Conversely the forward action is continuous in the $C^\infty$ topology by multiplication and differentiation of smooth sections. The saturation $U_A\cap\mathcal A_\infty^*$ is open, and $V_A^\infty$ is open in the quotient because the quotient map is open: the saturation of any open set is a union of its open gauge translates. The restricted map $S_A^\infty\times\bar{\mathcal G}_\infty\to\pi_\infty^{-1}(V_A^\infty)$ is therefore a homeomorphism for the actual quotient topology, and it is equivariant. This proves the smooth-space topological principal bundle claim.

proof_steps.claim: To obtain derivative decay, fix $\alpha<\alpha'<\sqrt\kappa$ and use step 3.3 at rate $\alpha'$. On each unit ball centered at large $z$, both $w$ and $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ are $O(e^{-\alpha'|z|})$. By [F3] and [F5], $w$ has a $C^{1,\beta}$ norm of that order on the concentric half-ball for some $\beta>0$. Thus the right-hand side has a $C^{0,\beta}$ norm of the same order, and [F4] gives $C^{2,\beta}$ decay on a smaller ball. Inductively, for each multi-index $\gamma$, differentiating $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})$ gives $\Delta D^\gamma w=\kappa e^{-w}D^\gamma w+G_\gamma$, where $G_\gamma$ is a finite sum of products of lower derivatives of $w$ and is exponentially small by the induction hypothesis. Applying [F3] and [F4] on nested unit balls gives the same $e^{-\alpha'|z|}$ bound for two more derivatives. Since $e^{-\alpha'|z|}\le e^{-\alpha|z|}$ outside a fixed disk, every finite derivative has the stated rate.

proof_steps.claim: Starting with a framed ASD connection, [A4] constructs its holomorphic Ward bundle; the exact coupled cohomology-vanishing and diagonal argument [[lem-qftx-asd-twistor-vanishing-and-monad-reconstruction]] reconstructs the normalized three-term monad. Starting with regular ADHM data, [A5] identifies its normalized real monad and projection connection with this Ward bundle and connection. The equality of the two constructions is the first-order and inverse-extraction clause in [A5], so it is conditional on that exact real block proof, not on the P² citation alone.

By [A5], both composites on framed isomorphism classes are identities: ADHM data produce the Ward bundle whose monad extraction returns the same $U(k)$ orbit, and an ASD connection produces a Ward bundle whose matrix extraction returns an orbit reconstructing that framed connection. The charge of each resulting connection is $q_N=-k$ by [F2]–[F3]. Thus the claimed bijection and charge statement follow conditionally on [A4]–[A5].

The finite-dimensional quotient and $\mathbb P^2$ sheaf maps are $T$-equivariant by [A1]–[A2]. The Ward construction is natural under rotations and framing transformations by [A4]; the exact raw monad torus factors are directly calculated in the new block lemma cited by [A5], while the equivariance of inverse normalization remains part of [A5]. These exact interfaces make the composite $T$-equivariant. The same composition on first-order families is valid only under the base-change hypotheses of [A2]–[A4] and the deformation compatibility of [A5]. This proves the stated conditional torus and tangent clauses and leaves the positive-FI boundary separate.
